sources.news_title: South Carolina Republicans are purists
sources.text:
South Carolina Republicans are purists
Republican voters in South Carolina faced a primary runoff between a nonentity who would function as an uncritical Trump lickspittle, and Darline Graham. They decided to go with the one who may not have even heard of Taiwan as of last week:
On Friday, Donald Trump made a rare appearance at a political rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on behalf of Darline Graham, telling voters to pretend he was on the ballot when they voted. On Tuesday, they listened.
Graham entered politics just six weeks ago, when she was appointed to fill the Senate seat vacated by the sudden death of her brother, Lindsey Graham. At first, she was a placeholder, but then she decided to run for a full term for the seat with Trump’s backing. The race immediately became a test of whether Trump’s backing could help Graham, a political neophyte known only to voters because of her last name, win a primary election in the deep-red state.
It turns out he could. On Tuesday, Graham pulled out a victory in the Senate runoff over Rep. Ralph Norman by a margin of 52.5 percent to 47.5 percent, making her the Republican nominee for Senate and the overwhelming favorite to win a six-year term in November.
As Graham herself admitted in her election-night victory speech, directly addressing the president via the medium of cable television, “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
She wasn’t merely flattering the president. Graham’s victory can be credited to the massive margins she ran up in the Pee Dee, the region of the state around Myrtle Beach where Trump campaigned for her. His rally appearance, along with the endorsement of local congressman Russell Fry, who was the third-place finisher in the first round of voting two weeks ago, transformed that region into a stronghold for Graham. Darline Graham got a higher percentage of the vote in the area than her late brother did when he won his primary in June, shortly before his death, in a far less competitive race.
Graham was also boosted by higher turnout in the runoff than in the first round of voting in the Senate special election two weeks ago. Traditionally runoffs in South Carolina have lower turnout as only the most motivated voters are willing to turn out for a second election in two weeks. This was not the case with Trump’s intervention; 33,000 more voters turned out on Tuesday than did so earlier in August. In contrast, for the regular Republican primaries in June, turnout fell off by more than 150,000 for those races where there was a runoff.
This as above all tribute paid by South Carolina Republicans to their decrepit god-emperor. But it has its own perverse logic. Graham’s late brother was the alleged foreign policy brains of the Republican conference, and in 2016 was one of Trump’s fiercest critics. And yet at the time when he died hoping for one last Meet The Press hit, Lindsey was (as he had long been) the biggest supporter of Trump’s catastrophic Iran invasion, as well as being one of Trump’s most enthusiastic cheerleaders.If Palmetto State Republicans see his wife as the closest approximation of what Lindsey left the Earth has, it’s hard to say tat they were wrong. The party is a hollow shell with a tacky orange toupee, and why deny the obvious, child?
…Here, for example, in her Being There way is Darline accurately describing the core health care position of the Republican Party (i.e. if you’re not rich, you don’t deserve healthcare.) Paul Ryan might make it sound fancier and be more willing to lie about the implications of his views, but they end up in the same place.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Can Still Win You a Certain Type of Election
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
On Friday, Donald Trump made a rare appearance at a political rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on behalf of Darline Graham, telling voters to pretend he was on the ballot when they voted. On Tuesday, they listened.
Graham entered politics just six weeks ago, when she was appointed to fill the Senate seat vacated by the sudden death of her brother, Lindsey Graham. At first, she was a placeholder, but then she decided to run for a full term for the seat with Trump’s backing. The race immediately became a test of whether Trump’s backing could help Graham, a political neophyte known to voters only because of her last name, win a primary election in the deep-red state.
It turns out he could. On Tuesday, Graham pulled out a victory in the Senate runoff over Rep. Ralph Norman by a margin of 52.5 percent to 47.5 percent, making her the Republican nominee for Senate and the overwhelming favorite to secure a six-year term in November.
As Graham herself admitted in her election-night victory speech, directly addressing the president via the medium of cable television, “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
She wasn’t merely flattering the president. Graham’s victory can be credited to the massive margins she ran up in the Pee Dee, the region of the state around Myrtle Beach where Trump campaigned for her. His rally appearance, along with the endorsement of local Rep. Russell Fry, who was the third-place finisher in the first round of voting two weeks ago, transformed that region into a stronghold for Graham. Darline Graham got a higher percentage of the vote in the area than her late brother did when he won his primary in June, shortly before his death, in a far less competitive race.
Graham was also boosted by higher turnout in the runoff than in the first round of voting. Traditionally, runoffs in South Carolina see lower turnout, as only the most motivated voters are willing to show up for a second election in two weeks. This was not the case with Trump’s intervention; 33,000 more voters came out on Tuesday than did so earlier in August. In contrast, for the regular GOP primaries in June, turnout fell off by more than 150,000 for those races in which there was a runoff.
The win reinforced Donald Trump’s standing within the Republican Party at a time when it has increasingly come into question. Although his status as the leader of the GOP is undisputed, 10 candidates he has endorsed this year, including three just last week, have lost their primaries. As Trump’s favorability nears an all-time low with the general electorate, a loss for Graham would have been a direct blow to his standing within the party only months before midterms and on the eve of the 2028 presidential primary beginning in earnest.
Trump’s success in South Carolina’s GOP primary Tuesday night (as well as his endorsed gubernatorial candidate winning a runoff in Oklahoma) is by no means a panacea for Republicans in November. Voters are still dealing with high gas prices, a shooting war in the Strait of Hormuz, and a trade war with Canada. But it does reinforce the dilemma that they face. Trump remains overwhelmingly popular with the Republican base and can single-handedly swing primaries. Even so, he remains deeply unpopular with the electorate as a whole. It means that swing-district Republicans must balance on a seesaw. They can’t separate themselves too much from the unpopular incumbent lest they alienate base Republicans. But they can’t tie themselves too closely, or else they may alienate swing voters.
Norman, the suburban Charlotte congressman whom Graham defeated, ran as a hard-right grassroots conservative. He warned of the dangers of socialism, berated Graham as a creature of the Washington “swamp,” and touted his disdain for Anthony Fauci and support for hydroxychloroquine as a treatment for COVID at the height of the pandemic.
However, Norman had piled up heresies against Trump. He supported his old friend Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary and repeatedly dithered on supporting the president’s priorities in the House. Norman always voted the way Trump wanted eventually, but he made things difficult when it was time to elect Mike Johnson as speaker or pass the extension of the 2017 tax-cut bill.
In addition, Norman was both helped and hurt by his mounting of a gubernatorial campaign months before. It helped because his prior campaign had recently spent millions introducing him to voters statewide. It hurt because it made him seem like a perennial candidate and reinforced Graham’s attacks on the five-term congressman as a career politician.
Graham benefited from not just Trump’s endorsement but a significant funding advantage over Norman, as well as from outside groups flooding the airwaves on her behalf. She was assisted too by last-minute intervention by Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc., which dropped over $800,000 on phone calls and text messages. That marked the first time this year that the group had spent in a race.
But she also faced a steep learning curve as a first-time candidate. Graham’s campaign was a gaffe-filled slog culminating in a stunning debate answer in which she stated onstage, “National security is not my thing.”
It wasn’t just that Graham seemed new to politics but that she often seemed unfamiliar with it entirely. She struggled with generalities and answering even rote questions. After her debate flub, Graham tried to spin it by saying she focused on “kitchen-table issues” such as affordability. However, when the incumbent senator was asked what specific proposals she had on affordability at a press conference on Monday, she simply said, “We’ll see about that when I get there.”
Voters at a polling place in Graham’s hometown of Lexington described the options as not quite between the lesser of two evils but rather “the lesser of two …,” before making the universal gesture for “meh.” As Bruce Corbett, a Lexington voter who supported his local candidate, said of his decision to back Graham, she was “the best of the two choices we had.”
Another Lexington voter, Sharon Mason, was so unenthused about her vote that she said, “I voted for what’s-his-name,” moments after leaving the voting booth.
Graham’s massive advantage in campaign advertising was clear, as many voters reiterated the negative television ads that flooded the airwaves about her opponent. “I’m tired of Norman being in there doing nothing and getting rich,” said Louise Geddings.
But other voters simply recoiled at having to select a candidate they viewed as entirely unqualified. “Why would I vote for Darline? She has no experience—she’s a legacy and only running because the governor appointed her,” said Thomas Cotten.
But despite that lack of résumé, Graham triumphed on Tuesday. Then again, with a major financial advantage and a flawed opponent, she didn’t need a résumé. After all, she had Donald Trump. The question is what that name will do for other Republicans in November’s midterms.

sources.news_title: U.S. Sen. Darline Graham Wins Runoff, Thanks God for Strength Amid Grief
sources.text:
After winning a special Republican primary runoff in South Carolina, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham credited God for sustaining her through the recent death of her brother, longtime U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham.
“First, I want to thank the good Lord who got us through these past few weeks and gave me and my family the strength to keep going,” Graham said in a victory speech Tuesday night (Aug. 25).
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” she added. “But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room.”
Graham also thanked President Trump for his backing and her supporters for their prayers. “The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family,” she said, “but you know what? We did it.”
After Trump ally Lindsey Graham died unexpectedly last month at age 71, the president recommended that Darline Graham, 62, complete her brother’s current Senate term. South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to that role two days after Lindsey’s July 11 death.
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham To Run in November Midterms
Before he died, Lindsey Graham had been running for his fifth Senate term. He handily won the South Carolina primary in June, with 57% of the vote.
In the Aug. 11 special primary, Darline Graham and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman were the top two finishers. By winning Tuesday’s special runoff, Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in the November midterm election. The victor will serve a full six-year term. South Carolina hasn’t had a Democratic U.S. senator in more than 20 years.
Graham, a political novice, has worked in vocational rehabilitation and blindness-prevention programs. She has a master’s degree in rehabilitation counseling and is a Certified Public Manager. Graham, president-elect of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind, is scheduled to begin that role in January.
RELATED: ‘Joni Lamb Was All About God,’ President Trump Shares During Memorial Service
Graham and her brother had a tight-knit relationship. Lindsey helped raise Darline after their parents died in the mid-1970s, and she was an avid supporter of his political career.

sources.news_title: Someone Stupid Heads From South Carolina to DC
sources.text:
The South Carolina special election to replace the late, great, peace-loving US Senator Lindsey Graham was held last night — this was a runoff after the initial multi-candidate initial round — and I can confidently say that the stupid won in a big way.
Let’s get the basics out of the way and then we’ll spend a little time in the cesspool that is South Carolina politics, including a look at the meltdown of cable TV star congressional Rep. Nancy Mace and the deep corruption of Dem. Rep. Jim Clyburn and his alliance with the state GOP.
Here’s the Wiki on the race to catch up.
Dumbass Darline Won, Really?
In the final stretch of the campaign last week Darline Graham put on a Hall of Fame bad performance, piling gaffe upon gaffe atop admissions of ignorance, all capped by a completely insane special rally appearance by POTUS Trump.
Here’s the basics from the AP:
Sen. Darline Graham — a political newcomer appointed to the seat held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — will win a special GOP primary runoff to replace her brother on the South Carolina ballot, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.
Graham, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman, a staunch conservative and member of the hard line Freedom Caucus, who had also advanced to the runoff, following South Carolina’s special Senate primary earlier this month.
Graham will face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November.
…
“Now, the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said during the rally to cheers. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”
Trump, later on, effusively praised Graham, saying “she only knows how to put America first.”
We should note that even Sainted Brother Lindsey didn’t go unchallenged, having won a 6 way primary just weeks before his tragic, tragic, tragic, death:
U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham walloped his GOP challengers Tuesday on the way to fulfilling his pledge to be President Donald Trump’s “best ally” in the U.S. Senate.
When The Associated Press called the race about 9 p.m., Graham had more than 58% of the vote to again avoid a primary runoff, continuing an unbroken record. In November, he will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who won a three-way primary for the chance to be South Carolina’s first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in 28 years.
First elected to the Senate in 2002, Graham has never needed a runoff.
Tuesday marked the third time he’s fended off crowded GOP fields: In 2020, he bested three GOP opponents with almost 68% of the vote. In 2014, he took 56% of the vote in a seven-way race.
He ended up with five GOP opponents in this primary, after one dropped out in April. With all votes counted, Graham had 57% of the vote, a 28-percentage-point lead over his closest challenger, according to unofficial state Election Commission results.
So the dude was popular with the SC GOP base, but not unchallenged.
But polling did show voters wanted a replacement just like Lindsey or did they? Per the Post and Courier:
Like any politician, Graham had detractors. Some South Carolina conservatives labeled him “Liberal Lindsey” for his one-time role in bipartisan talks to address perennially thorny and unsolved political issues like illegal immigration.
Meanwhile, moderate conservatives, as well as Democrats, detested Graham’s unwavering support of President Donald Trump — especially after he initially broke with Trump over the president’s role in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.
“All I can say is count me out. Enough is enough,” Graham said after the riot, before soon reversing course and becoming one of Trump’s closest allies as well as a regular golfing buddy.
But for all the grousing, Graham rarely faced serious competition, easily fending off challengers from the right and left. None of his opponents could claim such personal proximity to a president.
…
A majority of voters interviewed by The Post and Courier said that even as Graham is gone, they hope his successor carries on his legacy, specifically by acting in the interests of South Carolinians while also exhibiting a deft touch in the realm of foreign policy.
They also expressed a hope the next senator lowers the temperature in Washington and works on behalf of all people, not just groups who are already in the victor’s corner.
Well that was funny, but wait til you see what they’re getting instead.
Darline, Political Natural, as In, She Put In No Visible Effort
Let’s check out a few clips to see Darline in action because nothing says rotten-corrupt-oligarchic-empire-clinging-to-the-empty-forms-of-a-republic like electing someone this obviously unfit for office, any office.
Darline on foreign policy:
Moderator: Senator, are Taiwan and the South China sea national security issues for the United States and if so, why?
Darline Graham: National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise but I support the military. pic.twitter.com/F0FEFmc6GW
— Acyn (@Acyn) August 19, 2026
Hannity helps out
Hannity: I bet based on all your time with your brother, that you know probably everything about the Middle East….
Darline Graham: Absolutely. I know national security is important. We have a wonderful commander in chief. I know that we need to stand with Israel… pic.twitter.com/Df6cVQHmyW
— Acyn (@Acyn) August 20, 2026
Darline on Affordability (Which means what, exactly? Inflation? Economics? Help me out here, I don’t watch enough cable news to keep up.)
Was this Darline Graham’s Nancy Pelosi moment?
Graham now says we’ll have to elect her to find out what her plans are on “affordablity.”
Graham was saying no one cares about her lack of knowledge of China because South Carolina voters only care about affordability.
So Ed… pic.twitter.com/VUq6Phguyo
— Tara Servatius (@TaraServatius) August 25, 2026
It was a professional, team effort:
🚨HOT MIC: A hot mic catches Darline Graham’s campaign staff telling a reporter, “Nothing too difficult here” before asking her a question.
Shes running a Joe Biden campaign‼️ pic.twitter.com/kwMcMwP5qN
— Ralph Norman Fan (@RalphNormanFan) August 20, 2026
And if that wasn’t enough to get any politician tarred and feathered and carried out on a rail in a functioning republic, POTUS Trump put on possibly his most deranged performance ever in Myrtle Beach the Friday before the election.
Doesn’t Get Any Trumpier Than This
This is the full hour plus rally which I’m including because it really is one for the history books blogs:
Roll Call has a complete transcript.
Self-appointed “political referee” and utter cipher (seriously he’s the blankest, emptiest professional reporter I’ve ever met in person) Chris Cillizza summed up the “27 Wackiest Lines”, some highlights:
Trump: “I’ll make you a deal that if Darline wins, I’ll come down and play the best golfer in Myrtle Beach in a match.
…
“I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me. That does not make me happy.
…
“I got the highest gay vote in the history of politics for a Republican.
…
“Tariffs, it’s my all-time favorite word. I love tariffs. I love the word. It’s made us rich as hell.
…
“Tariff is my fifth favorite word – after God, religion, wife, children.
…
“I’m going to be impeached. They’re gonna impeach me.”
“These are lunatics. These are people that are vicious, violent, that weaponize the justice system, the Justice Department, and they wanna destroy our country. They wanna see that our country failed. They want our country to fail.
…
“I’m doing this to honor Lindsey. I’m doing this to honor Lindsey. That’s why I’m here. I don’t have to be here on a Friday. I don’t have to be here. Although I must say I love it. And now that I am here, we got plenty of time to talk, right?
…
“So the Democrats hate our country. They’re communists. They’re radical left lunatics. And frankly, they’re, in many cases, horrible, horrible people.
Somehow this worked with SC GOP voters.
Her Opponent Explains
Rep. Ralph Norman re-enacted the ancient SNL “I can’t believe I’m losing to this guy” sketch instead of writing a concession speech:
Rep. Norman zeroed in on Trump’s endorsement of Graham and the funding she received from super PACs.
“You know the president got involved. He has that right. That’s his prerogative,” Norman said, sparking a series of boos from the crowd.
“Y’all, his policies are good,” he said in response to the boos. “I never understood why he got in this race to beat, you know, but it is, it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”
Norman said, “All our money came from South Carolina and from my personal account.”
“The other, my opponent’s, the money came from outside PACs,” he said. “We had $8 million spent against us. I couldn’t, we couldn’t come up with that much money, but people were great to me.”
Norman reluctantly said he would back Graham in the general election while also saying of the outcome, “I really hate it for the state.”
“I’m not supporting the Democrat. So I will support her, Darline, as best I can,” he said.
Go team!
Norman did have a few million points about the money in the race, although this isn’t the usual AIPAC or data center money we’re used to seeing piling in:

They hit his 2024 Nikki Haley endorsement: “Trump doesn’t want Ralph Norman to be South Carolina’s senator.” | E&E News / Politico |

Note: that $251,000 cash-on-hand figure is reported as Darline Graham’s by Legis1 and as Ralph Norman’s in other summaries of the same AP story.
Note the Green Energy money organized by former MoveOn.org boss Tom Matzzie. Also note that Norman is probably wildly over-stating how much of their money went into that race.
I wonder if Darline will be amenable to their influence?
So how did this happen?
How South Carolina’s Open Primaries Work for the Uniparty
Some states limit primary participation to registered party members, others, like S.C., limit voters to one party per election cycle but otherwise voters are free to mingle.
From Ballotpedia:
As South Carolina does not provide for registration by party, party primaries are open. Voters may choose which party’s ballot they wish to vote on in the primary, but may only vote in one party’s primary. Winners in primary contests are determined by majority vote. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff election is held two weeks following the primary.
In 23 states, at least one political party utilizes closed primaries to nominate partisan candidates for congressional and state-level (e.g. state legislators, governors, etc.) offices. In 18 states, at least one party utilizes open primaries to nominate partisan candidates for these offices. In 13 states, at least one party utilizes semi-closed primaries. Darline Graham wins Republican primary runoff for U.S. Senate
Published 2:00 pm Wednesday, August 26, 2026
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
Darline Graham secured her position on the general election ballot for U.S. Senate, winning the Republican primary runoff with 52.45% of the vote against U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman’s 47.55%. In total, Graham received 193,396 votes, while Norman garnered 175,327 votes.
“I’m honored to carry my brother’s legacy forward and ready to fight for South Carolina,” said Graham after her victory, emphasizing her commitment to the values that her brother represented. Her campaign gained significant momentum following an endorsement from former President Donald Trump, who actively campaigned for her in the state.
Graham, whom Gov. Henry McMaster appointed to fill the remaining months of her brother Lindsey’s term, faced Norman in a runoff after neither candidate won in a special election held earlier this summer.
As she prepares for the November election, Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a physician from Charleston who has been vocal about her intent to challenge the status quo in South Carolina. The general election will take place on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP nomination to replace her late brother in US Senate - WXXV News 25
sources.text:
Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP nomination to replace her late brother in US Senate
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.
Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham’s sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump’s rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president’s backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he’s doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham’s inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham’s answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham’s experience level “wasn’t really cutting it for me.”
Sellers also said he wasn’t swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. “If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP runoff
Graham defeated hard-right challenger Rep. Ralph Norman
What happened
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Tuesday won the Republican primary to succeed her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, defeating hard-right Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) 52% to 48%. At President Donald Trump’s urging, Gov. Henry McMaster (R) last month appointed Graham to serve out the last six months of her brother’s term.
Trump’s pick for Oklahoma governor, businessman Mike Mazzei, also narrowly beat state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in Tuesday’s GOP runoff primary. In Georgia’s heavily Democratic 13th Congressional District, former school board chair Everton Blair Jr. won a special election to fill out the term of Rep. David Scott (D), who died in April.
Who said what
The South Carolina runoff was “seen as a test of Trump’s endorsement power,” The Wall Street Journal said, and he “flexed his political muscles in the final days of the campaign” to get Graham “over the finish line.” Trump “did more to support her than he had for any other Republican candidate this year,” The New York Times said, and it took the strength of his “political capital” — including a rally and $830,000 from his MAGA Inc. super PAC — to “overcome her inexperience” and a “flubbed” debate answer about national security.

sources.news_title: South Carolina Primary Results: Darline Graham Wins GOP Senate Nomination With Donald Trump's Backing
sources.text:
South Carolina Primary Results: Darline Graham Wins GOP Senate Nomination With Donald Trump's Backing
Political novice Graham — sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham — won after Trump's last-minute campaigning and substantial spending from his allied super PAC
President Donald Trump secured an important political victory on Tuesday, 25 August, as the closely watched South Carolina primary results showed Darline Graham securing the Republican Senate nomination. She narrowly defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in a bitter special primary runoff.
The result followed a difficult stretch for the president's political operation. Trump-backed candidates have suffered losses in at least 10 primary races this year, including contests in Iowa, Georgia, Tennessee, Florida and Wyoming.
Graham's victory therefore provided the president with a high-profile win in a race in which he invested significant political capital.
From Placeholder to Trump's Handpicked Senator
To recall, Graham is the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. Governor Henry McMaster appointed her to fill the remaining months of her brother's term after he died in July. Her appointment initially appeared likely to be a short-term role before the special election.
Trump, however, fundamentally changed the trajectory of her political career. He encouraged Graham to seek a full six-year term, later saying publicly, 'I asked her to do it. I got her into this whole thing.' She announced her candidacy shortly after being sworn into the Senate.
Her political profile has become closely linked to the president. This marks a notable contrast with her late brother, who made national security and foreign policy central to his Senate career.
Darline Graham entered the contest with little previous political experience but powerful Republican endorsements.
The final tally was close in a state accustomed to strong Republican performances. Graham captured about 52.5 per cent of the vote, while Norman trailed with about 47.5 per cent, according to unofficial results.
Trump Launches a Late Rescue Effort
Graham had struggled to consolidate Republican support during the initial 11 August primary. She finished first but received about one-third of the vote, forcing a runoff against Norman two weeks later.
When the race appeared increasingly competitive, the president personally intervened. He flew to Myrtle Beach to rally his supporters behind Graham. 'Pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot,' Trump told the Republican crowd on Friday.
Financial reinforcements quickly followed the president's visit. His aligned super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent more than $825,000 (£612,000) on get-out-the-vote calls and text messages supporting Graham.
The spending marked the first time this year Trump's political operation had deployed a substantial portion of its cash reserves in a primary contest.
The victory was particularly notable given Graham's limited political experience. During a recent televised debate with Norman, she struggled with a foreign policy question and admitted that she was 'not that informed on national security.'The remark drew criticism because foreign policy had been a defining issue for her late brother.
Norman, meanwhile, faced attacks over his previous endorsement of former Governor Nikki Haley during her 2024 presidential primary campaign against Trump. Graham's allies repeatedly highlighted that endorsement as they questioned Norman's loyalty to the president.
Ripple Effects Across the Nation
Norman addressed his supporters on Tuesday night after conceding the race. 'The president got involved. He has that right,' the congressman said. He then added, 'I never understood why he got in this race. But it is what it is, and I'll accept it.'
Meanwhile, Graham celebrated with supporters at her victory party. 'South Carolina is truly Trump country,' she declared. She specifically thanked the president, stating, 'Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful.'
Graham now advances to face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews this November. Andrews, a paediatrician, immediately challenged the Republican to at least three televised debates.
She argued that 'no appointment, endorsement, or family connection entitles anyone to six years.' Graham will enter the general election as the favourite in heavily Republican South Carolina.
The president also notched a secondary, albeit extremely narrow, victory in Oklahoma. Mike Mazzei won the Republican primary runoff for governor over state Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
That race served as another test of Trump's endorsement power in a strongly Republican state.
The primary also featured disagreement over a proposed $4 billion (£2.94 billion) aluminium smelter at the Tulsa Port of Inola. Trump supported the project, while Drummond had taken legal action challenging aspects of its development.
In Georgia, Democrat Everton Blair won a special election runoff to fill the remainder of the late Representative David Scott's term.
Blair defeated Scott's daughter, Marcye Scott, and will serve through 3 January 2027. Blair will become the first openly gay man elected to Congress from Georgia, marking a historic first for the state.
His tenure, however, will last only several months. Neither Blair nor Marcye Scott is running for the next full term, meaning Tuesday's result determined only who would complete David Scott's unfinished term.

sources.news_title: Sen. Darline Graham wins South Carolina primary – The Horn News
sources.text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political newcomer.
Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham’s sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump’s rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president’s backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he’s doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham’s inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham’s answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham’s experience level “wasn’t really cutting it for me.”
Sellers also said he wasn’t swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. “If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.
The Associated Press contributed to this article

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Wins Primary Runoff After Big Push from Trump
sources.text:
Darline Graham Wins Primary Runoff After Big Push from Trump
Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, has won the runoff to replace him as the Republican candidate on the November ballot.
Graham, 62, was appointed to temporarily fill the position by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, a Republican, in July after her brother’s sudden passing at the age of 71.
However, it was the support of President Donald Trump that likely pushed Darline Graham over the top on Tuesday. While she was the top vote-getter in an Aug. 11 special primary, she didn’t get more than the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff with the second-place finisher, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman.
With over 95 percent of the vote counted, Graham was ahead of Norman by a 52 percent to 48 percent margin, according to The Associated Press. She’ll now face the Democratic candidate, pediatrician Dr. Annie Andrews, in November.
Despite Darline Graham’s relative inexperience, the seat is considered a “likely Republican” hold by the election news website Decision Desk HQ.
Trump and his allies viewed the race as a test of his strength in a party stronghold. The last Democrat to win a Senate race in South Carolina was the late Fritz Hollings in 1998. However, with the headwinds of a midterm cycle where Republicans control both houses of Congress and the White House, Darline Graham’s relative inexperience compared to Rep. Norman was considered to be a potential stumbling block to her nomination bid.
During a debate with Norman last week, she was seen to have flubbed a question regarding Taiwan and the South China Sea, telling moderators that “national security is not my thing.”
However, she was able to play it off as being the “honest” mistake of someone who wasn’t a career politician.
Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) is asked at #SCSen debate about Taiwan and the South China Sea: “I’m just going to be honest here; I’m not that informed on national security, so — but I do support the military. My brother was in the Air Force for 33 years…I’m not a polished… pic.twitter.com/c6WsSjWz6C
— CSPAN (@cspan) August 19, 2026
“I’m just going to be honest here; I’m not that informed on national security,” she said. “I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
Norman, meanwhile, said Taiwan was “a definite ally” and commended Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.”
Both sides put big money into the race — including a final push of $1 million by Norman, a wealthy real estate developer before he entered the House.
During a Friday rally in Myrtle Beach, Trump said that he asked Darline Graham personally to run to replace the seat held by her brother, one of Trump’s closest allies, “because everyone loves her, everyone respects her.”
“She only knows how to put America first,” Trump said, according to NBC News. “You vote for her, you’re going to be very proud of that vote.”
Speaking in Columbia, South Carolina, Graham honored her late brother in her victory remarks.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart. But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room,” she said.
“Mr. President, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country,” Graham added.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
Norman, meanwhile, acknowledged the effect of Trump’s intercession in the race during his concession speech.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “But it is, it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”
He added that getting involved was Trump’s “prerogative” and that “his policies are good.”
Lindsey Graham was considered a shoo-in for a fifth term when he died at his Capitol Hill home of an aortic dissection on July 11, just one day after returning to the United States from a trip to Ukraine.
In addition to serving 23 years in the Senate, he served for eight years in the U.S. House and was a House impeachment manager during the impeachment trial of then-President Bill Clinton in 1999. He launched a brief campaign for the presidency during the 2016 cycle, but withdrew before the primaries began.

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham has won the Republican nomination to keep her late brother’s Senate seat, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s runoff on Tuesday after neither won the 50% needed to secure the nomination outright earlier this month.
Graham had never held political office before Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to serve out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham’s term following his death last month. She then won the backing of President Donald Trump, who campaigned for her in South Carolina last week.

After Norman conceded, Graham quickly turned her attention to November.
“We cannot and must not allow democratic socialists to gain a foothold in our conservative state like South Carolina,” she told supporters Tuesday night.
She added, “Liberals believe if they can defeat conservatives in South Carolina, then they can defeat us anywhere. Once again, they’re coming for us and the South Carolina values we hold dear.”
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in the general.
Oklahoma runoffs
And Trump’s endorsement paid off in another runoff Tuesday night. Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei, a Tulsa businessman, narrowly won the Republican nomination for Oklahoma governor.
Trump backed Mazzei and attacked his opponent, state Attorney General Gentner Drummond, in the closing days of the race. Mazzei also poured millions of his own money into his campaign.
He’ll face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in November.
Meanwhile, nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won Oklahoma’s Democratic Senate primary runoff. Thomas, a democratic socialist, will face Republican Congressman Kevin Hern in November.
Hern is favored to win former Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s open seat. Mullin vacated his Senate post to serve as the secretary of homeland security.
Dan Sullivan on the ballot
In Alaska, there officially will be two Dan Sullivans on the November Senate ballot.
Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan has advanced to face Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Democrat Mary Peltola and one other candidate in the general election. The fourth candidate has not yet been determined.
An upset in Georgia
And former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair has won Georgia’s special election to serve out the remainder of former Rep. David Scott’s term, defeating Scott’s daughter, Marcye Scott.
The win was an upset. Blair trailed Scott 46% to 38% in last month’s all-party special election, but neither won a majority, forcing Tuesday’s runoff.

sources.news_title: Trump pick Darline Graham wins GOP Senate runoff in South Carolina
sources.text:
Trump pick Darline Graham wins GOP Senate runoff in South Carolina
WASHINGTON — Sen. Darline Graham narrowly won South Carolina’s Republican Senate primary runoff on Tuesday, after President Donald Trump flexed his political muscles in the final days of the campaign to get her over the finish line.
With 99% of the vote counted, Graham had 52%, while Rep. Ralph Norman, who represents a district in the northern part of the state, had 48%, according to the Associated Press.
Graham's victory is being seen as evidence of Trump's continuing influence over the Republican Party.
The sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham is currently serving in the Senate as a temporary replacement for her brother, who died suddenly in July. She had never previously run for elected office.
Republicans and Democrats also held primaries in several other states on Tuesday, as they narrowed down their field of candidates for the midterm elections.
Political experts expect that Graham will now go on to succeed in the November election. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate for decades.
The midterms more generally will decide which party controls the US Congress - which in turn will have a bearing on the second half of Trump's presidency.
Graham was running against right-wing Republican Congressman Ralph Norman, who sought to portray his opponent as a puppet of Washington politicians.
The head-to-head was set up after the pair emerged as the top two from a wider field of candidates during an initial contest earlier this month.
Norman is a supporter of Trump and has voted in favour of many of his policies. But in 2024, he initially backed Trump's primary opponent Nikki Haley as his pick for Republican presidential candidate.
In a post on X, she thanked her supporters and the president, and said she was "deeply honored and humbled" by the result.
During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling during a foreign-policy question during a recent debate.
Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "I'm not that informed on national security." She added: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."
Trump's influence over the party was also tested in Oklahoma, where Mike Mazzei, a former state lawmaker endorsed by the president, took on Gentner Drummond, the state's attorney general.
The winner is widely expected to become the next governor in the heavily Republican state.
South Carolina was not the only state that held an election on Tuesday to replace a deceased lawmaker.
In Georgia, voters in the Atlanta area were tasked with choosing a replacement for Democratic Congressman David Scott, who died in April.
Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late congressman, was among those seeking office. But projections in US media show she was beaten by opponent Everton Blair.
Blair will therefore serve out the remainder of the term, which ends in January. In November, two other candidates will run to take over his seat in the new year.

sources.news_title: Trump Blessing Brings 'Very Nice Lady' A Win In SC Senate Race
sources.text:
The Trump endorsement wins again, this time in the Palmetto State’s special primary runoff where Darline Graham secured the GOP nomination for the Senate seat her late brother long held.
Graham beat proven conservative Rep. Ralph Norman by 5 percentage points (52.5% to 47.5%), with primary voters opting for a “woefully” unprepared “very nice lady” over a five-term congressman and Freedom Caucus member who is informed on national security.
Graham will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November’s general election. Ruby red South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to Senate since before the turn of the 21st century.
Gov. Henry McMaster tapped Graham to serve out her brother Lindsey Graham’s current term after South Carolina’s senior senator died in July — less than four months before November’s midterm election. Now Darline Graham stands an election away from keeping the seat her brother had held for four terms, and was running for a fifth.
‘Our Victory Would not have been Possible’
“I want to thank President Trump for all of his support and his endorsement,” the Republican nominee said following her win. Speaking to her biggest benefactor, Graham said her brother truly loved the president and thought of Trump as one of his closest friends.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” the senator said.
She couldn’t have been more correct.
During his concession speech, Norman told supporters that he never understood why Trump got involved in the South Carolina race. Darline Graham is thanking her lucky stars that he did.
But Democrats may have helped Graham’s cause, too. She was viewed by many as the weaker of the two candidates in the GOP runoff — the one Dems would rather face in November. As conservative activist Tyler Bowyer noted, the Democrats who did not vote in the primary could opt to vote in the Republican primary runoff “for a second dip” in South Carolina’s open primaries.
“Totally screwed up system that benefits moderate Republicans with Dem votes, not just ONCE but TWICE,” Bowyer wrote on X.
Lindsey Graham may have been a staunch Trump ally, but he was no warrior for the MAGA cause. His sister, critics argued, is untested without a history of pro-Trump positions. The big fear: Darline Graham will become an empty vessel for Senate RINOs who have shrugged off much of Trump’s agenda as if that agenda didn’t put Republicans back in control of the Senate.
Just days before Tuesday’s runoff, Graham stumbled badly, saying national security wasn’t her “thing” when asked about U.S. foreign policy in Taiwan and China during a debate.
“I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security, so,” adding that “national security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
“It very much confirmed many of our suspicions that while she might be a very nice lady, she is woefully underprepared or unprepared to be one of the 100 U.S. senators in the Senate,” state Rep. Jordan Pace, a Norman supporter, told Politico in an interview.
But the Trump endorsement once again proved more than enough to compensate for candidate weaknesses.
Heading into Tuesday’s primaries Trump had posted a 97 percent win rate for candidates he’s endorsed this election cycle — 254 victories in 262 races.
‘Helping Us Across the Finish Line’
Trump padded his endorsement record on Tuesday in Oklahoma’s governor runoff election, with former state Sen. Mike Mazzei’s paper-thin win over Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond. The Republicans fought a bruising battle, with Drummond holding a slight edge in June’s primary, which set up Tuesday’s runoff.
Mazzei, whose campaign coffers were bolstered by his personal $11.6 million loan, also received the support of Trump Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who had served Oklahoma in Congress for 13 years, 10 years in the House and three in the Senate. He had the state GOP’s backing, too.
“We wanted to keep you on the edge of your seats for a little while, or at least on the edge of my seat,” a relieved Mazzei joked with supporters at his watch party in Tulsa after the race was called.
“Thanks, of course, to President Donald J. Trump for helping us across the finish line,” Mazzei said to loud applause from attendees of the watch party, Nondoc reported.
‘Decoy Dan’ Makes the Cut
Also on Tuesday, the final vote tallies came in from Alaska’s Aug. 18 primary election, showing “Decoy Dan” Sullivan advancing to November’s general election under The Last Frontier’s rigged ranked-choice voting system. The Democrat plant is accused of running to confuse voters considering casting their ballots for the incumbent Republican senator, also named Dan Sullivan.
“Make no mistake, the entire purpose of this man’s candidacy is to siphon votes away from Sen. Sullivan by confusing voters,” The Federalist’s John Daniel Davidson reported Monday. “He even initially tried to register with the Alaska Division of Elections as ‘Dan S. Sullivan,’ adopting the incumbent’s middle initial so that the two names would appear identical on the ballot. He then created a website that was markedly similar (in format, color scheme, etc.) to Sen. Sullivan’s reelection site.”
Despite Decoy Dan advancing to the four-person RCV ballot in November, the race ultimately will come down to the incumbent and former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. But the other Dan Sullivan could grab enough votes from Sen. Dan Sullivan to push Peltola and the Democrats over the top — exactly how the Dems planned it in a red state that Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham’s sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week. Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day. “The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said. With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother. “Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said. Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November. On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly US$830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham. Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination. After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor. Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official. On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things. “I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.” In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate. Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president. Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her. “I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.” Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump’s rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president’s backing for the candidate was enough to win his support. “Trump wants her, he’s doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said. Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham’s inexperience Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk. During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley. A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than US$1 million in the closing week. Graham overcomes debate flub Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on. Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations. She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.” Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham’s answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office. Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham’s experience level “wasn’t really cutting it for me.” Sellers also said he wasn’t swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother. “Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. “If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.” No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin. That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever. ___ Collins reported from Rock Hill, South Carolina. Meg Kinnard And Jeffrey Collins, The Associated Press

sources.news_title: Lindsey Graham's sister wins Republican primary to contest Senate seat in November
sources.text:
Darline Graham wins primary to contest late brother's US Senate seat
Voters in South Carolina have chosen Darline Graham, the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham, as the Republican candidate to contest his US Senate seat in November.
Graham's bid received strong backing from President Donald Trump, who travelled to the state to campaign for her. Graham's victory is being seen as evidence of Trump's continuing influence over the Republican Party.
Graham is currently serving in the Senate as a temporary replacement for her brother, who died suddenly in July. She had never previously run for elected office.
Republicans and Democrats also held primaries in several other states on Tuesday, as they narrowed down their field of candidates for the midterm elections.
Political experts expect that Graham will now go on to succeed in the November election. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate for decades.
The midterms more generally will decide which party controls the US Congress - which in turn will have a bearing on the second half of Trump's presidency.
Graham was running against right-wing Republican Congressman Ralph Norman, who sought to portray his opponent as a puppet of Washington politicians.
The head-to-head was set up after the pair emerged as the top two from a wider field of candidates during an initial contest earlier this month.
Norman is a supporter of Trump and has voted in favour of many of his policies. But in 2024, he initially backed Trump's primary opponent Nikki Haley as his pick for Republican presidential candidate.
With counting almost complete, Graham had received 52.5% of the vote, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In a post on X, she thanked her supporters and the president, and said she was "deeply honoured and humbled" by the result.
During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling during a foreign-policy question during a recent debate.
Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "I'm not that informed on national security." She added: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."
Trump's influence over the party was also tested in Oklahoma, where Mike Mazzei, a former state lawmaker endorsed by the president, took on Gentner Drummond, the state's attorney general.
The winner is widely expected to become the next governor in the heavily Republican state.
South Carolina was not the only state that held an election on Tuesday to replace a deceased lawmaker.
In Georgia, voters in the Atlanta area were tasked with choosing a replacement for Democratic Congressman David Scott, who died in April.
Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late congressman, was among those seeking office. But projections in US media show she was beaten by opponent Everton Blair.
Blair will therefore serve out the remainder of the term, which ends in January. In November, two other candidates will run to take over his seat in the new year.

sources.text:
Election 2026: Graham clips Norman for Republican U.S. Senate ticket
By Alan Wooten
The Center Square
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham will have the place of her brother Lindsey on the Nov. 3 ballot, having defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s U.S. Senate special Republican primary runoff on Tuesday.
About 2 hours and 15 minutes after polls closed, Graham led Norman 52.6%-47.4% with more than 340,000 ballots counted when the race was called by multiple media outlets. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician, is the Democratic opponent in November and is joined on the ballot by Libertarian Kasie Whitener.
The special election became necessary when Lindsey Graham died July 11. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to fulfill the remainder of the term in the 119th Congress that ends on the first of January, and she decided to seek the six-year term by succeeding her brother on the Nov. 3 ballot.
From a crowded field, and after a failed run for governor in the June primary, Norman emerged second to Graham in the special primary two weeks ago. Without achieving 50% plus one of the votes, a runoff was necessary.
Graham, within hours of her brother’s death, carried the support of second-term Republican President Donald Trump. The eve of the runoff included an injection of voter calls and text message blasts valued at $830,000, paid for by the MAGA Inc. super PAC supporting the president and aligned with Republicans.
Graham took a debate punch on foreign policy tied to national security. She later said as she traveled the state, not a single voter asked her about Taiwan and the South China Sea. They did ask, she said, about rising healthcare costs and day-to-day affordability.
In addition to Trump, she had the backing of Republican South Carolina U.S. Sen Tim Scott and Republican South Carolina U.S. Rep. Russell Fry.
Norman, a leading fiscal hawk in the House of Representatives, had endorsements of Florida Sen. Rick Scott and Utah Sen. Mike Lee. Usually with Trump, he broke in 2024 to support former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley’s bid for president.
This Senate seat is one of 33 in regular rotation for the 2026 midterms nationwide, and there are also two special elections. Majority control rests with Republicans at 53 seats, and contests in North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Michigan, Maine, Iowa, New Hampshire, Alaska, Texas and Montana figure to determine if Trump's agenda the next two years will stall in the chamber.
Graham will be heavily favored against Andrews. There hasn’t been a Democrat from the state in the U.S. Senate since Sen. Fritz Holdings retired in 1998.
Republicans have also dominated statewide offices for more than a decade. And they've done so in legislative districts.
Today's state Senate is 34-12 Republican majority, and the House of Representatives is 88-36 Republican majority. Republicans have had majorities for seven four-year cycles in the Senate, dating to 2000, and 16 two-year cycles in the House, dating to 1994.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham, boosted by Trump backing, wins South Carolina Senate race
sources.text:
Darline Graham, boosted by Trump backing, wins South Carolina Senate race
Graham’s victory means that Trump holds a near-perfect record with his Senate primary endorsements during his political career, even as some of his gubernatorial and House picks have fallen short this year
Megan Varner/ Getty Images
Boosted by an endorsement from President Donald Trump and a preelection rally from the state’s leading Republican figures, Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) survived a challenge from Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) to win the GOP nomination for her late brother’s Senate seat.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart, but I know he’s looking down, very proud,” Graham said in her victory speech Tuesday night.
Graham prevailed narrowly (52%-48%) despite facing serious questions about her experience and readiness for a full term in the Senate during the compressed campaign. She expressed ignorance about foreign policy in the race’s lone debate when asked about her thoughts about Taiwan’s security. She had also said she wouldn’t be as focused on foreign policy as her brother, whose hawkish national security record defined his political legacy.
Norman, a hard-line fiscal conservative, proved to be a lackluster opponent, winning in his home base in northwestern South Carolina but losing across the rest of the state. He alienated Republican leaders by initially opposing Trump’s presidential campaign in 2024 (he was one of Nikki Haley’s leading endorsees) and holding out support of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) during the 2023 House GOP leadership fight.
Norman wasn’t able to offer a generational contrast, either — at 73, he would have been one of the oldest freshman senators in recent memory. He was badly outspent in the race by Graham and allied groups, including Trump’s well-financed super PAC, which hasn’t gotten involved in many races this cycle.
“His policies are good, I never understood why he got in this race … it is what it is. I’ll accept it,” Norman said in his concession speech of the president’s involvement.
Graham’s victory means that Trump holds a near-perfect record with his Senate primary endorsements during his political career, even as some of his gubernatorial and House picks have fallen short this year. Trump’s decision to spend valuable political capital — both in time and money — clearly played a pivotal role in the competitive runoff.
Graham herself offered a nod to Trump’s influence, saying in her election night speech, “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
In November, Graham will face pediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat who has been a strong fundraiser, especially given the challenges the party faces in winning South Carolina, a solidly conservative state that backed Trump by 18 points in the 2024 presidential election.

Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP senate nomination
Darline Graham has won the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate in South Carolina, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman after a close runoff election to determine the GOP nominee for the seat vacated after the passing of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.
Dig deeper:

South Carolina has been a firm Republican state for years, making the race a difficult challenge for Democrats. Darline’s brother, Lindsey, represented the state in the Senate since 2003, winning reelection in 2020 by about 10 percentage points.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Scores Major Win in Primary Runoff With Darline Graham
sources.text:
Donald Trump secured a much-needed primary victory Tuesday when South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in the Republican Senate runoff. The result strengthens Trump’s standing in a party where several of his preferred candidates have recently fallen short. Graham now moves toward a November contest in a heavily Republican state.
Darline Graham beats Ralph Norman to win in South Carolina primary
The win carries a personal dimension for Graham. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her in July to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly at 71 (via CNBC). Darline had never won elected office before taking the seat. She will now face Democrat Annie Andrews in November, although the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the race “Solid R.”
Trump made Graham’s campaign a priority from the start. He flew to South Carolina last week for a joint appearance, then used a tele-rally Monday before issuing another endorsement on Truth Social. He argued that nobody could better carry on Lindsey Graham’s legacy and described Darline as a lifelong “WINNER,” giving her his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
Graham’s path to the runoff wasn’t exactly smooth sailing. A debate moment over Taiwan gave Norman an opening when she admitted she was “not that informed on national security” while discussing the island’s significance to America.
Graham later brushed off the criticism on Fox News, saying she simply doesn’t “speak politician.” Norman seized on the stumble, pitching himself as the battle-tested conservative and dismissing Graham as a “propped-up candidate.”
Graham’s victory comes as Trump’s endorsement record faces scrutiny following several losses by his preferred candidates. Several candidates he backed have already stumbled in Republican races across Iowa, Wyoming and Florida. In South Carolina, his endorsement also failed to lift Pamela Evette into the next round after Trump ultimately backed her and Alan Wilson. CNN found that 10 Trump-backed candidates have lost this cycle, the same number of primary defeats he suffered across the 2018, 2020 and 2024 elections combined.
