sources.news_title: Reports of Trump's Waning Influence Have Been Greatly Exaggerated
sources.text:
Donald Trump's presidency is unraveling. Don't believe me? You obviously don't read the New York Times.
"European leaders have refused to join his war with Iran," writes the Times' Peter Baker. "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel flatly rejected his Gaza plan. Gulf Arab states forced him to abandon plans to charge a shipping toll in the Strait of Hormuz," he adds.
Baker has more: "Universities and law firms are rebuffing his directives rather than signing on the bottom line. Bond markets are rebelling against his fiscal policies. Even the ABC network, whose $16 million payment to settle a Trump lawsuit was seen as an early example of yielding to the president, has discovered that it did not buy peace and is now suing his administration for threatening its broadcast licenses."
Wow. Baker thinks Trump has one foot on a banana peel and the other poised over a bear trap.
Indeed, Donald Trump's approval numbers are predictably underwater. The RealClearPolitics average is anemic at 39.5% approval. Nate Silver's average has Trump at 38.1% approval.
Then, for the love of Mike, would these experts tell me why political novice Darline Graham, sister of the deceased Sen. Lindsey Graham, managed to win the South Carolina Senate race primary despite healthy skepticism that she could prevail?
Graham made an unforced, rookie mistake in the one debate between her and her primary opponent, Rep. Ralph Norman, last week. She admitted she didn't know a lot about foreign policy, specifically Taiwan.
Norman must have thought the electoral gods were on his side. "By her choice, she's running for the United States Senate. It's a six-year term. You need to get fully versed in what issues you're going to be dealing with. This isn't a get training on the job, you can't do that."
After that gaffe, some political observers believed it would take a miracle for Graham to pull off a victory.
Enter a miracle.
Donald Trump rode to Graham's rescue on Friday, showing up at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center and, before an enthusiastic house, gave a ringing endorsement for Darline. He defended her debate gaffe by arguing that she was simply "being honest" rather than offering a typical politician's response.
"I'm doing this to honor Lindsey. That's why I'm here... So, Darline, we got to win that race." He directly appealed to attendees to treat the contest as if he were on the ballot himself.
Appearing with GOP heavyweights Sen. Tim Scott and Gov. Henry McMaster, Trump backed up his trip by having his MAGA super PAC pour $800,000 into a massive get-out-the-vote effort. It was an over-the-top success. The turnout in Myrtle Beach was spectacular. Graham won 73% of the vote, bettering her brother's 64% in the last primary, and won all 125 precincts. Statewide, she won 197,000 votes to Norman's 175,000.
Must've been a nice day because nothing else contributed to the large turnout, right?
Trump's approval may be underwater, but he still drives the GOP bus. And since the midterms are predicated largely on getting your supporters to the polls in greater numbers than your opponent, Trump's ability to drive voters to the polls will be critical if the GOP hopes to maintain control of Congress.
President Donald Trump didn't just endorse Graham – sharing a stage with her in South Carolina on Friday, he declared that he too was "on the ballot."
A day before the primary runoff, he appeared to hedge his bets: For "a few" of the candidates he endorsed it was "almost impossible for them to win," he posted on Truth Social, but he felt "obligated" to back them. He did not specify which candidates he was referring to, though the post came amid concerns about the viability of Graham's campaign.
By late Tuesday, however, it was clear she had pulled it off. While Norman performed well in his home base of Greenville, Graham outperformed him in much of the rest of the state – including a resounding win in the area surrounding Myrtle Beach, where Trump campaigned with her last week.
It was a much-needed win for Trump, facing mounting public concerns over inflation, the conflict with Iran and an escalating trade war with Canada.
I think it's clear at this point, less than two months before the election, that no one — not pollsters, not prediction markets, not "experts," not anyone — knows what the voters will say on November 3. What pollsters are telling us about what issues are "important" isn't tracking with the reality we're seeing on the ground.
Trump, as usual, is the wildcard. Where he's popular, he will help. Where he's not as popular, he will probably hurt, but not as much as some might project. One aspect of Trump's effect on the races that won't be reflected in any poll or survey is that the 35% of the electorate that supports Trump are more enthusiastic than almost any Democrat, and therefore, more likely to vote. That's what the South Carolina runoff tells us.
I'm not predicting a GOP win in the midterms. But these confident predictions of a GOP disaster aren't based on reality. There's a disconnect between the polls and what's happening on the ground. And elections are won and lost on the ground.

Appointed Republican Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s South Carolina GOP Senate primary runoff, defeating U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman to secure the party nomination for the seat formerly held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
Neither candidate managed to secure an outright majority in the 10-candidate special primary on August 11, which eliminated eight contenders, including Republican Rep. Russell Fry, and sent Graham and Norman into Tuesday’s head-to-head contest.
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to the seat after Sen. Lindsey Graham died on July 11. Former President Donald Trump quickly backed her bid for a full term, campaigning in Myrtle Beach on Friday and hosting a tele-rally with her on Monday.
During the call, Graham noted that because Trump “got her into this whole thing, I have to make sure she gets in.”
Federal Election Commission filings show Graham raised more than $346,000 between July 23 and August 5. The pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. also spent upwards of $827,000 on phone calls and text messages supporting her candidacy.
Graham’s campaign generated resistance among several local party figures and lawmakers. South Carolina Freedom Conference Chairman Jordan Pace stated to the Daily Caller that the party did not favor Graham serving a full term, while state Rep. Jay Kilmartin cited grassroots frustration regarding her platform and governing approach.
Foreign policy emerged as a central point of debate during an August 18 forum hosted by Newsmax.
Asked by moderator Greta Van Susteren whether Taiwan and the South China Sea represent national security priorities for the United States, Graham responded, “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security. So … But I do support the military.” The stance contrasted with that of her late brother, who long advocated an interventionist foreign policy, including U.S. aid to Ukraine and direct military action abroad.
Norman mounted a competitive campaign with backing from high-profile conservative figures and organizations, including the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC), Florida Sen. Rick Scott, Utah Sen. Mike Lee, South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace, and former governor Mark Sanford. Former Virginia Rep. Bob Good also endorsed Norman in a social media post on Tuesday, calling on South Carolina voters to “reject birthright senatorship.”

sources.news_title: Sister of pro-Israel stalwart Lindsey Graham secures GOP Senate nomination
sources.text:
South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham defeated U.S. House Rep. Ralph Norman in a special primary runoff on Tuesday, putting her in a dominant position to win the Senate seat left vacant with the death in July of her older brother, the pro-Israel stalwart Lindsey Graham.
The Associated Press called the race two hours after polls closed at 9:01pm. By the time 99% of votes were tallied, Darline Graham had secured 52.3% of the votes to Norman’s 47.7%.
“Tonight is a great victory, but it’s not the finish line,” Graham told her supporters on Tuesday night. “In fact, it is the starting line for an even bigger fight, which lies ahead.”
If Darline Graham goes on to win November’s general election against Democrat Annie Andrews, she will have big shoes to fill. Her brother served 23 years in the Senate and eight in the U.S. House. He traveled to Israel about a dozen times between Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attack on the Jewish state and his death at age 71.
Heading into the primaries, analysts expressed no doubt that Darline Graham would be pro-Israel. But matching Lindsey Graham’s level of foreign policy activity, they warned, would be a formidable task. Meanwhile, her campaign to date has largely avoided discussion of international affairs. Instead, she has focused on domestic concerns like reducing spending, securing borders and promoting Trump-backed policies.
During a debate aired on C-SPAN last week, Graham struggled to respond to a foreign policy question about Taiwan and the South China Sea, ultimately admitting that she’s “not that informed on national security.”
“I’m not a polished politician up here,” she said. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
Later addressing issues of affordability, Graham linked the domestic economic situation to the war in Iran and said she trusts President Donald Trump “to get the Strait of Hormuz open.” She also voiced her preference for financial sanctions over putting troops on the ground.
Asked about the country’s relationship with Israel, Graham described the Jewish state as “one of our strongest allies.” Recognizing her brother’s close relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, she added that during a recent meeting with the Israeli premier, she vowed to “continue supporting Israel in any way” she can.
“We have to stand with Israel,” Graham said.
At their previous face-off, Graham had secured 33% of the vote, while Norman came in second place, at 25%, against eight fellow Republicans. But South Carolina requires primary winners to earn a majority of votes in order to avoid a two-candidate runoff. In the November general election, Graham will contend with Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is unlikely to prevail in the solidly Republican state.
Tuesday’s runoff marked the third time in two months that South Carolina Republicans came to the polls to select a Senate candidate. Lindsey Graham, won the first primary in June but died suddenly the next month from an aortic dissection.
A few days later, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, a Republican, appointed Darline Graham to finish her brother’s term. Though she only had minimal policy experience, including a leadership role at the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, she earned President Donald Trump’s endorsement and declared her candidacy in the full race.
Trump celebrated Graham’s nomination in a Tuesday night Truth Social post, writing that “Darline Graham rides Trump endorsement to win GOP nomination for brother’s South Carolina seat.”
Graham thanked Trump profusely during her Tuesday night acceptance speech, recognizing the president as one of her brother’s “closest friends” and crediting him for helping her secure a victory.
Norman, meanwhile, thanked his supporters on Tuesday night for their “prayer crusade of a campaign,” stressing that he “did not prepare a concession speech.” He accused “outside PACs” of spending $8 million opposing him and blamed the Democrats for this situation, adding that “they got what they wanted.”
He recognized Trump’s role in the race as a supporter of Graham, noting that he “never understood why he got involved” but that it is the president’s prerogative to do so. Nonetheless, Norman pledged that there “won’t be any tears” and that he planned to back Graham.
“I’m not supporting a Democrat, so I will support her, Darline, as best I can,” he added. “We’ll live to fight another day.”

Lindsey Grahams sister-Darlene wins South Carolina Republican primary runoff for US Senate - The Tribune
sources.text:
Washington, DC [US], August 26 (ANI): Darline Graham Nordone, the sister of late US Senator Lindsey Graham, secured the Republican nomination to succeed him on South Carolina's general election ballot, Politico reported.
Nordone defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in Tuesday's special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after both candidates emerged at the head of a 10-way primary field, the report added.
Her victory underscores the decisive impact of high-profile backing, as the US President went to great lengths to push her over the finish line, encouraging her entry with an early endorsement, standing by her after a debate fumble, and holding a rally in Myrtle Beach, a level of direct involvement rarely seen this election cycle.
Extending well beyond campaign appearances, the financial muscle behind her candidacy proved formidable. Politico reported that MAGA Inc., Trump's primary super PAC, poured over USD 827,000 into targeted phone calls and text messages for Graham, providing the kind of heavy backing that Republicans in competitive battlegrounds have eagerly sought.
The decisive outcome reaffirms that Trump's endorsement remains a dominant force in Republican politics when backed by total and active engagement.
Following the primary triumph, Graham will officially replace her late brother on the ballot in November as the Republican nominee, placing her on a direct path to securing a full Senate term in deep-red South Carolina.
This sustained backing was especially vital during the intensive two-week runoff sprint, when Norman and his allies targeted her over political inexperience following a foreign policy debate slip. However, sharing the stage with the President at a closing rally allowed her to seal the contest by reaffirming her direct alignment with Trump, Politico reported.
The win marks an extraordinary turn for a figure previously unknown in public politics. Having never held elective office, Graham was appointed to the Senate by GOP Governor Henry McMaster after Lindsey Graham's sudden death in July. Prior to her appointment, she had headed South Carolina's Commission for the Blind since 2019, following a tenure at the state's Vocational Rehabilitation Department.
In contrast, her opponent Norman, a House Freedom Caucus veteran with nine years in Congress, struggled to convert his legislative track record into votes. Politico noted that while Norman broadly supported the administration's policy vision, he had occasionally clashed with Trump over federal spending.
Ultimately, Norman's congressional background proved insufficient against Graham's momentum, while he simultaneously faced severe opposition from the solar industry, which deployed USD 1 million in targeted spending to derail his bid. (ANI)

sources.news_title: ‘It's put up or shut up time’: Battleground Republicans want the Darline treatment
Darline Graham wins South Carolina Republican Senate runoff
sources.text:
Diyar Guldogan and Darren Lyn
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s Republican primary runoff for the South Carolina Senate seat previously held by her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.
 
Darline Graham, 62, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman 52.5% to 47.6%. 
 
The two had emerged as the top candidates in a crowded Republican primary earlier this month. Neither candidate had secured enough votes to win the Aug. 11 contest outright, sending the race to a runoff.
 
The victory puts Darline Graham on track to appear on the November ballot as the Republican nominee for a full six-year Senate term. She will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.
 
Lindsey Graham, 71, died unexpectedly in early July after more than two decades in the Senate. He had won the Republican nomination for another term in the initial June primary before his death.
 
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to temporarily fill the vacant Senate seat. She subsequently announced her campaign for a full term and received the backing of President Donald Trump.
 
In her victory speech, Graham said she "humbly" accepts the nomination to serve as the Republican nominee for the upper chamber.
 
"I want to thank President Trump for all of his support...South Carolina is truly Trump country!" she said.
 
Norman, for his part, said he “hates it for the state" and "never understood" why Trump got involved.
 
"He has that right, that's his prerogative ... his policies are good, I never understood why he got in this race to beat but it is what it is, and I'll accept it," he said.
 
The state of Georgia also held a special Democratic runoff election for the 13th Congressional District to replace the late US Rep. David Scott, who passed away in April. Scott's daughter Marcye lost in a close battle to her opponent Everton Blair by a count of 54% to 46%.
 
Blair will serve out the remainder of David Scott's term in office, but neither candidate is on the November ballot for the next full congressional term. The nominees who will face off in the midterm election for the 13th Congressional District are Democrat Jasmine Clark and Republican Jonathan Chavez.
 
Several key primary races took place in the state of Oklahoma, including the race for US Senate. In the Republican primary, US Rep. Kevin Hern, who was endorsed by Trump, easily beat his four opponents with 69.8% of the vote. Hern will face Democratic nominee N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, who achieved an overwhelming victory over Jim Priest.
 
The race to replace Hern in Oklahoma's 1st Congressional District is also headed to a runoff in the Republican primary between Mark Tedford and Trump-backed Jackson Lahmeyer. The winner will face Democratic nominee John Croisant, who ran unopposed.
 
In the race to replace Oklahoma Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, who cannot run for re-election due to term limits, there will be a runoff between Trump-endorsed former state Sen. Mike Mazzei and Gentner Drummond. The winner will face Cyndi Munson, who won the Democratic primary, beating her two opponents with 74.9% of the vote.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham wins Republican U.S. Senate runoff in South Carolina
Darline Graham wins S.C. GOP nomination to replace her late brother in Senate
Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP nomination to replace her late brother in US Senate
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., gives a speech to supporters after winning a special Republican primary runoff to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., in the November general election, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in Columbia, S.C.
COLUMBIA, S.C. — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.
Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham's sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."
Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

sources.news_title: Lindsey Graham's sister wins. The War Party wins. We lose, again.
sources.text:
Darline Graham won the Republican primary Tuesday and will likely win a full-term to fill her late brother Lindsey Graham’s U.S. Senate seat in the ruby red state of South Carolina in the upcoming November election.
According to the latest tallies Tuesday night, Graham, who was appointed to her brother’s seat after his death in July, beat her opponent Rep. Ralph Norman, 53% to 46%.
It’s a curious turn of events in a modern era where there are very few displays of hereditary power, but she had the full backing of the Republican establishment and the fulsome endorsement of President Donald Trump days before today’s primary runoff.
To be sure, her self-confessed lack of foreign policy experience or even knowledge won’t be a bad thing for Trump. Graham has all but said she will follow her brother’s career-long support of a militarized U.S. foreign policy, which means she is likely to be no critic of Trump’s failing war in the Middle East. A win for the War Party, but a loss for the rest of us.
Graham was given a chance to display her merits last Thursday when she was asked in a debate with Norman if Taiwan and the South China Sea were national security issues for the United States.
“I’m just going to be honest here. I’m … not that informed on national security,” Graham replied. “But I do support the military."
Many thought this gaffe would sink her. Not a chance.
This just wasn’t Norman’s time. He has a mixed foreign policy record, yet campaigned on “peace through strength” and now-dated MAGA “no more forever wars” sloganeering. In the same debate Graham flubbed, he said of the Iran War, that “(Trump’s) going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take if the Straits of Hormuz are still dominated by a country that’s supposed to be decimated.”
Despite having voted more with Trump’s agenda than any other South Carolina Republican, Norman could not compete with the idea that Lindsey Graham’s sister somehow deserved the president’s endorsement more. Don’t think her potential rubber stamp for the military didn’t have a lot to do with that.
Trump told reporters at the Graham rally four days ago that “she’s going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants.”
What the “military wants”? What the “president wants”? Is that the role of a U.S. Senator representing South Carolina?
(Graham’s) candidacy has been bolstered by support from at least three political action committees, coordination with a national Republican Party group, and donations from “large business executives”, while Norman has done more self-fundraising, The State newspaper in Columbia reported on August 19.
Some of Graham’s big backers include the PAC raising funds on behalf of major aerospace manufacturer Boeing, the CEO of private equity firm Blackstone, the head of public policy for TikTok, and an executive at Palantir, one of the most influential defense and surveillance technology contractors in the world today.
Super PAC "Security is Strength", which was created for her brother a decade ago, pledged $900,000 for Graham in July. Palmetto Action spent $1.26 million targeting Norman, according to Federal Election Commission records.
There was something ironic in the Security is Strength support of Graham after she admitted national security wasn’t her strength. Still this Columbia-based “neocon PAC”, which says it “is dedicated to promoting a strong national defense, conservative judicial philosophy, and the protection of traditional values,” was created in 2015 to support Lindsey Graham's 2016 Republican presidential primary run — the key purpose of which was to kill any potential momentum for fellow candidate and restraint advocate, Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY).
The late Graham was clear a decade ago about who was bankrolling this PAC. “If I were a defense contractor, I’d be big time for Lindsey Graham, because I’ve been forward-leaning on rebuilding our military," he said at the time.
“It’s not surprising, then, that the same warmongers who subsidized Graham are now subsidizing his sister — fully aware of her unwavering allegiance to Trump’s escalating war in Iran,” wrote Will Folks of South Carolina-based FITS News in July.
Having an unquestioning Iran war supporter in Lindsey Graham’s seat certainly seems important to Sean Hannity, who promptly hosted Darline Graham on his Fox News show the night after her disastrous debate gaffe.
“I bet based on all your time with your brother, that you know probably everything about the Middle East,” Hannity said to her, as if she received this knowledge through osmosis.
“Absolutely,” she replied. “I know national security is important. We have a wonderful commander in chief.”
“I know that we need to stand with the Israel,” Graham also exclaimed (emphasis added).
Next to Graham on screen was a "Darline's Graham's Policy Positions" scroll letting Fox News viewers know the totality of her ostensibly conservative positions.
Graham attempted to clarify and divert, “I tripped up on one question last night, regarding Taiwan. I don't speak politician. I was just honest. Of course, Taiwan is our friend.”
“But I think people in South Carolina are more worried about boys in girls sports,” she went on.
On Monday, Hannity made clear that he was supporting Graham and also interviewed South Carolina’s other senator, Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to explain why he, too, was supporting her.
The reliably hawkish Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) and neocon pundit Mark Levin had already endorsed Graham.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Nordone Wins Runoff in South Carolina’s Special GOP Senate Primary
sources.text:
South Carolina Republicans voted to try to keep one of the state’s U.S. Senate seats in the Graham family, as Darline Graham Nordone, who was appointed to fill it temporarily, has won the runoff for the special Republican primary election to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham on the ballot in the November general election.
The Associated Press called the race at 9:01 p.m. ET, as Nordone led with about 52.5% of the vote.
Nordone said in a speech after securing the nomination that she has mixed emotions about her primary victory and that she misses her brother.
“There is still a big hole in my heart,” Nordone told supporters at a rally, “but I know he’s looking down right now very proud of everyone in this room.”
She then added that her nomination is merely “the starting line for an even bigger fight which lies ahead.”
Nordone will next face off against the Democratic candidate Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who won her primary in June. The upper chamber seat, though, is unlikely to flip in Democrats’ favor; the Cook Political Report rates the race as “Solid Republican.”
In June, Graham won the Republican primary race to compete for his fifth term as Senator, but after his death the following month, a special primary election was called for Aug. 11. While Nordone, who was appointed by South Carolina’s Governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term, earned the highest share of the vote on Aug. 11, she fell short of the majority she needed to win the race, triggering the runoff. Nordone earned nearly 33% of the vote on Aug. 11, while her opponent, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, came in second, with nearly 25%, sending both candidates to the runoff race.
President Donald Trump had championed Nordone in the race, publicly encouraging her to run for a full term before she had even announced her plans to do so. In a Truth Social post in July, Trump called Nordone “a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot.”
“Lindsey was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known, and his sister shares his deep love of our Country, and the State of South Carolina,” Trump said in his post. He added that he asked Nordone to run for a full term, saying, “I hope Darline does this, in that there would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.”
Although Nordone was a strong supporter of her brother’s political career over the years, she had never before held elected office. Her lack of political experience was the subject of scrutiny during her campaign, particularly after a debate against Norman leading up to Tuesday’s runoff. When asked during the debate if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S., Nordone replied: “I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security, so.”
Her opponents were quick to criticize her for the remark. Nikki Haley, Trump’s former U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. who endorsed Norman in the race, shared a clip of Nordone’s response to the debate question on X, saying, “Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate.”
Nordone responded to the backlash in an interview on Fox News.
“I tripped up on one question last night,” she said. “But you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician. You know, I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

sources.news_title: Graham wins South Carolina Senate primary, vindicating Trump
sources.text:
The News
South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s primary for a full term, riding President Donald Trump’s endorsement to a narrow victory after a quick special election.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” Graham said of Trump at her victory party in Columbia. She immediately pivoted to the general election against Democrat Annie Andrews, warning that she advocates “turning confused little boys into little girls and vice versa.”
Graham, who’d never sought office before being appointed to replace her brother Lindsey in the Senate, was backed by most of the state’s GOP leadership, and her allies — including MAGA Inc., the president’s super PAC — outspent her primary competitor, Rep. Ralph Norman.
“We had $8 million spent against us,” Norman told his supporters, bemoaning the president’s decision to endorse Graham. “His policies are good. I never understood why he got in this race. It is what it is.”
Graham built an insurmountable lead in the 7th Congressional District in and around Myrtle Beach, where Rep. Russell Fry endorsed her after losing his own Senate bid, and where the president flew in for a weekend rally. Norman carried his district and the upstate, where the Grahams were raised and where conservative voters had been most critical of the late senator.
In the rest of the state, Graham prevailed — including in the Charleston area, where former governor and congressman Mark Sanford endorsed Norman after his own Senate campaign faltered. She linked herself directly to the president, telling voters that, unlike her brother, she’d get rid of the filibuster to pass Trump’s voter ID law, and said she’d never support amnesty for undocumented immigrants.
The president was on the verge of getting another endorsee over the line in Oklahoma, where former state Sen. Mike Mazzei beat Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the runoff for the GOP nomination for governor. Mazzei did best with votes cast on Election Day, after Drummond had criticized the president’s plan to import beef to ameliorate the effects of his tariffs.
“When he gets it wrong, I will speak up,” Drummond said of Trump.
In this article:
David’s view
Graham’s campaign, powered by her brother’s old political operation, impressed Republicans. Graham’s candidacy sometimes didn’t. After last week’s only runoff debate, where the senator punted a question on Taiwan and explained that “foreign policy” wasn’t her expertise, Republicans upped their expectations for Norman, a House Freedom Caucus member who ran to Graham’s right.
But she won, and the president got to claim another victory, which she was happy to attribute to him. His intervention in Oklahoma was just as impressive: Mazzei, whose top issue is ending the state income tax, didn’t have a political legacy to run on like Graham’s.
Notable
- Ben Jacobs covered the final days of the South Carolina runoff for Slate, including the in-person Myrtle Beach rally that the president attended: “It’s never an ideal sign when a candidate’s support at an election-eve rally is less than unanimous.”

sources.news_title: Trump gets a much-needed South Carolina win and other takeaways from Tuesday’s elections
sources.text:
President Donald Trump demonstrated his might with Republican primary voters Tuesday in South Carolina, as Darline Graham — the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and the president’s pick in the state’s special Senate primary runoff — claimed the GOP nomination.
Now favored to win a full term in November, Darline Graham is, in many ways, a senator of Trump’s own making. The president lobbied South Carolina’s governor to appoint her to fill the remaining months in her brother’s term after he died in July. Then, he privately and publicly pressed her to run for a full six-year term.
And when it looked like her rival in the runoff, Rep. Ralph Norman, might win, Trump visited Myrtle Beach to rally Republican loyalists to Graham’s cause, as his super PAC, MAGA Inc., disclosed spending more than $827,000 to support Graham.
Graham’s win is narrow — she led by just a few percentage points Tuesday evening — but symbolically significant for the president in a month full of political setbacks, with six of his endorsed picks losing Republican primaries.
Trump notched another win in Oklahoma, where the Republican he endorsed won a primary runoff in the race for governor — defeating a rival who has sought to slow the construction of a massive aluminum plant the president supports.
And in a low-turnout special election runoff in Georgia, Democrats filled a vacancy in the narrowly divided House.
Here are takeaways from Tuesday’s elections in South Carolina, Oklahoma and Georgia:
A badly needed win for Trump
Darline Graham took to the stage at her victory party Tuesday night and declared: “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
Unlike her brother, who was close to the late Sen. John McCain and built a reputation as a foreign policy hawk independent from Trump, Darline Graham’s political profile was tied entirely to the president.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” she said in a message directed at Trump.
For Trump, the win was badly needed — a victory in one of his highest-risk interventions in Republican primaries this year, after a string of several losses this month and with midterm elections just over two months away. It could serve to remind Republican lawmakers who might be looking to distance themselves from an unpopular president of the potential political costs of being at odds with Trump.
Norman acknowledged Trump’s role in the race’s outcome, telling his supporters Tuesday night that “the president got involved. He has that right.”
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said as some members of the crowd booed the president. “But it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”
Graham is now set to face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in November. Andrews on Tuesday challenged Graham to at least three televised debates, saying in a statement that “no appointment, endorsement, or family connection entitles anyone to six years” in the Senate. Still, Graham is heavily favored to win the deep-red state in the general election.
A senator of Trump’s making
Trump has endorsed a slew of candidates this year, but rarely has he put his own political capital on the line like he did in South Carolina.
When Trump initially talked up Darline Graham to fill the seat of her late brother, and Gov. Henry McMaster complied, it seemed like a short-term gig. The seat was already on the ballot for a full six-year term in November, so she’d have been a placeholder for a few months, until South Carolina voters nominated and elected one of the state’s myriad experienced Republicans who had been waiting decades for a Senate vacancy.
But Trump doubled down three days after she was sworn in, urging her on social media to seek a full term. And, days later, she announced she would do so.
The president’s “complete and total endorsement” wasn’t enough to clear the field. After all, Darline Graham had no political experience, and her brother wasn’t exactly beloved among conservative voters in South Carolina: He’d earned just 57% of the vote in his primary two months earlier against a handful of relative unknowns.
The results of the August 11 primary suggested she could be defeated in the runoff. She finished first, but with just shy of 33% of the vote.
There were reasons to believe Trump’s influence might be limited. After all, his choice in South Carolina’s GOP primary for governor, Lt. Gov. Pam Evette, lost to state Attorney General Alan Wilson — who Trump also endorsed at the last minute when it was clear his preference was on course for defeat.
The president did not have the luxury of the same face-saving tack here: Norman had endorsed and campaigned with former Gov. Nikki Haley as she ran against Trump for the 2024 GOP presidential nomination.
Graham’s inexperience was on display during a debate with Norman earlier this month, when she declined to answer a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea, saying that national security was “not my thing.”
But Trump carried Graham over the finish line. He visited South Carolina on Friday, telling Republicans that he’d personally lobbied her to run for a full term. “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he urged GOP voters.
Another endorsement test in Oklahoma
Trump notched another victory in Oklahoma — this one even narrower — with his preferred candidate in the governor’s race, former state Sen. Mike Mazzei, winning a Republican primary runoff against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
The two are vying to take on Oklahoma House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson, the Democratic nominee, in the race to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt in November.
The race was another test of Trump’s influence — and there were significant questions over whether his endorsement would be enough for Mazzei, after Trump’s picks in Republican gubernatorial primaries in Georgia, Iowa and Minnesota all lost earlier this year.
A key divide in the primary was a proposed $4 billion aluminum smelter at the Tulsa Port of Inola, estimated to bring about 1,000 jobs to the area. Trump touted the plant, claiming on Truth Social that it “will be one of the best projects ever conceived or built, not only in the Great State of Oklahoma, but in the United States, itself.” But, amid local concerns about pollution and damage to the livestock economy, Drummond has sued, asking a federal court to block the plant’s construction.
Georgia Dems fill a House seat
Democrat Everton Blair, a former Gwinnett County School Board chair, won the special election for Georgia’s 13th District House seat vacated by the late Rep. David Scott’s death in April.
But he won’t hold that seat for long.
Blair, who will be the first out gay member of Congress from Georgia, defeated the longtime lawmaker’s daughter Marcye Scott in the special election runoff on Tuesday. He campaigned on a pledge to be a stronger opponent to Trump and advocate for a more progressive affordability agenda than both the late congressman and his daughter.
However, Blair finished a distant third in the regular House primary earlier this year, so he won’t be on the ballot in November.
State lawmaker Jasmine Clark is the Democratic nominee for a full two-year term in the deep-blue district in November. She did not run in the special election because under state law, she would have had to resign her seat in the Georgia House — costing Democrats a seat just as Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was launching an unsuccessful push for mid-decade redistricting.
In the meantime, Blair’s win, and the special election of state Sen. Aisha Wahab in California last week, will help Democrats further narrow the already razor-thin GOP majority in the House.
CNN’s Katie Doran and Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

Three takeaways from Tuesday's South Carolina Republican Senate primary
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 - South Carolina Republicans on Tuesday nominated Darline Graham to run in November's general election for her late brother's U.S. Senate seat, as she defeated Representative Ralph Norman in a primary runoff.
Here are some takeaways from the result:
TRUMP ENDORSEMENT PAID OFF
President Donald Trump didn't just endorse Graham – sharing a stage with her in South Carolina on Friday, he declared that he too was "on the ballot."
A day before the primary runoff, he appeared to hedge his bets: For "a few" of the candidates he endorsed it was "almost impossible for them to win," he posted on Truth Social, but he felt "obligated" to back them. He did not specify which candidates he was referring to, though the post came amid concerns about the viability of Graham's campaign.
By late Tuesday, however, it was clear she had pulled it off. While Norman performed well in his home base of Greenville, Graham outperformed him in much of the rest of the state – including a resounding win in the area surrounding Myrtle Beach, where Trump campaigned with her last week.
It was a much-needed win for Trump, facing mounting public concerns over inflation, the conflict with Iran and an escalating trade war with Canada.
Only 33% of Americans approve of his performance, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, but Tuesday's result shows he still has singular influence among Republican voters.
The president's ability to boost turnout among his party faithful will be a key factor in determining whether Republicans are able to retain control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in November's midterm elections.
MAGA INC. MEGA MONEY
A political action committee, MAGA INC., established to support Trump, spent $827,711 to bolster Graham's campaign, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.
While Trump has given his vocal endorsement to Republicans in races across the country, his PAC has rarely contributed to their campaigns.
It appears to have paid off for Trump, and could embolden MAGA INC. to keep the money flowing to the president's favored candidates in key races going forward.
GRAHAM AN UNLIKELY REBEL IN THE SENATE
The late Senator Lindsey Graham became a close ally of Trump's after a rocky start in 2016 when, as a candidate in the Republican presidential primaries, he referred to Trump as a "bigot" and "complete idiot."
He would go on to become a frequent golfing companion of the president and one of his most loyal supporters in Congress.
Darline Graham so far has followed in her brother's footsteps, and would appear to be another ally in the making for Trump. It is still unclear, however, whether Republicans will be able to hold onto their slim Senate majority next year.
Whether they do or not, Graham is looking like she could be in the mold of many first-term senators who have held to another tradition, keeping their heads down during their maiden year and following their leadership's desires. REUTERS

sources.news_title: Graham’s win in South Carolina shows Trump’s still got sway
sources.text:
Graham’s win in South Carolina shows Trump’s still got sway
Loading...
| Washington
For President Donald Trump, this one was personal.
Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina won the Republican primary runoff Tuesday to replace her brother – the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a close Trump ally – on the November ballot for a full six-year term. With more than 95% of the vote in, Ms. Graham was leading by 52% to 48%.
It may have been President Trump’s support, including a big rally last week in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, and a tele-rally Monday night, that made the difference. After Lindsey Graham’s death last month, the president had urged the state’s governor to appoint the senator’s sister to Mr. Graham’s seat for the remaining months of the current term, then encouraged her to run in her own right in November.
Why We Wrote This
Voters have rejected more Trump-endorsed candidates in this year’s primary season than in previous cycles. But Darline Graham won South Carolina’s U.S. Senate nomination Tuesday, as the president’s backing outweighed her lack of experience.
The new Senator Graham, a political novice, stumbled in her Aug. 18 debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, the second-most vote-getter in the first round of primary voting two weeks ago.
“I’m not that informed on national security,” Ms. Graham said to audience boos when asked about U.S. policy toward Taiwan.
Mr. Trump was undaunted, putting his political reputation on the line.
“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot!” he urged the crowd at the Graham rally in Myrtle Beach.
In Monday’s tele-rally, Mr. Trump again centered the race on himself. “I asked her to [run],” he said. “I got her into this whole thing, I have to make sure she gets in.”
The senator thanked the president in her Tuesday night victory speech. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Not long ago, a Trump endorsement almost guaranteed victory in a Republican primary. This year, that has not necessarily been the case. Before Tuesday, 10 Trump-backed candidates for statewide office or Congress had lost their primaries in 2026, equal to the figure for all of 2018, 2020, and 2024 combined, according to a CNN analysis based on data from Ballotpedia.
But on Tuesday, more than one Trump-endorsed candidate won a competitive primary. In Oklahoma, Tulsa businessman Mike Mazzei edged out state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in a runoff for governor. Mr. Mazzei will confront Democrat Cyndi Munson, the Oklahoma House minority leader, in the November election.
With the Oklahoma outcome and Ms. Graham’s high-profile win, Mr. Trump has shown he still has political mojo, staving off the growing whispers of “lame duck.”
Still, for some voters, the idea of sending a fresh face to Washington, one who might understand their everyday struggles, may also have held appeal. Ms. Graham had a career in vocational rehabilitation for disabled people before suddenly becoming a U.S. senator. She and her older brother were close; after their parents died when Darline was a young teen, Lindsey became her legal guardian and later her adoptive father.
Representative Norman offered voters a different kind of political value, as a seasoned legislator who knows the ropes in Washington and could advocate for the state.
But Mr. Norman has long had an uneasy relationship with Mr. Trump, particularly on fiscal matters. sources.news_title: Senator Darline Graham wins GOP primary runoff in South Carolina to replace her late brother in US Senate - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — US Senator Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.
Darline Graham defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Darline Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after her brother’s sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly notched an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
She went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the novice candidate with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unknown, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump’s rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president’s backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he’s doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham’s inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Senators Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative US House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the US has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham’s answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham’s experience level “wasn’t really cutting it for me.”
Sellers also said he wasn’t swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. “If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

sources.news_title: Trump-backed Graham wins South Carolina runoff in boost for president
sources.text:
Darline Graham, the political novice appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham, defeated veteran congressman Ralph Norman after Trump invested heavily in the contest, campaigning in the state and urging supporters to vote as though his own name were on the ballot, according to projections from CNN and NBC.
Her victory interrupts a bruising run for Trump, whose endorsed candidates had lost 10 Republican contests this cycle, including six in the previous two weeks, even as his own approval ratings fell sharply.
The result is also a personal vindication for Trump, who had insisted days earlier that his endorsements were “stronger than ever” and dismissed recent losses as acts of loyalty to candidates he knew faced difficult races.

The Trump-supporting MAGA Inc political organisation also spent more than US$827,000 on voter calls and text messages – a rare deployment of its reserves in this year’s primaries.

Trump’s influence is also being tested in Oklahoma, another Republican stronghold, where his favoured candidate Mike Mazzei faces state attorney general Gentner Drummond for the party’s gubernatorial nomination.
Drummond narrowly finished ahead of Mazzei in the first round in June, with both taking around a quarter of the vote. More than US$9 million has since been spent on the runoff, according to US media.
Trump has repeatedly attacked Drummond as a “fake Republican,” in part because the attorney general opposed a proposed US$4 billion aluminum smelter backed by the president, arguing that the project could damage local land and communities.
Mazzei, a wealthy former state senator, publicly embraced the project shortly before Trump endorsed him.
Victories in either state would help Trump steady a primary record battered by recent defeats in Florida, Wyoming, Minnesota and Tennessee, among others.
Any further losses would add to questions over whether Republican voters remain as willing to take his direction when Trump himself is not on the ballot.

sources.text:
UPDATED, 8/26/26 | Recently-appointed U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won a chance Tuesday to run for a six-year term in November after a rough-and-tumble primary runoff with U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman for the spot to replace her brother on the GOP ballot.
The Associated Press called the race for Graham two hours after the polls closed Tuesday. By the time all of the state’s 2,311 precincts reported, Graham had a 4.9% lead – 18,069 more votes than Norman out of more than 370,000 ballots cast. Interestingly, turnout in the special primary runoff was slightly higher than the 335,000 people who voted in the special primary two weeks ago, Winthrop University political scientist Scott Huffmon noted.
An emotional Graham told supporters Tuesday night that recent weeks have been challenging for her family, referring to the unexpected July 11 death of her brother, U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, and her whirlwind new role as U.S. senator and candidate.
“But you know what? We did it,” she said, also thanking President Donald Trump for his key endorsement and the relationship he and her brother had, according to the Associated Press.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
In November, Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews of Charleston and some third-party candidates in a state where the legislature is overwhelmingly controlled by Republicans.
Andrews immediately called for Graham to participate in three televised debates.
“Republicans nominated a candidate who was appointed to this seat because of her last name and elevated by Donald Trump’s endorsement and political machine,” Andrews said in a statement. “But no appointment, endorsement, or family connection entitles anyone to six years in the United States Senate. This seat belongs to the people of South Carolina.”
Huffmon reminded, however, that Republicans have a 10-point advantage over Democrats in a generic S.C. race.
“If Graham can stick to talking points, not give Dr. Andrews any ammo with gaffes and refuse to be baited into fighting with Andrews where Andrews has the high ground, Graham just has to play defense,” Huffmon told the Charleston City Paper.
Battle for the soul of the GOP
A South Carolina map of results shows a clear schism between Republican runoff voters highlighted in Norman’s commanding leads across the Upstate.
But Graham won the rest of the state – in the Midlands, Lowcountry and Grand Strand, where President Donald Trump on Friday publicly rallied Republicans to vote for her.
In Horry County, for example, Graham trounced Norman with 26,459 votes to Norman’s 9,618 – a 3-1 margin. She also tallied victories in Charleston County, where she got 56% of the vote, Berkeley County (64%), Dorchester County (66%), Richland County (60%) and Aiken County (62%).
Norman had a dominating Upstate showing in Greenville and Spartanburg counties in the 4th congressional district. He tallied two-thirds of votes, but the number of votes told the real story. Some 74,000 voters in those two counties picked Norman – one of every five votes statewide. The number of votes cast in those two counties was slightly more than in Horry, Charleston and Beaufort combined. Norman also had convincing wins in his 5th congressional district around York County and in the Upstate’s nearby 3rd district, which includes Graham’s home county, Oconee.
Norman, who placed third in June in a broad Republican gubernatorial primary, thanked supporters Tuesday night, but criticized outside PAC money and questioned the involvement of the president in the race.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman told supporters, later adding, “It is what it is and we accept it.”
In the days ahead of the race, pundits frequently mentioned how the Tuesday vote would be a test of Trump’s power to back winning candidates. But while some say the power of his endorsement has been shaky lately, it wasn’t in South Carolina.
It also didn’t hurt that MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans, “infused nearly $830,000 into Graham’s campaign for voter calls and text message blasts” on Monday.
Lindsey Graham died July 11. Two days later, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed his sister, a political unknown, to fill his seat until January. Some were uncertain she would run for a full six-year term, but she did with Trump’s strong backing. He said her interim appointment was a “fabulous tribute” to her brother and urged her to run in the special primary. He even endorsed her before she made her candidacy official, the AP reported.
But uncertainty about her candidacy rose after a recent televised debate with Norman in which Graham fumbled a foreign policy question about Taiwan. She admitted that “national security is not my thing” – a stark contrast to her hawkish brother who was in Ukraine the day before he died of a tear to his aorta.
Nevertheless, on Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump made a simple request to South Carolina voters: “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he said. “Just come and vote. It’s so important.”
A majority of GOP runoff voters did just that.

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — Cynthia Womble was all smiles as she left Beach Church, 577 George Bishop Parkway, after voting in the Senate runoff election Tuesday between Sen. Darline Graham and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman.
"It's always exciting to be a part of history," said Womble, who said she voted for Graham. "We are helping shape the future of our country."
Womble was one of 36,077 people who turned out to vote in Tuesday’s runoff election in Horry County. Graham won 26,459 of those votes, or 73%.
Her performance in Horry County was even stronger than that of her late brother, Lindsey Graham, who won 68% of the county’s vote in June.
Graham also swept all 125 precincts that were open across Horry County on Tuesday.
Graham won Tuesday's statewide runoff with 193,360 votes or 52.4% of the votes cast in South Carolina.
Graham will face Democrat nominee Dr. Annie Andrews in November's midterm election for the Senate seat.
Graham gathered support in Horry County on Friday after U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed her at an event in Myrtle Beach that drew thousands.
"I went to that and was so excited that she might get another six years in Washington," Myrtle Beach resident Shelia Kostreiwa said Tuesday afternoon after leaving Tuesday afternoon from the polling station at the Myrtle Beach Fire Station No. 5 at 79th Avenue. "Washington could use someone like her."
Graham was sworn in as South Carolina’s first female United States senator on July 14 after Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fulfill the remainder of her brother’s fourth term following his unexpected death days earlier.
Norman is a long-time member of the U.S. House of Representatives and is a member of the House Freedom Caucus. Norman ran for governor earlier this year, but failed to make it to the runoff race alongside fellow Republican Rep. Nancy Mace, who endorsed him for Senate. Former governor Mark Sanford also endorsed Norman.
In contrast, U.S. Congressional hopeful Jenny Honeycutt, U S. Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming), U.S. Senator Tim Scott (R-S.C.), and U.S. Rep. Russell Fry also supported Graham during Friday's event in Myrtle Beach.
"It's drawn a lot of attention," said Phillip Armstrong, election clerk at the polling station at Beach Church. "It's been pretty steady all day and has definitely been a strong turnout for a special election like this."
Armstrong, a retired educator, thanked each of the voters that came to the location Tuesday and invited them back to vote in the midterm elections in November.
"That's when it gets really crazy," Armstrong said of the polling station at the church. "There will be a line out of the door and circling around the building.
"And that's just the midterm elections," he said. "During a presidential election, it can be about a three-hour wait in this precinct."
Rita Conner, election clerk at the polling station at Grace Christian Fellowship on Highway 57 North in Little River, said her site also had higher than anticipated traffic for a special runoff election.
"We are a smaller precinct, but it's been going well," Conner said early Tuesday afternoon. "It's been really steady ... we are really pleased with the turnout so far."
Les Hunkele, the election clerk at Myrtle Beach Fire Station No. 5, said he "wasn't really surprised" with the high turnout Tuesday.
"Personally, if there is 10 people on the ballot, it gets confusing," Hunkele said. "If there is only two people on the ballot, I think people come in with a more informed decision."
The fire station also had accommodations for handicapped voters, offering an option for curbside voting during the day.
"We actually had our first curbside voter about 7:15 a.m. today," Hunkele said. "We don't get a lot of curbside voters, but it's important to the people that need it.
"Their vote counts just as much and we are happy to help them cast it," he said.
Ring said the Horry County Voter Registration and Elections Office was grateful to both the election workers and the voters who participated in Tuesday's election.
"It really does take a village to pull something like this off," she said.
North Myrtle Beach resident Evelyn Hurley said she was just happy to be a part of the Democratic process on Tuesday.
"I was raised to believe that every vote counts," Hurley said. "And people that don't vote have no business complaining about it after the elections."

sources.text:
South Carolina Republicans have chosen U.S. Sen. Darline Graham to defend her late brother’s Senate seat, rewarding President Donald Trump’s handpicked candidate days after she admitted that national security was “not my thing.”
Decision Desk HQ projected Graham the winner of Tuesday’s runoff against U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman at 8:38 p.m. EDT. With roughly 90 percent of the expected vote reported at 9:05 p.m., Graham led 52.4 percent to 47.6 percent.
She will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and clinical researcher, on November 3. The winner will begin a six-year term in January.
Related: Lindsey Graham’s sister Darline, a current U.S. senator, admits national security is ‘not my thing’
Graham entered the race with no legislative experience. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to complete Lindsey Graham’s term after he died from an aortic dissection in July. Before her appointment, she led the South Carolina Commission for the Blind.
Trump urged her to seek a full term, campaigned with her in Myrtle Beach and held a telephone rally Monday. His MAGA Inc. super PAC spent more than $827,000 supporting her in the closing days, the Associated Press reports.
But Graham’s inexperience became unavoidable during her only debate with Norman. Asked last Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea matter to American national security, the sitting senator could not explain how a consequential potential conflict would unfold.
Related: Trump wildly claims hospitals are performing ‘reverse surgery’ on trans patients ’at my order'
“I’m just going to be honest here,” she said. “I’m not that informed on national security.” “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise,” she continued. “But I do support the military.”
Graham also claimed South Carolina had 50 million residents. It has approximately 5.5 million. When she tried to recover on national TV after the poor performance, Graham pivoted from her own lack of preparation to transgender athletes.
“Of course, Taiwan is our friend,” she told Fox News. “But I think people in South Carolina are more worried about making ends meet. They are concerned about boys in girls’ sports.”
At a campaign event with Graham, Trump claimed that "at my order" transgender people were now receiving "reverse surgery." That is not happening.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Wins SC GOP Senate Runoff for Brother’s Seat
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham won Tuesday’s South Carolina special Republican Senate primary runoff, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman and moving closer to securing a full term in the seat once held by her late brother.
Graham (R-SC), who entered the race with President Trump’s endorsement and encouragement after the shocking death of longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham last month, led Norman (R-SC) 53% to 47% in the Palmetto State runoff with more than three-quarters of ballots counted.
Her runoff victory followed a crowded Aug. 11 special GOP Senate primary, where she finished ahead of Norman and several other Republican contenders, including former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC), businessman Mark Lynch and others.
Fry, who drew about 20% of the vote and placed third in the first round of voting, moved quickly to endorse Graham after ending his own Senate campaign.
Graham, 62, also benefited from a powerful lineup of Republican support, including endorsements from Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) and South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, along with more than $800,000 in backing from the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc.
“We have known each other for a long time — She is a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on the eve of the runoff.
The president also praised her late brother, saying, “Lindsey was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known, and his sister shares his deep love of our Country, and the State of South Carolina.” He added that “there is nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother.”
Trump had pressed South Carolina Republicans to turn out for Graham in the final stretch of the campaign, telling supporters at a packed Myrtle Beach rally last week to “pretend” he was on the ballot and warning they would “lose everything” if she failed to win the Senate race.
During the primary race, Graham differentiated herself from her brother by highlighting her interest on domestic issues, including affordability, immigration, gun rights, election integrity and opposition to DEI.
“I loved my brother Lindsey, and I miss him so much every day. But on illegal immigration, I’m tougher than he was,” she said at the Myrtle Beach rally. “It’s simple. If you are here illegally, you got to go.”
Graham, a political newcomer, had never held elected public office prior to being tapped to step in for her late brother, who died from an aortic dissection on July 11.
On the campaign trail, she embraced being a Washington outsider.
“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at the rally with Trump.
“And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job,” she added.
Graham’s inexperience showed during a debate against Norman earlier this month, when she stumbled over a question about the relevance of Taiwan and the South China Sea to US national security.
“I’m not that informed on national security — so,” she replied. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
While Norman’s supporters seized on the apparent gaffe, Trump downplayed the effect the moment would have on the race.
“All she was is being honest. She’s very smart, and she was being honest,” Trump told reporters last week.
“I mean, she’s into the price of groceries, the price of food, the price of beef, and it’s not — it hasn’t been her thing, but she’s surrounded by very good people, and she said that she’s totally for the military,” the president added.
In contrast, Norman, a five-term congressman, declared foreign policy and national security to be one of his “top concerns,” along with reining in federal spending.
“I’m going to be a CHAMPION for fiscal conservatism in the Senate,” he wrote on X Tuesday. “Why? You can’t have military superiority WHEN YOU’RE BROKE!
“My opponent doesn’t get that, but I do!”
Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley and outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace were among the notable pols that backed Norman’s campaign.
Graham will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election.
South Carolina is a solidly red state and Graham will likely be heavily favored against the Democrat.

sources.news_title: Trump pick Darline Graham wins election despite struggling over Taiwan question
sources.text:
Trump pick Darline Graham wins election despite struggling over Taiwan question
The political newcomer wins Republican Senate nomination after failing to answer questions about South China Sea issues
According to results released on Tuesday at 9pm, Graham won 52.4 per cent of the vote, defeating Representative Ralph Norman in the run-off and will advance to the November election.
South Carolina is a Republican stronghold, and whoever wins the Republican nomination is widely expected to win in November. Graham and Norman advanced from an earlier August primary in which neither candidate won more than 50 per cent of the vote, forcing Tuesday’s run-off.
The campaign was not without geopolitical drama. During last week’s debate, Graham was asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the United States. She appeared unprepared for the topic, first asking the moderator to repeat the question, then acknowledging that she was not an expert on national security.
“I am not that informed on national security,” she said, after a pause. “But I do support the military.”
The moment drew widespread press and social media attention, with critics questioning whether she has the experience and qualifications to serve as a senator. It also highlighted a sharp contrast with her late brother, who spent decades building a reputation in Washington as a prominent foreign-policy hawk.
On the same debate stage, Norman gave a more detailed answer, calling Taiwan “a definite ally” and highlighting the island’s semiconductor industry. Norman has also been a strong Trump supporter.

Darline Graham Nordone has won the South Carolina Republican Senate runoff, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman by 53-47 percent and giving President Donald Trump a huge win on Tuesday. The race was called by Decision Desk and NBC News.
