sources.news_title: Trump Picks Name Over Qualifications as Darline Graham Wins South Carolina Senate Runoff
sources.text:
President Trump threw his full weight behind Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate runoff. He held the rally. He spent the PAC money. He told voters to pretend he was on the ballot. And in doing so he passed over a proven, battle-tested conservative for a political novice whose biggest credential is her last name.
The race has been called and Graham came out victorious.
Ralph Norman was the better choice. Full stop. The five-term congressman and House Freedom Caucus member has spent years fighting the spending machine in Washington, owning a business, and delivering consistent conservative votes. Darline Graham, appointed to finish her late brother’s term after Lindsey Graham’s sudden death in July, has been a senator for roughly six weeks. She has no legislative record of consequence.
When asked in the only debate whether Taiwan and the South China Sea constitute national security issues for the United States, she answered with stunning candor: “I’m not that informed on national security… National security is not my thing.”
That is not a gaffe. That is a disqualifier. The United States Senate is not a training ground. It is the body that confirms generals, funds the military, and debates whether American blood and treasure get committed overseas. Lindsey Graham spent decades immersed in those questions and used this knowledge to advance his NeoCon priorities for the Military Industrial Complex.
His sister openly admitted she has not. Even fellow NeoCon Nikki Haley, who backed Norman, put it plainly: this is not something you inherit.
Trump’s loyalty to Lindsey Graham is understandable on a personal level. The late senator was a reliable ally on many fronts. But personal loyalty is not a governing philosophy. South Carolina Republicans deserved a senator who already knows the difference between a strategic strait and a talking point. Instead they got a candidate who leaned hard on the family brand, the governor’s appointment, and the president’s endorsement while offering little more than assurances that she would “finish what he was doing.”
Norman has flaws. He endorsed Haley over Trump in 2024, which likely contributed to Trump not backing him. Yet his voting record and fiscal conservatism remain far more consistent with the America First agenda than a blank slate whose campaign spent more time explaining away inexperience than demonstrating readiness.
He has actually legislated. He has actually fought the swamp from the inside. Graham’s defenders call her lack of political polish a virtue. Voters should have called it a risk.
The race became a test of whether a famous surname and a presidential endorsement can paper over a thin resume. Trump poured more personal effort into this contest than he has into several tighter midterm fights. His super PAC dropped more than $800,000 in the final stretch. Tim Scott and Henry McMaster fell in line. The machinery worked hard to deliver the result the president wanted.
Yet the underlying problem remains. Conservatives have spent years demanding competence and backbone from their elected officials. Elevating someone who admits national security is “not my thing” undercuts that demand.
Norman may not have been the purest MAGA vessel, but he was the more qualified conservative. Qualifications still matter. Experience still matters. Knowing the difference between Taiwan and a state agency still matters.
As it is written, “He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.”
South Carolina deserved a senator who already met that standard rather than one still learning the job on the public’s dime. Trump’s endorsement of Darline Graham put loyalty ahead of that standard. Ralph Norman was the stronger conservative choice. The party will live with the consequences either way.
None of this changes my appreciation of and loyalty to President Trump and the MAGA movement. I just wish he’d made a better choice in this race.
Two Storms, One Harvest
Every food crisis in living memory has been a one-shock event. The 2008 price spike was a commodity bubble. The 2020 shortages were a logistics failure. The 2022 grain scare was a war on one exporter’s ports. Each time, the system bent, adjusted, and recovered, and each time the experts assured us afterward that global markets are simply too big and too diversified to fail.
What nobody in Washington seems eager to discuss is that 2026 is shaping up to be something the modern food system has never actually faced. Two independent shocks, one climatic and one geopolitical, are converging on the same harvest cycle at the same time. Not sequentially. Simultaneously.
Start with the weather. The Pacific Ocean is currently building toward what forecasters now openly call a record event. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center puts the odds of at least a strong El Niño near 88 percent, with roughly two in three odds it reaches “very strong” status, the tier reserved for perhaps three or four events in the entire satellite era. Every major global model now projects a median peak in Super El Niño territory, and most of them project it exceeding the 2015-16 event, which until now held the modern record. Sea surface anomalies were already brushing the super threshold in mid-July, months before these events normally peak. The atmosphere has already shifted into El Niño mode, and the event is forecast to crest in late fall and early winter.
This is not about “climate change.” It’s about the standard cycles of weather, and the cycle we’re currently in is one that has likely devastated societies in the past. We’re better prepared as a society today, but not all Americans are equally prepared.
Serious households have started doing the quiet math on their own. Grocery bills tell part of the story, and the forecast maps tell the rest, which is why long-term food storage has moved from fringe hobby to mainstream line item in the family budget, with established suppliers like Heaven’s Harvest seeing demand from people who five years ago would have rolled their eyes at the idea. That instinct is not paranoia. It is pattern recognition, and the pattern is worth walking through carefully.
Editor’s Note: Heaven’s Harvest IS a sponsor, but the warnings of this article are real and would be written even if we didn’t have a survival food sponsor. With that said, those who take advantage of what they offer can use promo code “Patriot” for 15% off.
The Fertilizer Clock Is Already Running
While the Pacific warms, the second shock has been unfolding in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict with Iran turned the world’s most important energy chokepoint into a contested waterway, and the consequences reach far beyond the gas pump. Roughly a third of global fertilizer trade moves through Hormuz, and the disruption sent urea prices up 86 percent year over year by March, with a 53 percent jump in a single month.
The World Bank projects energy prices rising about 24 percent in 2026 and fertilizer about 31 percent. By its own accounting, fertilizer prices ran 35 percent higher in the first five months of this year than the same period last year.
Here is the mechanism the nightly news will not explain. Fertilizer is not a grocery item. It is a time-delayed input. The nitrogen a farmer in Iowa or Punjab could not afford to apply this spring does not show up as a problem this spring. It shows up as a thinner harvest six to twelve months later.
The World Bank’s own food security brief concedes that the effects of reduced applications earlier this season “are likely to become visible only later in harvest outcomes.” Translate that from institutional language into plain English and it means this. The damage is already done, it is already in the ground, and we are simply waiting for it to arrive on the shelf.
Now check the calendar. Six to twelve months from the spring planting season lands us squarely in late 2026 and early 2027. Which is precisely when the strongest El Niño in the instrumental record is forecast to peak, bringing its signature droughts to Southeast Asia, Australia, southern Africa, northern Brazil, and South Asia, the very regions that grow the world’s rice, sugar, and oilseeds.
The World Bank warns openly that a strong El Niño “could disrupt multiple crop belts simultaneously” on top of the conflict-driven input costs. Their baseline projection assumes the Middle East disruptions ease by autumn. What in the last two years of Middle East history suggests that assumption is safe?
The System Has No Slack Left
The comfortable answer is that global markets always adjust. But adjustment requires slack, and the slack is gone. Global cereal production is expected to decline from last year’s records even before El Niño does its work. The UN World Food Programme, hardly a den of right-wing preppers, is calling this the most significant disruption to its supply chains since Covid and the invasion of Ukraine, and its supply chain director put the stakes bluntly.
Today’s supply chain challenges are tomorrow’s hunger crisis.
There is also a political dimension that markets cannot price. When food gets scarce, governments do not behave like economists. They behave like politicians. Export bans, hoarding mandates, and panic buying at the national level turned the modest rice shortfall of 2008 into a global crisis, and analysts are already warning that import-dependent nations are the first dominoes.
The 2015-16 Super El Niño, a far weaker event than what is now forecast, threw tens of millions into food stress across Africa and Asia. This one is projected to be stronger, and it arrives with fertilizer already rationed by price and shipping lanes already contested by missiles.
What Joseph Knew
Scripture does not treat preparation for lean years as faithlessness. It treats it as wisdom delivered in advance to those willing to act on it.
Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt.
Joseph did not respond to that warning with a hashtag or a committee. He stored grain during the years of abundance, and when the famine came, Egypt stood while its neighbors begged. The lesson is not that famine is certain. It is that the time to prepare is precisely when preparation still looks optional.
Nobody who filled a pantry in a year of plenty has ever regretted it, and nobody standing in an empty aisle has ever been glad he waited for certainty.
None of this calls for panic, and panic is the enemy of sound judgment anyway. It calls for the same unglamorous prudence our grandparents considered ordinary. Keep some cash margin, know your local growers, and put real food in deep storage while it is cheap and available, because the entire arc of this story is that cheap and available is a closing window.
Families looking for a straightforward place to start can visit Heaven’s Harvest and use promo code Patriot for 15 percent off long-term storable food. The forecasts may yet soften, the strait may yet reopen, and we should pray they do. But hope is a fine thing to hold and a foolish thing to eat.

sources.news_title: Election 2026: Graham clips Norman for Republican U.S. Senate ticket
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – U.S. Sen. Darline Graham will have the place of her brother Lindsey on the Nov. 3 ballot, having defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s U.S. Senate special Republican primary runoff on Tuesday.
The race was called about 2 hours and 15 minutes after polls closed. Graham defeated Norman 52.5%-47.6% with 100% of precincts reporting the 12.2% turnout (369,014 votes). Dr. Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician, is the Democratic opponent in November and is joined on the ballot by Libertarian Kasie Whitener.
The special election became necessary when Lindsey Graham died July 11. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to fulfill the remainder of the term in the 119th Congress that ends on the first of January, and she decided to seek the six-year term by succeeding her brother on the Nov. 3 ballot.
From a crowded field, and after a failed run for governor in the June primary, Norman emerged second to Graham in the special primary two weeks ago. Without achieving 50% plus one of the votes, a runoff was necessary.
Graham, within hours of her brother’s death, carried the support of second-term Republican President Donald Trump. The eve of the runoff included an injection of voter calls and text message blasts valued at $830,000, paid for by the MAGA Inc. super PAC supporting the president and aligned with Republicans.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” Graham said of Trump in her victory speech.
Norman said he respected the president’s “prerogative” to inject his presence in the race, though his comments indicated he did not like it. He said he does like the policies of the 80-year-old whose mercurial domination of party direction has run roughshod over those who cross him since he bullied through a 17-candiate field in the 2016 presidential cycle a decade ago – Lindsey Graham among them.
“I really hate it for the state,” Norman said. “I don’t hate it for me. I hate it for the state. But the public of South Carolina made the decision.
“I never understood why he got in this race.”
Darline Graham took a debate punch on foreign policy tied to national security. She later said as she traveled the state, not a single voter asked her about Taiwan and the South China Sea. They did ask, she said, about rising costs in healthcare and day to day affordability.
In addition to Trump, she had the backing of Republican South Carolina U.S. Sen Tim Scott and Republican South Carolina U.S. Rep. Russell Fry.
Norman, a leading fiscal hawk in the House of Representatives from the 5th Congressional District, had endorsements of Florida Sen. Rick Scott and Utah Sen. Mike Lee. Usually with Trump, he broke in 2024 to support former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley’s bid for president.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” Graham said. “But I know he’s looking down right now very proud of everyone in this room.”
Turnout Tuesday was about 23,000 better than two weeks earlier for the crowded primary. In June, the state’s regular election cycle primary drew about 465,000 voters.
Graham won 34 of 46 counties. And whereas Fry won eight counties in the Pee Dee two weeks ago, Graham won them all backed by Fry’s endorsement and Trump’s visit to Myrtle Beach on Friday.
Norman won Oconee and Abbeville counties that had been won by Graham on Aug. 11.
This Senate seat is one of 33 in regular rotation for the 2026 midterms nationwide, and there are also two special elections. Majority control rests with Republicans at 53 seats, and contests in North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Michigan, Maine, Iowa, New Hampshire, Alaska, Texas and Montana figure to determine if Trump's agenda the next two years will stall in the chamber.
Graham will be heavily favored against Andrews. There hasn’t been a Democrat from the state in the U.S. Senate since Sen. Fritz Holdings retired in 1998.
Republicans have also dominated statewide offices for more than a decade. And they've done so in legislative districts.
Today's state Senate is 34-12 Republican majority, and the House of Representatives is 88-36 Republican majority. Republicans have had majorities for seven four-year cycles in the Senate, dating to 2000, and 16 two-year cycles in the House, dating to 1994.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina Republican primary runoff for U.S. Senate
sources.text:
Darline Graham, sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, won the Republican primary runoff in South Carolina for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, according to U.S. media projections, in a triumph for President Donald Trump.
Graham, who was appointed to hold the Senate seat until the beginning of January following her brother’s death on July 11, defeated Representative Ralph Norman and will run in November’s election for a full, six-year Senate term.
Trump endorsed her candidacy and backed that up with large campaign contributions from his MAGA INC super PAC. Rallying for her on Friday in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, Trump placed the spotlight on himself and proclaimed, “I am on the ballot.” Graham, 62, will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the general election and is expected to prevail easily in the deeply conservative state.
This primary was one of a series of tests of Trump’s sway with voters in this year’s midterm elections, as he tries to use his bully pulpit to prevent Democrats from wresting control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate from his Republican party. But his record of endorsements this cycle has been mixed, with polls showing he continues to be weighed down by rising consumer prices and an unpopular war with Iran.
Trump’s MAGA INC., spent $827,711 in support of Graham, according to its filing on Monday with the Federal Election Commission, in a rare instance of the president putting financial support behind his favoured candidate.
For her part, Graham used Friday’s rally to try to recover from what has been cast as an earlier debate misstep when she said she was not knowledgeable about national security issues – the kind that helped define her brother’s career in the Senate.
“Guilty as charged,” Graham proclaimed at the rally. Instead, she focused her remarks on domestic issues, including Trump’s immigration clampdown and anti-abortion advocacy.
She had never held public office until her appointment to the Senate, having previously held positions advocating for persons with physical disabilities.
South Carolina has overwhelmingly embraced Trump in all three of his runs for president and is not likely to play a role in the battle for the control of Congress. Norman, 73, a long-time real estate developer, has spent nearly a decade in the U.S. House. His defeat on Tuesday comes on the heels of an unsuccessful bid for governor. He has been a leading member of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus, but endorsed the more moderate Nikki Haley, a former governor of South Carolina, in her 2024 failed presidential bid.
Earlier this month, Graham and Norman were the two top vote-getters in the Republican primary’s 10-candidate field, but neither garnered enough support to avoid Tuesday’s runoff.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Wins GOP Runoff for Late Brother's S.C. Senate Seat
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham won South Carolina's Republican U.S. Senate runoff Tuesday, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman after President Donald Trump mounted a late push to help the political newcomer secure the GOP nomination for a full six-year term.
Graham's victory, coming a month after she was appointed to fill the remainder of the term of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, preserved Trump's perfect record in U.S. Senate Republican primaries this year. Trump-endorsed Senate candidates had won or advanced in every primary contest entering Tuesday's runoff.
Newsmax and Decision Desk HQ called the race for Darline Graham more than 90 minutes after polls closed. With 69% of the vote counted, she had 52.5% to 47.5% for Norman.
Darline Graham will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a Charleston physician, in November. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.
Darline Graham, 62, entered the two-week runoff as the favorite after finishing first in the Aug. 11 special Republican primary with about 33% of the vote. Norman, a five-term congressman and member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, finished second with about 25%.
Neither received the majority required to win the nomination outright.
Trump endorsed Darline Graham before she formally entered the race and intensified his support in the closing days, traveling to Myrtle Beach on Friday to campaign with her and holding a tele-rally Monday.
"I want it to happen," Trump told supporters at Friday's rally. "Good luck, Darline."
MAGA Inc., the super PAC aligned with Trump, also spent nearly $830,000 on calls and text messages supporting Darline Graham in the final days.
She overcame questions about her political experience, particularly after stumbling during the candidates' only runoff debate when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were national security interests for the United States.
"National security is not my thing," Darline Graham said. "I'm not that informed on national security."
Norman seized on the remarks to argue she was not prepared for the Senate.
"This isn't a 'get training on the job.' You can't do that," Norman said during the debate.
Darline Graham countered by emphasizing her three decades in state government and focusing her campaign on domestic concerns, including healthcare costs and affordability.
Norman, 73, sought to make the race a choice between Darline Graham's backing from Trump and his own record as an experienced conservative lawmaker. He received support from former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley; former Sen. Jim DeMint; Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla.; and Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Turning Point Action.

Trump-backed Darline Graham wins South Carolina Senate runoff
sources.text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.
Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham's sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."
Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Beats Back Ralph ‘Marshall Law’ Norman To Clench Senate Nom
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) in Tuesday’s South Carolina runoff, securing the Republican nomination for the state’s Senate seat — which had been occupied by her brother, late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), until earlier this summer.
With some 91% of the votes counted, per the AP, Graham had 52% to Norman’s 48%.
Graham will run in the general election against Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician.
Graham was tapped for the role by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) after her longtime senator brother passed away unexpectedly last month. Shortly after she started her temporary role — to finish her brother’s current term — Graham announced she was running to keep the seat for the next six years.
Graham got President Donald Trump’s endorsement for her campaign. Trump had also recommended McMaster appoint the late senator’s sister to serve the remainder of his term.
Graham was able to defeat the five-term congressman despite a recent hiccup on the debate stage that highlighted her lack of experience as an elected official.
“I’m just going to be honest here,” Graham said in response to a question about the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests during a debate against Norman. “I’m not that informed on national security so — But I do support the military.”
Norman tried to take advantage of that debate moment, calling out Graham for her lack of understanding in foreign policy and seeking to align himself with the MAGA movement’s resistance to “forever wars.”
“South Carolina deserves a Senator who UNDERSTANDS Foreign Policy,” Norman said on social media. “I’m a PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH supporter! No more forever wars!”
This is the second big loss Norman took this year.
Before his bid for the Senate, Norman ran to be the Palmetto State’s governor. He lost that bid, finishing third in the gubernatorial primary over the summer.
Norman has represented South Carolina’s 5th congressional district since 2017. Norman started out on Capitol Hill after winning a special election to replace former Rep. Mick Mulvaney (R-SC), who vacated his House seat after Trump appointed him to be the director of the Office of Management and Budget during his first term.
A member of the House Freedom Caucus, Norman holds a strict anti-abortion and a pro-Second Amendment voting record. He opposes federal gun control and universal background check legislation. Norman also consistently votes against debt ceiling increases and large spending bills.
Most notably, as TPM reported, he urged White House chief of staff Mark Meadows to invoke the “Marshall Law!!” just days before Joe Biden’s inauguration in 2021.
Despite his publicly MAGA loyalist persona, Norman and Trump have had a tumultuous relationship.
Norman initially endorsed former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary. And it is no secret that Trump holds grudges against those in the Republican Party who at one point or another questioned his dominance.
Norman has also been vocal about his opposition to “endless wars” amid Trump’s war on Iran.
When will they ever learn?

sources.news_title: Darline Graham Secures the Nomination for Senate Despite Late Campaign Gaffes
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman for the Republican nomination for Senate in South Carolina, a victory that was also one for President Donald Trump, who pushed for her to stay on in the seat held recently by her late brother.
The Associated Press called the race at 9:02 p.m. Tuesday for Graham, whom Trump endorsed, campaigned for and backed with an $800,0000 last-minute effort from MAGA Inc. to turn out her voters.
“We got the vote out where we needed to,” senior Trump political adviser James Blair told NOTUS. “Great win for the President and for Darline.”
Norman had initially sought the South Carolina governorship and later bid for the open Senate seat, leaving South Carolina’s 5th Congressional District with an open race. The congressman is known for being adversarial at times to both House Republican leaders and Trump; Norman endorsing former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential election and routinely criticizes his party’s agenda in Congress.
Trending
Graham’s win bolsters Trump’s influence ahead of the midterms, despite several candidates losing their primaries while carrying his endorsement.
Graham was appointed, at the president’s urging, to fill the remaining months of her brother Lindsey Graham’s term after his sudden death in July. Trump had touted her candidacy as a way to “honor the legacy of her beloved brother.”
Though there was little public polling ahead of the special election due to the tight timeline, a Trafalgar Group poll of the race released late Monday found the two candidates deadlocked at 48% each with a 2.9% margin of error. Some Republicans began to view a Graham victory as increasingly unlikely, NOTUS reported, after some campaign missteps.
In a televised debate on Aug. 18, Graham said she was “not that informed on national security” — a statement that stands in sharp contrast to her late brother’s deep investment and hawkish positions on foreign policy. The blunder was quickly picked up by Norman, who billed himself as an experienced “true conservative” while casting Graham as a candidate propped up by “left-wing Democrats.”
Trump traveled to South Carolina on Friday to stump for for Graham, urging voters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.” When asked about her awkward answer in the debate, Trump told reporters, “All she was is being honest.”.
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s Senate term and officially endorsed her for the full term ahead of the runoff election.
Lindsey Graham’s passing left Republicans scrambling to find a replacement because the late, four-term senator had already won the primary for his seat in June. The Republican field quickly expanded to 10 candidates — including Graham, Norman, Rep. Russell Fry, businessman Mark Lynch and Mark Sanford, the former congressman and governor.
The most prominent candidates knocked out in the primary split their endorsements, with Fry backing Graham and Sanford and Lynch throwing their support behind Norman.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November in the general election for the Senate seat, which is rated “Solid R” by the Cook Political Report.

sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC) won her South Carolina Senate primary campaign against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC), officially winning a full term in the seat once held by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC).
During the campaign she was endorsed by President Donald Trump, who she vowed to staunchly support in a full Senate term throughout the campaign.
She overcome harsh criticisms: Graham was often accused of overreaching due to her complete lack of previous political experience. That inexperience was highlighted during her debate against Norman when she admitted that she did not know anything about America's relationship with its close ally, Taiwan. The United States has repeatedly pledged to protect Taiwan if it is invaded by China, which claims the nation to be part of its own territory.
After being asked about Taiwan during the debate with Norman, Graham admitted "national security is not my thing" and "I'm not that informed on national security."
She also said that, because of her brother's extensive experience in handling foreign policy, she felt comfortable discussing domestic issues like affordability. By contrast, Norman described Taiwan as "a definite ally" and claimed Trump was "enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China."
Speaking to the Associated Press, Norman — who often criticizes Trump, although he generally supports the president's agenda — had more detailed foreign policy problems with his fellow Republican.
"(Trump) did a great job of taking out the nuclear threat that we had for 40 years. … but there’s still a lot of work to be done," Norman told the AP. "The American people do not understand the Strait of Hormuz not being completely controlled by America. That’s what I hear. And gas prices, as a result, are staying high. And I think one of the worst things the president wants is the public to turn on him because he’s not ending it."

sources.news_title: South Carolina Republicans Nominate Darline Graham, As Trump Told Them To
sources.text:
WASHINGTON ― South Carolina Republicans did as they were told by President Donald Trump on Tuesday and voted to make Lindsey Graham’s younger sister their nominee to replace him in the U.S. Senate after his sudden death last month.
Darline Graham, who had never publicly evinced a desire to run for public office prior to being asked by Trump to run for her brother’s seat, defeated congressman Ralph Norman in the runoff election. She will now face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November and, given the state’s recent political history, is likely to win.
“I think Trump making this a referendum on himself meant that MAGA voters in key places turned out and voted for the candidate he endorsed,” said Scott Huffmon, a political scientist and pollster at South Carolina’s Winthrop University. “Given Trump‘s recent losses in primary endorsements, that was not a sure thing when polls opened this morning.”
The race had divided the world of Trump’s followers and supporters, with a considerable number breaking with Trump and backing Norman. The American Conservative Union, for example, which stages the various “Conservative Political Action Conferences” in the United States and abroad, and which in recent years has essentially become a propaganda arm for Trump, backed Norman over Graham.
To counter this, Trump expended considerable time and effort to ensure that steadfast ally Lindsey Graham’s vote was replaced by someone who owed her political career entirely to him.
While most Trump GOP primary “endorsements” ― which in the majority of cases are for incumbents without serious opposition or candidates with clear polling leads ― involve little more than a post or two on Trump’s personal social media platform, he pulled out all the stops to back Graham.
He staged a rally for her on Friday in Myrtle Beach, one of the most conservative regions of the state and where the hometown congressman, Russell Fry, had done the best in the Aug. 11 primary. Trump persuaded Fry, who is now seeking reelection to his House seat, to endorse Graham, and Trump followed up Friday’s trip to the state with a “tele-rally” ― in which he phones in to a gathering of the candidate’s supporters ― on Monday evening.
Those efforts appear to have paid off. Graham won handily in counties within Fry’s congressional district in the northeast part of the state. In Myrtle Beach’s Horry County, where she won 35% compared to Fry’s 42 and Norman’s 8 in the Aug. 11 primary, Graham was leading Norman 73-27 with 75% of the vote counted.
“Horry turned out significantly for Graham,” Huffmon said. “They could have stayed home after their original choice of congressman Fry lost, but they decided to heed Trump‘s call and vote as if he were on the ballot.”
Tuesday’s runoff was necessary because South Carolina is among the southern states that retain a Jim Crow-era requirement that a candidate must secure an outright majority to win, a rule originally created to prevent Black people from winning public office.
Trump’s public backing of Darline Graham failed to clear the field for her, and she wound up with nine opponents on Aug. 11. She won just under a third of the ballots cast, while Norman received 25%.
Lindsey Graham, who was 71, died on July 11 of a tear in his aorta, a consequence of long-term arterial sclerosis. Darline Graham, who is nine years younger, was appointed by Trump ally and South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster on July 13 following Trump’s urging to fill the remaining five months of the term, and took office the following day.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP Senate runoff
Darline Graham wins GOP nomination for next US Senate term following her brother's death • SC Daily Gazette
sources.text:
Darline Graham wins GOP nomination for next US Senate term following her brother’s death
After all votes were counted, Graham won with 52.5%, a 5 percentage-point margin, according to unofficial election results
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham thanks supporters at her election night watch party Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after being declared the winner of the special GOP runoff. On stage to her right are Gov. Henry McMaster and first lady Peggy McMaster. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
COLUMBIA — Voters elected Darline Graham to take her late brother’s place on November ballots, as the full backing of President Donald Trump helped overcome criticism of her political inexperience.
When The Associated Press called the GOP runoff election at 9:01 p.m., Graham had 52% of the vote over U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, with 89% of votes counted.
Graham’s win ensures the first elected female U.S. senator from South Carolina will be sworn into office in January. Sworn in exactly six weeks ago as the appointed senator, Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election.
The 62-year-old younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham led the 10-candidate primary two weeks ago with 33% to Norman’s 25%. But a runoff win was far from guaranteed. Some polling showed Norman ahead hours before precincts opened.
“We did everything we could do,” Norman, 73, said to a round of applause from supporters at his election watch party in Rock Hill.
He didn’t have a concession speech, since he didn’t expect to lose, he told the crowd. “But I accept it and I will forever be grateful for each one of y’all who supported us.”
Graham, who took the stage later in Columbia, said she had mixed emotions, including grief and “immense gratitude.”
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” she said. “But I know he’s looking down right now and he’s proud.”
Losing her brother was a tragedy for the entire state, Graham said.
“But tonight, you know what? We stand back up, the way South Carolinians have done and look forward to the future,” she said. “South Carolina was founded by fighters, and we are fighters.”
Trump, who urged Darline Graham to seek the next six-year term, pitched her candidacy as a tribute to her brother, his best friend: Lindsey Graham died suddenly July 11 in Washington, D.C., of a ruptured aorta, one month after trouncing five GOP opponents on his way to a fifth term.
“She’s the perfect person to carry on the legacy of her brother,” Trump told people who called in to a tele-rally Monday night. He congratulated her by phone Tuesday night before she walked on stage.
His all-in endorsement included traveling to ruby red Myrtle Beach, where he told thousands of supporters Friday to pretend his name is on the ballot. Voting for Graham, he said, is voting for someone who “fully supports the Trump agenda.”
He recognized he would take the credit or blame.
“I asked her to do it. I got her into this whole thing,” he said Monday night. “I have to make sure she gets in because there will be nobody better.”
In a state where Trump won every time he was actually on the ballot, the runoff results were expected to reflect his strength or waning influence. In November 2024, Trump won South Carolina by 18 percentage points. When Trump got behind Graham’s candidacy pre-filing, political commentators outside South Carolina assumed that made her a shoo-in.
But Trump’s surprise pick of a political novice caused many South Carolina voters to rebel. Graham was expected to be the honorary placeholder — an appointment that gave no one the benefit of incumbency in South Carolina’s first open Senate race in 22 years — not the handpicked successor.
Norman attempted to turn that into an advantage. The support and money lining up behind Graham “shows the elite establishment has already picked their candidate. Same ol’ playbook. Same ol’ insiders. I’m not their choice,” he said in an ad.
Following an unsuccessful campaign for governor when he sought the outsider label — repeatedly saying he’s not a career politician — Norman juxtaposed his record over more than two decades in elected office against Graham’s first-time candidacy. He’s the proven conservative, he argued: “You know how I’m going to vote.”
Graham embraced her status as unskilled at being a politician.
“They say I’m not a politician. I say guilty as charged,” she repeated Monday night.
Norman, first elected to the state House in 2004, has won two previous special elections, including the 2017 race that sent him to Congress. He opted to seek the governor’s office this year instead of re-election to the U.S. House but placed third in the June GOP primary.
She used that against him.
“He’s run for office 14 times, always chasing the next office. To me, this is just desperation,” Graham told callers Monday. “I am not a career politician.”
She pointed to 30 years of experience in state government, to include the last seven leading the state Commission for the Blind. And she emphasized her humble roots in relating to Americans’ economic struggles, saying that, like her brother, a childhood growing up in the back of their parents’ restaurant and pool hall also instilled a hard work ethic.
“Whatever it was that made Lindsey strong has made her strong,” Gov. Henry McMaster said during a campaign event with her Monday. The perspective she gained in her roles helping people with disabilities is also a strength, he added.
McMaster, who appointed her last month for the term ending in January, endorsed her for the full term on Friday, just before the Trump rally.
He called Graham the better candidate for keeping the Senate seat red.
Norman was the more polarizing candidate. A member of the hardline Freedom Caucus in the U.S. House, he ran for governor as the ticket furthest to the right on the political spectrum. His pick as a running mate was former Rep. Adam Morgan, founding chair of the affiliate caucus Norman helped launch in the state House in 2022, which has feuded with the majority GOP caucus ever since.
“Keep this in mind: There is another election after this one,” McMaster said. “We’ve got to win this election in order to win that election in November.”
Norman supporters
For David and Ann Casey of Rock Hill, their votes for Norman came down to time spent in office. They also wanted someone who could push back against Trump.
“Darline’s a great person, but my vote was more for experience,” said Ann Casey, a 63-year-old dental hygienist, after voting at a church off Interstate 77 in Rock Hill.
“I had concern about Darline being a ‘yes’ person to the Trump administration,” added David Casey, a 64-year-old financial advisor. “(Norman’s) capable of hitting the ground running, and he’s not going to be told what to do.”
Graham’s non-response to a question about Taiwan during the only runoff debate sunk her for some voters.
Matthew Gusmer, a farmer in western York County, supported Norman in the governor’s race and in Senate GOP primary two weeks ago but was on the fence about whether to continue supporting him in the runoff — that is, until Graham’s performance in the Aug. 18 debate in Newberry.
“Probably the number one thing that swayed me was in the debate the other night with her comment about foreign policy,” he said.
Asked whether Taiwan is a national security issue for the United States, Graham blanked, eventually acknowledging she’s not informed on the issue.
“I’m just going to be honest up here,” she said. “I’m not a polished politician. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
“That really just kind of floored me,” Gusmer said. “With everything going on between Russia, Iran, every front, it just really turned me off.”
As a farmer, Gusmer said foreign policy and the impact it can have on things such as prices at the pump, fertilizer, and seed, as well as the cost of land in fast-growing South Carolina, are major issues and he wants a candidate who is well-informed.
Voters for Graham
But for Graham’s supporters, her lack of political experience was a plus.
“I like the fact that she’s not a politician,” said Tommy Wood, a 66-year-old engineer from Irmo. “She’s not seeking the job, so she’s willing to serve, where all the opponents are wanting the job.”
Graham kept the same staff as her brother, which brings their institutional knowledge, Wood said. He and his wife, Phyllis Wood, were longtime supporters of Lindsey Graham.
“That’s invaluable,” Tommy Wood said of his staffers committing to her.
When the Woods watched Graham flub the answer on Taiwan during the GOP debate, they felt bad for her, but their opinions never swayed, they said.
“She was nervous and blindsided, and it didn’t look good,” said Tommy Wood. But, as he heard someone else say, “I don’t care if she knows the difference between Taiwan and Timmonsville,” a tiny town in Florence County.
The couple noted that Norman ran for Senate only after losing the nomination for governor. If he wanted to be a senator, he should have made that his primary goal, they said.
“I didn’t like that,” said Phyllis Wood. “Not cool,” Tommy Wood added.
Sandra and John Jackson, of West Columbia, felt her support for South Carolina is more important than her opinions on foreign policy.
“She’s going to keep South Carolina at the forefront of her mission in Washington, D.C.,” said Sandra Jackson, a 69-year-old retired flight attendant.
What Graham lacks in political experience, she makes up for in life experience, the Jacksons said.
“She’s a mother, and she’s run the Commission for the Blind,” Sandra Jackson said. “She has experience.”
“Anybody who runs for office for the first time doesn’t have any experience,” added 78-year-old John Jackson.
Jessica Holdman contributed to this report from Rock Hill, and Skylar Laird contributed from Columbia.
- 10:35 pmThis article has been updated with comments by Ralph Norman and Darline Graham after she was declared the winner.

sources.news_title: Trump-endorsed Darline Graham beats back Norman in South Carolina Senate GOP runoff
Graham Nordone wins South Carolina Senate runoff
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham Nordone (R-SC) won South Carolina’s Republican Senate special primary runoff Tuesday, defeating Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) and moving one step closer to securing a full term in the seat previously held by her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.
With 89% of the vote counted, Graham Nordone had 52.3% of the vote compared with Norman’s 47.7%, according to the Associated Press.
Recommended Stories
Graham Nordone’s victory caps an unusual and abbreviated campaign that began after Lindsey Graham died unexpectedly in July, leaving Republicans scrambling to replace the longtime senator both in Washington and on the November ballot.
Gov. Henry McMaster (R-SC) appointed Graham Nordone to temporarily fill her brother’s seat just days after his death. President Donald Trump then encouraged her to seek a full six-year term and quickly endorsed her bid.
Graham Nordone, who had never previously held elected office, emerged from a crowded 10-candidate Republican primary earlier this month as the top vote-getter. She received roughly 33% of the vote, while Norman finished second with about 25%, sending the two Republicans to a runoff after neither received the majority required to win outright.
The race quickly became another test of Trump’s influence over Republican primary voters. Norman, a five-term congressman who recently finished third in the GOP gubernatorial primary, sought to make the case that his years in elected office and conservative record made him better prepared for the Senate. Graham Nordone, meanwhile, leaned into her status as a political outsider while highlighting Trump’s support and her family’s long ties to South Carolina politics.
Trump traveled to Myrtle Beach in the closing days of the runoff to campaign alongside Graham Nordone, standing by his endorsed candidate after a debate performance that raised fresh questions about her lack of political experience.
During the debate, Graham Nordone acknowledged that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked about Taiwan and the South China Sea. The comment quickly drew criticism from Norman and other Republicans, including former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who backed Norman.
Trump defended Graham Nordone following the debate, praising her for being candid about what she did not know and reiterating his support for her campaign during his South Carolina rally. The president’s intervention came as Republicans divided over which candidate should succeed Lindsey Graham.
Graham Nordone picked up endorsements from several prominent Republicans, including Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) and Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC), who finished behind Norman in the initial primary. Norman, meanwhile, secured the backing of former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, who cited Norman’s focus on federal spending and the national debt in announcing his support.
Graham Nordone will now face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November. The Republican nominee will enter the general election as the favorite in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in decades. Lindsey Graham won reelection in 2020 by roughly 10 percentage points, while Trump carried South Carolina by an even wider margin in 2024.
For Graham Nordone, Tuesday’s result also represents a rapid political ascent. Before entering the Senate last month, she spent much of her career working in disability services and most recently led the South Carolina Commission for the Blind.
GRAHAM NORDONE LEANS ON TRUMP TO RESCUE SENATE BID AFTER DEBATE GAFFE
Her relationship with her brother has also been central to the unusual circumstances surrounding the race. After their parents died when the siblings were young, Lindsey Graham became his younger sister’s legal guardian and later adopted her so she could receive military benefits.
Graham Nordone has sought to honor her brother’s legacy while also drawing distinctions between the two, particularly by emphasizing domestic concerns such as affordability rather than the foreign policy issues that became a defining feature of Lindsey Graham’s Senate career.

sources.text:
Darline Graham wins South Carolina’s GOP Senate primary runoff election for brother’s seat
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman Tuesday in the South Carolina special Republican Senate primary runoff election, moving one step closer to holding on to her late brother’s seat in the upper chamber for a full term.
Graham (R-SC), who was endorsed and encouraged by President Trump to run for Lindsay Graham’s seat following the longtime senator’s shocking death last month, topped Norman (R-SC) 52-48% in the Palmetto State primary runoff, with more than 95% of the ballots counted.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” Graham said in her victory speech.
Fighting back tears at times, she described the “mixed emotions” she endured on election night and since her brother’s passing.
“I’m still feeling grief, heartache and immense gratitude,” she said.
“During the past several weeks, I’ve been amazed at the number of people Lindsay personally impacted and the legacy he left behind,” Graham continued. “Our state and nation are much better and safer because of him.
“Thank you, Lindsay, for your service to South Carolina and to this country. It’s just not the same without you here.”
She previously bested Norman and several other contenders, including former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R), Rep. Russell Fry (R-SC), businessman Mark Lynch, and more, in the initial Aug. 11 special GOP Senate primary.
Fry, who received about 20% and placed third in the initial primary, quickly endorsed Graham after losing his Senate bid.
Graham, 62, also secured key endorsements from Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) and South Carolina Republican Gov. Henry McMaster and more than $800,000 in financial support from pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc.
“We have known each other for a long time — She is a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot,” Trump said of Graham in a Truth Social post on the eve of the runoff.
“Lindsey was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known, and his sister shares his deep love of our Country, and the State of South Carolina,” the president continued, adding that “there is nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother.”
Trump urged South Carolinians to get out and vote for Graham last week, telling his supporters at a packed Myrtle Beach rally to “pretend” he’s on the ballot and warning that they’ll “lose everything” if she doesn’t win her Senate race.
During the primary race, Graham differentiated herself from her brother by highlighting her interest on domestic issues, including affordability, immigration, gun rights, election integrity and opposition to DEI.
“I loved my brother Lindsey, and I miss him so much every day. But on illegal immigration, I’m tougher than he was,” she said at the Myrtle Beach rally. “It’s simple. If you are here illegally, you got to go.”
Graham, a political newcomer, had never held elected public office prior to being tapped to step in for her late brother, who died from an aortic dissection on July 11.
On the campaign trail, she embraced being a Washington outsider.
“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at the rally with Trump. 
“And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job,” she added.
Graham’s inexperience showed during a debate against Norman earlier this month, when she stumbled over a question about the relevance of Taiwan and the South China Sea to US national security.
“I’m not that informed on national security — so,” she replied. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
While Norman’s supporters seized on the apparent gaffe, Trump downplayed the effect the moment would have on the race.
“All she was is being honest. She’s very smart, and she was being honest,” Trump told reporters last week.
“I mean, she’s into the price of groceries, the price of food, the price of beef, and it’s not — it hasn’t been her thing, but she’s surrounded by very good people, and she said that she’s totally for the military,” the president added.
In contrast, Norman, a five-term congressman, declared foreign policy and national security to be one of his “top concerns,” along with reining in federal spending.
“I’m going to be a CHAMPION for fiscal conservatism in the Senate,” he wrote on X Tuesday. “Why? You can’t have military superiority WHEN YOU’RE BROKE!
“My opponent doesn’t get that, but I do!”
Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley and outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace were among the notable pols that backed Norman’s campaign.
Graham will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election.
South Carolina is a solidly red state and Graham will likely be heavily favored against the Democrat.
It was a good primary night for Trump, as another of his endorsed candidates, Mike Mazzei, won the GOP primary runoff for governor in Oklahoma.
Mazzei, a former state senator, beat Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond by less than a percentage point, or about 2,000 votes, in the contest.
Trump excoriated Drummond in a Truth Social post last week, accusing the AG of being a “fake Republican” over donations made to former President Joe Biden and the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, as well as for filing a lawsuit to block an aluminum plant project backed by the president.
The Drummond campaign has said the Biden and Lincoln Project donations were mistakenly made by the attorney general’s wife under the Gentner Drummond name.
Mazzei will face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the November election to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt.

Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham defeated Republican South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s GOP Senate primary runoff race, according to The Associated Press.
Graham and Norman advanced to Tuesday’s primary runoff because neither garnered a majority of the vote during the August 11 special primary. They defeated eight other candidates, including Republican South Carolina Rep. Russell Fry.
Republican South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to replace her brother, former Republican South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, who passed away on July 11. (RELATED: Will South Carolina Enter A Post-Graham Era)
President Donald Trump endorsed Graham and encouraged her to serve a full term. Graham held a tele-rally with Trump Monday, saying that because he “got her into this whole thing, I have to make sure she gets in.”
Trump held an in-person rally for Graham in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on Friday.
Graham failed to answer Newsmax host Greta Van Susteren’s question about China’s threat to Taiwan and the South China Sea during an Aug. 18 debate.
“Senator, are Taiwan and the South China Sea national security issues for the United States? If so, why?” Van Susteren asked.
“I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham said. “So … But I do support the military,” Graham replied.
Q: Are Taiwan and the South China Sea national security issues for the United States?
Sen. Darline Graham: I'm just going to be honest here… I'm not that informed on national security. pic.twitter.com/bJsCjqb7VT
Graham raised over $346,000 between July 23 and Aug. 5, according to the Federal Elections Commission (FEC). MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC, spent over $827,000 on text messages and voter phone calls to support Graham.
Norman received endorsements from Republican Florida Sen. Rick Scott, Republican South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace, Republican Utah Sen. Mike Lee, former Republican South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford and the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC). Former Republican Virginia Rep. Bob Good endorsed Norman in a Tuesday X post, urging South Carolina voters to “reject birthright senatorship.”
Trump-endorsed candidates tend to be successful in their primaries, although former Republican Florida congressional candidate Catalina Lauf lost to businessman Jim Schwartzel in an Aug. 18 primary despite Trump’s endorsement.
Many South Carolina Republicans were caught off guard when Graham entered the race. South Carolina Freedom Conference Chairman Jordan Pace told the Daily Caller that the party did not support her serving for a full term.
Republican South Carolina state Rep. Jay Kilmartin said many grassroots Republicans were frustrated with Graham’s policies and governing style.
Graham’s late brother was known for being a war hawk and a supporter of U.S. involvement in wars. He called for the assassination of Russian President Vladimir Putin when the Russia-Ukraine war broke out, supported the Iran war and said billions of dollars being sent to Ukraine were the “the best money [the U.S. has] ever spent,” in a May 2023 statement.

sources.news_title: Sen. Darline Graham wins the Republican Senate primary runoff in South Carolina
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Republican primary runoff, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump, who recruited, endorsed and campaigned for her following her brother Lindsey Graham’s death six weeks ago.
With nearly all of the vote tallied, Graham was leading Norman roughly 52% to 48%.
At her election night party in Columbia, Graham paid tribute to her late brother and credited Trump for getting her across the finish line.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart. But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room,” she told her supporters.
“Mr. president, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country,” Graham continued. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
An hour north in Rock Hill, Norman said he had not prepared a concession speech and lamented Trump’s involvement, though he said he accepted the results and planned to call Graham.
“I really hate it for the state. I don’t hate it for me. ... I hate it for the state. But the public of South Carolina made the decision,” Norman told his supporters. As for Trump’s involvement, Norman said, “He has that right. That’s his prerogative,” adding that “his policies are good.”
But Norman added, “I never understood why he got in this race. ... But it is, it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”
Trump had gone all in for Graham, who decided to run for a full six-year term after she was appointed to the seat by Gov. Henry McMaster. The president held an in-person rally for her Friday in Myrtle Beach and a tele-rally Monday evening, and his allied super PAC made a late $830,000 push to boost her.
During the Friday rally, Trump recounted how he asked her to run “because everyone loves her, everyone respects her.” He also said he’s supporting her to “honor Lindsey,” who had been one of his closest allies in Washington.
“She only knows how to put America first,” Trump told the crowd. “You vote for her, you’re going to be very proud of that vote.”
Graham, 62, will now face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election, and is the heavy favorite in the deep-red state where her brother served in the Senate and House for more than 30 years.
To beat Norman, who’s spent nearly a decade in Congress, Graham had to overcome GOP attacks of nepotism and inexperience. She had never held or run for elected office before, though she did lead a 130-person state agency that helped blind people. In the initial primary earlier this month, Graham finished first with 33% of the vote, short of the 50% needed to avoid a runoff.
And the final week of the truncated, two-week runoff campaign was dominated by Graham’s blunder at a debate with Norman where she replied that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were important national security priorities.
“National security is not my thing,” she said.
It was a particularly notable moment given that her senator brother had served more than three decades in the Air Force and was one of the leading voices on national security on Capitol Hill.
Darline Graham said that she would be more focused as a senator on domestic policy issues, such as affordability.
“Her brother was very much about the world. … That’s good, that’s fine. But she’s more about affordability,” Trump said about the Graham siblings, who have both talked about their humble beginnings being raised in a single room next to their family’s bar and pool hall.
In the closing days of the campaign, she touted herself as someone who would continue her brother’s legacy and also be a reliable vote for Trump. In one ad, she noted she was the lead sponsor of a tough Russia sanctions bill that was renamed for her brother, and she highlighted her vote to confirm Todd Blanche, Trump’s nominee for attorney general.
Graham’s victory caps a tumultuous six-week stretch in South Carolina Republican politics. Fresh from a trip to Ukraine, Lindsey Graham died the night of July 11 from what doctors preliminarily said was a tear in the aorta due to the hardening of the arteries.
Three days later, Darline Graham was sworn in to serve out the rest of his term. Despite her appointment and Trump’s endorsement, the primary to replace her brother attracted a crowded field of candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry, former Gov. Mark Sanford and wealthy self-funding businessman Mark Lynch.
Norman first irritated Trump when he became the only House Republican to endorse former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary race.
Since then, he’s been a constant thorn in Trump’s side. Last year, Norman, a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, clashed with Trump and GOP leaders by initially opposing the president’s landmark tax-and-spending cuts package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” But he eventually voted yes after successfully negotiating to speed up work requirements for Medicaid recipients and the elimination of Biden-era wind and solar tax credits.
The runoff was a rare race that divided conservatives.
While Darline Graham had Trump, McMaster and Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., in her corner, Norman secured endorsements from former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, who now lives in the state; Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., his onetime rival for governor; former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, who had run in the special Senate primary race; and former Sen. Jim DeMint, R-S.C., who previously led the Heritage Foundation.
As expected, Norman performed well in the upstate areas in and around his congressional district. Graham, meanwhile, bested Norman in populous areas along the coast and around the capital city of Columbia.
Trump’s visit to South Carolina and Fry’s endorsement seem to have boosted her in Horry County, where the Myrtle Beach rally was held.
In the initial GOP primary two weeks ago, Fry won the county with nearly 14,000 votes. But in the Tuesday runoff, Graham crushed Norman there, winning more than 26,000 votes to his nearly 10,000.

Interim U.S. Senator Darline Graham has secured the Republican nomination for a full six-year term after defeating U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in a tightly contested runoff election on Tuesday night.
The contest followed the death of her brother, longtime Senator Lindsey Graham, on July 11. Governor Henry McMaster appointed her on July 13 to complete the remainder of the term, which runs through early January 2027. She announced her candidacy for a full six-year term shortly afterward with the backing of president Donald Trump.

Other candidates included U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, who took roughly 20 percent, and former Governor Mark Sanford. Because no candidate reached a majority, South Carolina law required a runoff.
As votes were tallied on runoff night, incomplete returns showed Graham holding a lead in the low-to-mid 50 percent range, with Norman trailing in the mid-to-high 40s. Outstanding votes, including remaining precincts and any late-counted ballots, continued to favor Graham. Norman underperformed relative to benchmarks based on his strength in the Upstate region and his congressional district during the first round of voting.

sources.news_title: Graham wins GOP nod in South Carolina Senate primary runoff for late brother’s seat
South Carolina Votes to Replace Lindsey Graham in GOP Senate Runoff
sources.text:
South Carolina Republicans delivered their verdict Tuesday night, choosing Darline Graham over Rep. Ralph Norman in a Republican Senate primary runoff that was as much a referendum on Donald Trump's grip on his party as it was on the candidates themselves. With nearly all votes tallied, Graham led Norman 52.3% to 47.7% — a margin that was comfortable enough to be decisive but narrow enough to reflect genuine unease among a significant portion of the Republican electorate about what, exactly, they were voting for.
The result was a significant win for Trump, who had made the race one of his biggest bets of the midterm primary cycle. He flew to Myrtle Beach on August 21 for a get-out-the-vote rally — one of his first major campaign stops of the 2026 midterms — and his super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent more than $827,000 on Graham's behalf. At the rally, Trump framed the race in personal terms: "I'm doing this to honor Lindsey. That's why I'm here. So, Darline, we got to win that race."
They got it. The question now is what winning it actually means.
At her election night party in Columbia, Graham paid tribute to her late brother and credited the president directly. "I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart," she told supporters. "But I know he's looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room." She then turned to the endorsement that made the night possible: "Mr. President, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you've done for our country."
An hour north, in Rock Hill, Norman did not go quietly. "I did not prepare a concession speech," he told his supporters. "I really hate it for the state. I don't hate it for me. I hate it for the state." On Trump's involvement, he was pointed: "He has that right. That's his prerogative. His policies are good. I never understood why he got in this race."
The contest was triggered by the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham on July 11 — a loss that sent South Carolina's Republican establishment into a whirlwind of political activity. Governor Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to fill the seat on an interim basis, and she was sworn in July 14, becoming a United States senator with no prior elected experience. She entered the August 11 ten-way primary as a relative unknown and emerged as the top vote-getter, with Trump's swift endorsement providing critical early momentum.
Norman, 72, finished second in the August 11 primary. A Freedom Caucus member who has represented South Carolina's Fifth Congressional District since 2017, he built a record as one of the chamber's most reliably conservative members and drew on that record to make an explicit electability argument: that the state needs an effective Senate advocate during a consequential period, and that a legislator seasoned by years of floor fights in Washington is better positioned to deliver than a political newcomer appointed by circumstance.
He was not without allies. Former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows and former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley — whose alliance with Norman predates this race — both endorsed him, and groups aligned with Haley spent several hundred thousand dollars on his behalf. It was not enough. Norman's estrangement from Trump, which dates to February 2023 when he became the first House Republican to endorse Haley's presidential campaign, proved a liability that institutional conservative backing could not overcome.
Graham's campaign ran on a different argument entirely — that the values her brother represented, and the relationships he built during his nearly three decades in the Senate, gave her a unique foundation from which to serve. She did not try to obscure her inexperience; she tried to reframe it. "Probably the biggest thing that sets me apart is they're politicians and I'm not," she said at a campaign stop in West Columbia. The line was effective. It was also, given the seat she is now positioned to hold, worth examining closely.
The two-week runoff campaign surfaced vulnerabilities that will follow Graham into November and beyond. During a debate last week, she said she does not know much about national security — a statement that brought a fresh round of questioning about her qualifications to replace one of Washington's most prominent foreign-policy voices. Her campaign's answer was to lean into the critique, invoking Trump's own outsider trajectory. "President Trump has never served in elected office before and I think he's done a damn good job," she told the Myrtle Beach crowd.
The anti-politician framing is a well-worn playbook in the Trump era, and it worked. But the seat she won carries specific demands that generic outsider credibility does not address. Lindsey Graham's committee positions, seniority and political networks were built over 23 years of negotiating in the Senate's corridors of power, and will not transfer to his sister. Republican leaders will decide her committee assignments, leaving her to establish her own standing in Washington from scratch.
That gap is not merely procedural. Lindsey Graham served on the Armed Services Committee for the entirety of his Senate career and was one of the chamber's most influential voices on military posture and the use of force abroad. His death came at a moment when the United States is simultaneously managing an active economic and military confrontation with Iran, a grinding war in Ukraine, and a fraught Korean Peninsula — the kind of multi-front environment in which seniority and institutional relationships determine whether a senator's voice carries weight in closed-door negotiations or gets politely noted and set aside.
Analysts have expressed no doubt that Darline Graham would be reliably pro-Israel, as her brother was. But matching Lindsey Graham's level of foreign policy activity, they have warned, would be a formidable task — and her campaign has largely avoided discussion of international affairs entirely.
South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since Fritz Hollings in 1998. Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in November — a general election that will be watched nationally but almost certainly won by the Republican regardless of the margin. The first woman to represent South Carolina in the United States Senate will in all likelihood remain in that seat for a full six-year term.
What Tuesday settled, then, is not whether Darline Graham goes to Washington. It is how she got there — and what that journey says about the Republican Party's current calculus. Norman ran explicitly on experience, on the argument that a Senate seat during an active multi-front conflict requires more than a famous name and an outsider's appeal. South Carolina's Republican primary electorate disagreed, or decided that Trump's judgment outweighed Norman's argument.
Whether a Senate built on institutional knowledge and long-term relationships can accommodate someone who arrived in Washington six weeks ago and openly acknowledges she has much to learn will take considerably longer to answer than one evening's vote count.
