sources.news_title: Results roll in as Darline Graham, Ralph Norman face off to replace Sen. Lindsey Graham on South Carolina Senate ballot
sources.text:
Results roll in as Darline Graham, Ralph Norman face off to replace Sen. Lindsey Graham on South Carolina Senate ballot
South Carolina Republicans will decide Tuesday who will replace Sen. Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November's midterm election, after a rushed campaign in the wake of his sudden death in July.
Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham, faced Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday's runoff election, with polls closing at 7 p.m. local time. The two candidates were the top two vote-getters in the special primary election on Aug. 11. Darline Graham was appointed to serve out the remainder of her late brother's term, which ends early next year. Lindsey Graham had been running for his fifth term when he died and had just won the Republican primary in June.
Darline Graham, who has no prior experience in elected office, has focused on domestic issues during the abbreviated campaign, which has drawn support from President Trump. Going into Tuesday's runoff, her lack of preparedness in foreign policy has raised some questions about her candidacy for the full term.
In a debate last week, she stumbled on a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea. Graham said she's "not that informed on national security," unlike her late brother, an outspoken foreign policy hawk.
"I'm not a polished politician," Graham said. "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."
Asked at a news conference whether she'd taken a closer look at the issue of Taiwan and the Indo-Pacific since the debate, she told reporters she had traveled around the state to talk with as many voters as she could.
"You know how many of them brought up Taiwan or national security? Not one," she said, adding that they were talking about "the rising cost of health care and affordability, so that's what's important to me."
But when CBS News' Ed O'Keefe later asked Graham whether she planned to bring up a specific proposal or legislation on those issues, she offered no plan, responding that we'll deal with that "when I get there." Graham, however, is already in the Senate and has been serving for about six weeks.
The winner of Tuesday's runoff will take on Dr. Annie Andrews, who won the Democratic primary in June. Although the South Carolina Senate race is usually a fundraising boon to Democrats, the state remains solidly Republican and has just one Democratic representative in Congress.
Mr. Trump, who had been close to Lindsey Graham, has thrown his support behind Darline Graham. He campaigned for her in South Carolina last week and held a tele-rally for her on Monday. And the Trump super PAC MAGA Inc surged $827,000 into her campaign for text messages and phone calls on her behalf, according to Federal Election Commission records. Until Darline Graham's Senate bid, MAGA Inc had spent only about $18,000 in 2026 on a midterm race. The super PAC spent about $1.7 million last year and by the end of the second quarter, it had raised $401 million.
Darline Graham has also garnered the support of South Carolina's other senator, GOP Sen. Tim Scott, who said after her first few weeks in the Senate and her first-place finish in the primary that he's "confident she's the real deal."
The newly minted senator has billed herself as "a problem solver, a critical thinker, and a leader," with decades of experience working for South Carolina. Darline Graham, 62, most recently served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind. Graham had a close relationship with her brother, who never married or had children.
She's cited their upbringing, where she and her brother observed their parents working long hours at their bar and liquor store in central South Carolina, for their shared work ethic.
And as she's pledged to carry out her brother's legacy, she's also emphasized that she would chart her own path in the Senate, which could be more conservative than her brother's. During last week's debate, she quickly made her views on transgender athletes in sports, abortion and gun rights known.
Meanwhile, Norman, who has represented South Carolina in the House since 2017, has presented himself as an experienced legislator with a track record as a conservative fighter, while calling Graham an "unknown candidate."
The real estate developer and longtime member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus was one of a handful of Republicans to jump into the special primary race despite the president's endorsement of Darline Graham. And for Norman, who was one of only two House Republicans to back former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in her bid to challenge Mr. Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024, it wasn't the first time he's been willing to break with the president.
Norman, 73, has the backing of Haley, who also served as ambassador to the U.N. during the first Trump administration, and called out Darline Graham's lack of experience after her debate performance.
"Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States' national security. Darline Graham admits she's not," Haley said on X. "This is not something you inherit. And it's critical in the U.S. Senate."

sources.news_title: Darline Graham, Ralph Norman battle to replace Lindsey Graham on ballot in South Carolina runoff
Trump's sway is tested as Graham, Norman compete in South Carolina special GOP Senate primary
sources.text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother on South Carolina’s general election ballot, notching another win for President Donald Trump after he threw his support behind the political novice.
Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after Lindsey Graham's sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly won an endorsement from Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham got emotional while addressing her supporters Tuesday night, saying she misses her brother every day.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said.
With McMaster, her family and U.S. Rep. William Timmons looking on, Graham went on to thank the president for his support and for the relationship he had with her brother.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you and we are truly grateful,” she said.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump’s picks in this year’s midterms — spent nearly $830,000 for voter calls and text message blasts in support of Graham.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump’s backing would be enough to boost the political newcomer with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unidentified, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Norman thanked his supporters at his Tuesday night watch party but decried Graham taking outside PAC money, and Trump for supporting her.
“I never understood why he got in this race,” Norman said. “It is what it is and we accept it.”
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."
Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.
Collins reported from Rock Hill, South Carolina.
Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

sources.news_title: Trump support propels Darline Graham to victory in South Carolina runoff
sources.text:
Trump support propels Darline Graham to victory in South Carolina runoff
President’s chosen candidate also prevails in Oklahoma gubernatorial run-off
South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham on Tuesday capitalized on the strong support of President Donald Trump to win the Republican primary runoff to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, on the November ballot.
With more than 95 percent of votes in, Darline Graham was leading Rep. Ralph Norman, 52 percent to 48 percent, The Associated Press reported.
Trump picked up another win Tuesday in Oklahoma, where his preferred candidate for governor, former state Sen. Mike Mazzei, narrowly prevailed in a Republican runoff against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
In South Carolina, the president was behind Graham every step of the way. She was initially appointed to fill the remainder of her brother’s term following his unexpected death from an aortic tear in July. She then announced she would seek a full six-year term after Trump encouraged her to run in the special election.
“Mr. President, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends,” Graham said during her victory speech, addressing Trump directly. “I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country. Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful.”
After she made it through the initial round of voting two weeks ago, Trump doubled down in his support: He hosted a rally for her in Myrtle Beach on Friday, opened the purse strings of his super PAC and encouraged other South Carolina Republicans — including Rep. Russell Fry, who finished third in the first round of balloting — to back her.
At the Myrtle Beach rally, Trump urged Republicans to turn out for Graham in a state he carried easily in three presidential elections: “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.”
Graham’s victory provides Trump with a key boost heading into November, when his sliding poll numbers could hurt the GOP’s efforts to maintain control of the House and the Senate. Trump’s endorsement, once viewed as a golden ticket to victory in Republican primaries, has lost some of its shine in recent months, with several Trump-backed candidates for House, Senate and governor falling short.
Norman, who has been in the House since 2017, is coming off an unsuccessful run for governor, in which he placed third in the June primary. A member of the hard-line House Freedom Caucus and a staunch conservative, he reflected Tuesday on Trump’s decision to support Graham.
“The president got involved. He has that right. That’s his prerogative,” the congressman told his supporters as a chorus of boos ran through the crowd. “His policies are good. I never understood why he got in this race. … But it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”
Graham, who led a state commission that provides services to blind people, stumbled during a recent debate, when she acknowledged that she was “not that informed on national security” matters. That was at odds with the legacy of her late brother, a well-known defense hawk who crisscrossed the globe to promote an interventionist foreign policy.
But Graham sought to deflect the criticism, presenting herself as a plainspoken everywoman who doesn’t “speak politician” and emphasized kitchen table issues over foreign affairs.
Fellow South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott, who also leads the National Republican Senatorial Committee, called his new colleague “the real deal.”
In her speech Tuesday night, Graham invoked her late brother, who became her legal guardian after their parents died.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” she said. “But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room.”
Graham enters the general election as the favorite against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades.
Not long after the runoff was called, Graham turned her attention to Andrews, calling her “the most radical liberal ever nominated for a statewide office by the South Carolina Democratic Party.”

sources.news_title: Darline Graham triumph in South Carolina reasserts Trump dominance over GOP, confounds critics
sources.text:
Darline Graham triumph in South Carolina reasserts Trump dominance over GOP, confounds critics
Graham notably won Horry County, which includes Myrtle Beach, by a wide margin, seemingly supporting the idea that Trump’s rally successfully whipped up support.
Sen. Darline Graham’s, R-S.C., victory in the South Carolina Republican Senate primary runoff on Tuesday was a pivotal victory for President Donald Trump that reaffirmed his kingmaker status within the party.
The president also scored a big win in a close race in Oklahoma, confounding critics who had celebrated a handful of rare primary losses the last few weeks.
Gov. Henry McMaster, R-S.C., appointed Graham to fill the seat of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., after he died unexpectedly last month. The move came with the support of the president, who quickly backed her for a full term even when she was polling with low numbers.
Graham then beat out South Carolina heavyweights to place first in the initial round of the special primary. After the campaign consolidated into a one-on-one race with Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Trump enthusiastically jumped into the contest with a Myrtle Beach rally on Graham’s behalf.
Former rivals split on whom to back in the runoff. While Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., backed Graham, former Rep. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., and candidate Mark Lynch broke for Norman.
In the leadup to the runoff, Graham appeared in trouble after she flubbed a debate question by admitting to knowing little about foreign policy, her brother’s signature issue. Ultimately, though, Trump’s endorsement and personal campaigning on her behalf, appeared to carry the day for Graham.
The Associated Press called the race for Graham at 9:01 p.m., at which time she led with roughly 53% of the vote to Norman’s 47%. Trump did not immediately react to Graham’s win, but did publish a graphic celebrating her victory as a Trump-endorsed candidate.
Whether Trump’s personal involvement was truly the deciding factor will be debated. Graham notably won Horry County, which includes Myrtle Beach, by a wide margin, seemingly supporting the idea that Trump’s rally successfully whipped up support.
But the contest represents a marked shift from how the Palmetto State reacted to the president’s endorsement in the gubernatorial race.
Trump backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, R-S.C., in the first round of the gubernatorial primary. Like with Graham, Evette placed first in that round. But unlike Graham, Evette failed to rally support from the voting bases of the eliminated candidates, most of whom rallied behind state Attorney General Alan Wilson.
The expectation of a lopsided win for Wilson prompted Trump to issue a rare double endorsement that saved his endorsement record. In the Senate race, he refrained from doing so and stuck by his choice of Graham.
The gubernatorial primary was followed by some rare defeats of Trump’s endorsed candidates, including in House races in Florida and Tennessee. Catalina Lauf, his pick to replace Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., lost out to businessman Jim Schwartzel.
This month alone, local media personality Ryan Elijah beat out the embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., while former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher knocked off Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn.
Perhaps the most embarrassing moment was the defeat of the Trump-backed Amir Hassan in his Michigan House race. Hassan lost to Thomas Smith, who suspended his campaign before Election Day.
Trump’s endorsement also failed to carry MyPillow founder Mike Lindell to the Minnesota GOP nomination for governor. The pillow monger and media mogul lost out to state Speaker of the House Lisa Demuth in that primary contest, despite his national profile and Trump’s endorsement.
But Graham’s win, at least, seems to have stopped some of the bleeding for Trump, and marked a single-cycle turnaround for a Republican-leaning state that previously bucked him. Whether he can ride that momentum to continue shaping party primaries in the coming weeks will be watched closely.
Trump scored another major victory Tuesday night in the race to succeed retiring Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt, as former state Sen. Mike Mazzei narrowly won the Republican nomination by defeating sitting state Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
Mazzei and Drummond advanced to a runoff in June and are seeking to replace Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt, who is restricted by term limits and cannot seek reelection. Mazzei will face Democrat Cyndi Munson in November in a state the GOP Kidd is heavily favored to win.
Ben Whedon is the Chief Political Correspondent at Just the News. Follow him on X.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Bet on Darline Graham Is No Sure Thing
sources.text:
Just six weeks ago, Darline Graham was known to politically tuned-in South Carolinians as the adored younger sister of veteran U.S. senator Lindsey Graham, holding down a low-profile if worthy state office as an advocate for services for the blind. Then Lindsey Graham suddenly died and Darline began occupying her brother’s Senate seat, initially as a caretaker but now as a candidate for a full term (Lindsey had recently won renomination for a fifth term). Despite quickly earning the backing of Donald Trump, Graham did not chase off opponents at all. But she did finish first in an August 11 special Republican primary, winning about a third of the vote against a large field that included two U.S. House members and a former governor. (Democrats had already chosen their November Senate candidate, pediatrician Annie Andrews.)
Now Graham is in a rare late-August runoff against one of those congressmen, Ralph Norman, a old-school hard-core conservative prominent in the House Freedom Caucus, in a contest that is also a test of the strength of Trump and his closest South Carolina allies (including that other U.S. senator, Tim Scott; two-term governor Henry McMaster, and the congressman who finished third in the primary, Russell Fry). Norman has won the backing of former senator Jim DeMint, former governors Nikki Haley and Mark Sanford, and out-of-state right-wingers Mike Lee and Rick Scott.
From the perspective of D.C. insiders and Norman fans, the runoff contest has been defined by a single moment in the candidates’ August 18 debate, as described by Politico:
Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are relevant national security priorities, Graham responded: “I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security, so.” She added that “national security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military. …”
Her response spread like wildfire on social media, with critics saying it proves she is “unprepared” to take office.
This take quickly spread throughout the Beltway echo chamber, where pundits expressed horror at Graham’s ignorance, which they treated as a virtual profanation of her brother’s memory. The reaction was also taken up, of course, by Norman’s partisans in South Carolina, such as Nikki Haley:
It’s worth noting that Norman endorsed Haley over Trump for president in 2024, which likely reinforced Trump’s decision to back Graham. And even as D.C. gabbers all but wrote off Graham as self-disqualified, the 47th president intervened personally in the runoff, holding a rally in her support in Myrtle Beach on August 21, along with Fry (who represents that city in Congress), Scott, and McMaster. Trump disparagers, noting his recently ragged record of endorsees losing a significant number of Republican primaries, have piled on to the Graham criticism, hoping she’d prove to be another presidential black eye (so far his candidates haven’t lost any Senate primaries, so this could be a first).
Is this realistic? The Bulwark’s Andrew Eggar is skeptical:
It’s Darline Graham’s contention that GOP voters don’t care about any of this. What they want their senators to be doing, she argues, is chasing a bunch of right-wing culture-war shibboleths: beating their heads against the wall of the DOA Save America Act, rabble-rousing about the elevenish male trans athletes a year who want to play in girls’ and women’s athletics. The Serious Men of the Senate flatter themselves that their job is more serious and important than this. But I suspect Darline might know what time it is better than they do.
It’s not easy to figure out what’s actually happening on the ground. There has been just one public poll of the runoff, from the Trafalgar Group, which shows the two candidates tied. Apparently internal candidate polls and the conventional wisdom suggest a close race. Prediction markets favor Graham, but not overwhelmingly. Figuring out the shape of the electorate is problematic, too: This is a rare late-summer standalone primary election in a place where it’s hot as blazes right now with kids adjusting to a new school year. About 10 percent of the state’s registered voters showed up for the August 11 primary; turnout on August 25 is likely to be lower. Will the bulk of voters be GOP ideologues favorable to Norman or MAGA folk willing to do whatever the boss tells them to do? Nobody is all that sure.
Team Graham has significantly outspent Team Norman, according to the Charleston Post and Courier:
A dizzying amount of money has been spent in the days since Graham and Norman advanced from the Aug. 11 primary to face one another in this month’s runoff. Most of it has been spent against Norman.
Of the total $3.2 million in advertisements booked for the final week of the campaign, Norman’s campaign was being outspent by Graham and her allied political action committees by a rate of two-to-one, adding to an already lopsided assault from his establishment-aligned opponent.
There has also been some visible advocacy-group skirmishing, most notably among anti-abortion militants. The big machers of anti-abortion politics, National Right to Life and Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, have endorsed Graham, while the more uncompromising Students for Life group has backed Norman (citing a campaign contribution Graham made to a Republican legislator who helped block a total abortion ban in the state).
In a low-turnout runoff, geography could also be a factor. Norman’s electoral base has been in the northwest and north-central parts of the state, which tend to generate heavy GOP voting. Graham lives in the Columbia suburbs, and she did best in the primaries in that Midlands region and in the southern coastal Low Country area. It’s no accident that Trump’s big rally was in Fry’s northern coastal base; his vote could be a crucial prize in the runoff.
Norman is a lame-duck member of the House after finishing third in the gubernatorial primary back in June; Graham’s interim Senate gig ends at year’s end too. So somebody’s political career — Norman’s stretches back to 2004, and Graham’s is spanking new — is going to take a turn for the worse on August 25, and returns are expected to tell the tale quickly.

S.C. Succession: Darline Graham Claims GOP Senate Nomination
sources.text:
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
by WILL FOLKS
***
Backed by U.S. president Donald Trump, endorsed by the National Republican Senate Committee (NRSC), propagandized by Fox News and bankrolled by millions of dollars in neoconservative dark money, interim U.S. senator Darline Graham Nordone stormed to a significantly stronger-than-expected victory over Freedom Caucus stalwart Ralph Norman in a special GOP runoff election for the U.S. Senate in South Carolina on Tuesday evening.
With her win, Nordone advances to face Democrat Annie Andrews, Libertarian Kasie Whitener, Constitution Party candidate Mark Hackett and several other independent candidates on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
The winner of that race will serve a full six-year term in Washington, D.C. beginning on January 3, 2027. Nordone has held the seat on an interim basis for the past month-and-a-half.
“I am deeply honored and humbled to accept your nomination as the Republican candidate for the United States Senate,” Nordone said. “Now, we turn our focus to November. Together, we will fight for our values, defend South Carolina, and keep America strong.”
***
South Carolina, I am deeply honored and humbled to accept your nomination as the Republican candidate for the United States Senate.
First and foremost, I thank the Lord for His blessings and guidance. To my family, President Trump, Team Graham, and the countless supporters… pic.twitter.com/R2nCBocrIf
***
According to the S.C. State Election Commission (SCVotes), with 99% of ballots counted, Nordone had received 193,396 votes (or 52.45% of ballots cast). Norman trailed with 175,327 votes (or 47.55% of all ballots cast).
That five percent spread was much larger than anyone projected. Even on the eve of the election, prominent (and pro-Trump) pollsters only had Nordone ahead by 0.1% – while the vast majority of internal campaign polls had Norman winning the race handily.
Norman acknowledged the surprising nature of Nordone’s victory when he told those assembled at his watch party that he hadn’t prepared a concession speech.
What else was larger than expected? The size of the electorate…
***
In South Carolina partisan primary elections, head-to-head runoff races – which occur when no candidate receives a simple majority of voters on the first ballot – typically have far fewer voters participating. In this case, though, voter turnout actually increased on the second ballot.
According to SCVotes, 369,014 ballots were cast on Tuesday – a participation rate of 12.23%. Two weeks ago, 335,693 GOP voters cast ballots (an 11.12% participation rate).
The GOP nomination for this seat was originally claimed by Nordone’s brother, the late Lindsey Graham, on June 9, 2026. Graham died suddenly a month later, though, triggering the special election to fill his spot on the ballot.
Two weeks ago, Nordone and Norman advanced out of a crowded GOP field to face each other in a head-to-head race that most believed Norman was well-positioned to win. The wealthy real estate developer stumbled badly out of the gate, though, firing most of his campaign staff and failing to counter a withering barrage of negative advertising launched at him by pro-Nordone political action committees.
Norman was massively outspent in the abbreviated contest, and Trump’s support was critical in swaying voters in the heavily MAGA seventh congressional district – where he kicked off his initial ‘First in the South’ presidential campaign a decade ago. Backed by Trump – and endorsed by her former rival, coastal congressman Russell Fry – Nordone won a staggering 73% of the vote in Horry County.
***
RELATED | A BACKROOM DEAL
***
Nordone won despite her late brother’s declining popularity, her embrace of discredited diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) propaganda, a lack of support from social conservatives and a debate gaffe that raised significant questions about her competence for the job.
Ultimately, GOP voters decided they didn’t care about any of that… and turned out in shockingly high numbers to back her candidacy regardless.
With Nordone duly anointed as her brother’s successor, GOP leaders are undertaking what would appear to be an especially arduous task of unifying a badly divided Republican electorate.
“Now that the voters have spoken, it is time for every Republican across South Carolina to come together and focus on the general election,” GOP gubernatorial nominee Alan Wilson said as the results were announced. “With money and manpower from the National Democrat Party, Democrats have assembled the most radical statewide ticket in South Carolina history. I believe our message of affordability, law and order, and keeping socialism out of our state is a winning vision. United as one team, we will march to victory in November to deliver for South Carolina families. The real work begins now.”
***
ABOUT THE AUTHOR…
Will Folks is the founding editor of the news outlet you are currently reading. Prior to founding FITSNews, he served as press secretary to the governor of South Carolina. He lives in the Midlands region of the state with his wife and eight children.

sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham clears GOP primary runoff, moves on to face Annie Andrews in November
Capping a whirlwind primary season in South Carolina, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican special primary runoff against U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman on Tuesday night, according to The Associated Press.
The race was called at 9:01 p.m.
Graham, boasting the endorsement of President Donald Trump and the late influx of cash from MAGA Inc., will now move on to face Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews in November's general election.
No Democrat has won a statewide elected office in South Carolina in two decades.
"I have a different background and vision for our state," Graham said of the contrast between her and Andrews. "I will continue to work to grow our economy and put South Carolina families first."
BACKGROUND | "South Carolina voters to pick Senate nominee in runoff for November ballot."
Graham, the sister of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly in July, surprised the political class in South Carolina when she opted to run for a full six-year Senate term.
When Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham last month, a person familiar with McMaster’s thinking but unauthorized to speak publicly about it said the governor had never contemplated that she would run for the seat herself, according to reporting from The Associated Press. However, with the urging of President Trump, Graham put her name on the ballot.
Tuesday night, McMaster joined her on stage to celebrate her primary victory. He was smiling ear to ear, flanked by Graham's family and closest supporters.
Early on, Graham was the subject of criticism for being in Washington, D.C., for Senate votes instead of on the ground in South Carolina, where many voters said they didn’t know anything about her or her policy positions.
And then in a debate, she stumbled on a question regarding whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Graham found the question difficult to answer before ultimately saying, "National security is not my thing.”
Norman seized on the misstep, using the waning days of the campaign to reiterate that the Senate was not the place for on-the-job training.
Despite the line of attack, Graham was able to convert Trump's remaining popularity within the Republican Party into a primary victory. At a rally in Myrtle Beach the Friday before election day, the president urged his supporters to pretend that he's on the ballot if that will help them get to the polls to vote.
It turns out that decision was enough.
During Norman's concession speech, he derided the outside PAC money spent against him and also questioned why the president even got involved in the race.
"My opponents, the money came from outside PACs," Norman said in his speech. "The president got involved. He has that right. That's his prerogative. I never understood why he got in this race... It is what it is."
The staunch conservative confirmed that, moving forward, he is willing to help Darline Graham any way that he can ahead of the general election.
"I'll support her, Darline, as best as I can," Norman said. "I will support the Republican. I will not support a Democrat."

sources.news_title: Sen. Darline Graham wins GOP primary runoff to replace her late brother in US Senate
sources.text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham on South Carolina’s general election ballot.
Darline Graham defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.
Despite being a political unknown, Darline Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after her brother’s sudden death last month. She was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly notched an endorsement from President Donald Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.
On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump's picks in this year's midterms — infused nearly $830,000 into Graham's campaign for voter calls and text message blasts.
Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump's backing would be enough to boost the novice candidate with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unknown, across the finish line to the nomination.
After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.
Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.
On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.
“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”
In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.
Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.
Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.
“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.
RELATED STORY | Aisha Wahab becomes first Afghan American elected to Congress
Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperience
Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.
RELATED STORY | Poll: El Sayed holds slight edge in Michigan Senate race, but struggles with older swing voters
Graham overcomes debate flub
Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.
Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.
She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”
Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.
Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."
Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.
“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”
No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.
That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

sources.text:
Darline Graham, Ralph Norman Virtually Tied Ahead Of Runoff
Darline Graham And Ralph Norman Virtually Tied Ahead Of South Carolina Senate Runoff
While most states have held their primary elections, several runoff elections remain before the midterms. Perhaps the most widely watched runoff is the special election in South Carolina, where Sen. Darline Graham is running to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham in the Senate.
The Hill reports that polling shows Graham in a virtual tie with her opponent Rep. Ralph Norman. The election will test both the weight of an endorsement from President Donald Trump and the value of name recognition. While Graham was appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to finish her brother’s term, the runoff will determine if she will go to the general election for a full, two-year term.
Graham’s campaign hit a snag during a recent debate where she said she was “not that informed on national security” in response to a question about Taiwan. Norman quickly took that line and ran with it in recent press appearances.
“Contrary to my opponent, foreign policy and national security is a top concern,” Norman told Fox Business host Brian Brenberg on Monday. Norman, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, has continually framed Graham as part of the Republican establishment. Despite Graham’s name recognition, Norman’s campaign has gained steam in recent weeks.
Graham has done her best to push back against Norman’s attacks about her debate performance in recent weeks. “I think people in South Carolina are more worried about making ends meet,” Graham said last Wednesday during an interview with Sean Hannity. “So, they are concerned about a lot of other things other than Taiwan.”
It’s a good spin, but this year has taught us how pronounced the impact of foreign policy is on kitchen-table issues. The misguided war with Iran has driven up the cost of gas and goods, with inflation once again outpacing wage growth. Not to mention that we’re currently in an unnecessary trade war with Canada that will undoubtedly add yet another increase in prices for the average U.S. citizen.
Trump has placed pronounced focus on Graham’s campaign, as the primaries have shown his endorsement doesn’t carry as much weight with conservative voters as it once did. “I think she’s great. I asked her to do it. I got her into this whole thing,” Trump said Monday night during a tele-rally for Graham. “I have to make sure she gets in, because there will be nobody better.”
Whoever wins the runoff will face Democrat Annie Andrews in the November election.
Trump’s endorsement record will also be tested in Oklahoma, where a runoff election is being held to determine the Republican nominee in the state’s gubernatorial race. The Washington Post reports that Trump has endorsed former state senator Mike Mazzei, who is running against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond. Drummond beat Mazzei by one percentage point in the primary but didn’t secure enough of the vote to win the nomination outright.
Polling shows the race between the two candidates is virtually tied, with both receiving 44% of the vote and the remaining 12% undecided.
While Drummond has previously criticized Trump’s tariff strategy, he said he’s aligned with the president’s agenda despite not receiving his endorsement. “I respect President Trump and the work he is doing for our country, but we are not going to agree on every issue. I am a conservative Republican, and I believe part of leadership is having the courage to stand your ground when it is in the best interest of the people you serve,” Drummond said in a statement shared with the Hill.
Trump has clearly taken that stance personally, as he’s called Drummond “just another grandstander” and a “total RINO.
Should both Graham and Mazzei add to Trump’s failed endorsement record, it could ultimately weaken Trump’s hold on the party as he enters the lame duck period of his term.

Sen. Darline Graham wins GOP nomination for U.S. Senate in South Carolina
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham wins GOP nomination for U.S. Senate in South Carolina
South Carolina U.S. senate runoff election will test Trump’s endorsement
COLUMBIA, S.C. — South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham has won the GOP nomination for the U.S. Senate, according to a race call by the Associated Press.
Her win came after an endorsement from President Trump, backing her for a full term in the seat formerly held by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
She beat Rep. Ralph Norman for the nomination in Tuesday's special election primary runoff after no candidate won the GOP special election primary outright earlier this month. She now faces Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in November in the heavily Republican state.
Trump had backed Graham, a political newcomer, as the interim replacement for her brother, who died from a heart condition on July 11 and South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve out the remainder of her brother's term.
Then Trump endorsed Graham to run for a full term.
Loading...
Trump holds onto primary influence
The race was one of Trump's biggest bets of the midterm primary cycle, staking Graham against more experienced members of the party establishment.
"I'm doing this to honor Lindsey. That's why I'm here," Trump said at a Myrtle Beach rally on Aug. 21. "So, Darline, we got to win that race."
Graham touted her connection to Trump. "The critics say I shouldn't run for the Senate. They say I'm not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged," she said during the rally. "By the way, President Trump has never served in elected office before and I think he's done a damn good job."
Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent more than $827,000 on behalf of Graham. His PAC wallet has been mostly shut during several close Republican primaries this election cycle.
The president's support has a mixed record this year, with losses in prominent races in Florida, Georgia, Iowa and Minnesota, among other places. Overall, his endorsement has won more than lost in the primaries, where he can flex his influence with the Republican base.
Ray Saldi, 60, voted for Graham and said the endorsements from officials in support of her were not what solidified the decision. The familiar last name and near-blank political slate pulled him in.
"I really liked her brother, Lindsey Graham. I just wanted to make sure that she's truly genuine to the people of South Carolina," he said.
Saldi said he felt Graham would be more willing to put South Carolina above all else.
An abbreviated GOP primary campaign
Despite her lack of political experience, Graham inherited a seasoned campaign machine. Her brother had been in elected office since 1995, when he initially served in the House. She told supporters in Aiken, South Carolina on Monday that her brother's legacy is one she wishes to continue in a full term.
"I want to continue to fight to finish what he was doing. He helped this state. He brought resources to this state. And you know what? If we don't bring them here, they're going to go somewhere else, right?"
During the only candidate debate leading up to the runoff election, hosted by NewsMax, Graham caught heat for her answer on a question about the significance of Taiwan and the South China Sea.
"I'm just going to be honest here," she said. "I'm not that informed on national security."
The response from Graham prompted 'boos' from the audience. Lindsey Graham was known for his aggressive defense on U.S. national security and dedicated his career to foreign policy issues.
Norman, on the other hand, did have political experience as a five-term Congressman and a member of the House Freedom Caucus. Earlier this year, Rep. Norman ran for South Carolina governor but came in third place. During his short campaign for Senate, Norman has leaned on his political experience as a reason why voters should send him to the chamber.
Voting earlier on Tuesday, Rep. Norman leaned into his underdog role in this race.
"I love being an underdog," he said. "I think our people are going to get out and vote. I think they're excited. The electricity that we've had has been great."
He also appealed to some Trump skeptics. While Norman aligned with the president politically, he endorsed his longtime friend former South Carolina governor Nikki Haley in her 2024 presidential bid against Trump.
Haley returned that support to the tune of more than $700,000 in outside money from PACs aligned with her.
However, voters across parties have been bucking the political class by voting for anti-establishment candidates this election cycle. Graham has definitely used the fact she isn't a career politician to her advantage.
South Carolina Public Radio's Luis-Alfredo Garcia contributed to this report.

Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important national security issues facing the U.S., Graham answered: “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not, on national security, I’m not that informed on national security, so, but I do support the military.”
She added: “My brother was in the Air Force for 33 years, so I will do everything I can to support the military. My dad was in the Army. I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise. But I do support the military.”
The answer drew concerns from some Republicans about Graham’s readiness to govern on national security and foreign policy issues — which were of pre-eminent concern for her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. — if she’s elected to a full term.
But Scott has no qualms about his endorsement of Graham or of her ability to continue to do the job. Scott expressed confidence that she would win tonight's runoff election. “I can tell you, as the senior senator for the great state of South Carolina, the person I want in the Senate with me, Darline Graham, representing the people of South Carolina. Easy choice.”
WATCH:
Tim Scott: Darline Graham is competent, qualified, and ready for prime time. There’s a reason she earned President Trump’s support and my support. pic.twitter.com/zck0pcHaWa
— Acyn (@Acyn) August 25, 2026
President Donald Trump has endorsed Graham and held an in-person rally for her on Saturday, where Graham had the opportunity to make her final case to voters — mainly that she is strongly pro-life, will always stand for the Second Amendment, and expressed determination to get the SAVE America Act passed.
WATCH:
"I Will Always Stand for the Second Amendment" Darline Graham Details the Ideals She Will Uphold - 08/21/26 pic.twitter.com/abgHwTvibF
— RSBN 🇺🇸 (@RSBNetwork) August 21, 2026
Early voting has been going on since August 18, and polls close at 7:00 PM Eastern. So, whatever might be motivating the voters, their turnout will be the decider of this dead heat runoff.
The betting markets have Graham winning by a 67-percent margin. Whoever the winner is will face Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and Democrat candidate in November.

sources.news_title: Darline Graham secures victory in runoff race to replace late brother on ballot
Republicans Brace for Darline Graham to Lose in South Carolina
sources.text:
Republicans Brace for Darline Graham to Lose in South Carolina
Trump’s dream of sticking the MAGA-compliant sister of the late Lindsey Graham in her brother’s Senate seat may be hitting the skids.
With hours on the clock until polls close, Republicans are betting that Senator Darline Graham—the temporary fill-in for her late brother, Lindsey Graham—will be iced out of South Carolina’s GOP runoff race. Graham is up against Representative Ralph Norman, a five-term lawmaker who has represented the Palmetto State in various legislative capacities since 2005.
The junior Graham took the reins of her sibling’s powerful office last month, after the 71-year-old suddenly passed away from an aortic dissection. Despite having zero relevant experience or qualifications, Graham gained the president’s endorsement and was subsequently appointed by South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster.
Within the span of a few short weeks, the 62-year-old undertook a gambit to make her interim responsibilities more permanent, throwing her name on the ballot to be formally selected by the state electorate. The money poured in behind her, with chief executives, lobbyists, and prominent Republican donors pumping thousands of dollars into her nascent campaign, violating the weekly thresholds set by the Federal Election Commission.
The country was stunned earlier this month when Graham pulled ahead of more than half a dozen candidates in the Republican primary—but now, some Republicans believe that may have been the zenith of her political career.
Public opinion on Graham plummeted last week when she flopped on a softball debate question regarding Taiwan, confessing that “national security is not my thing.” In the same debate, Graham forgot the population of her own state, falsely claiming that South Carolina’s population is 50 million people—more than New York and Florida combined. Fact check: The state’s population is fewer than six million people.
Multiple Republican sources told NOTUS that, despite Donald Trump’s efforts, the sexagenarian is increasingly unlikely to win South Carolina’s primary runoff.
“You’re running a campaign with a virtual unknown that took on all of her brother’s unfavorables without any of the goodwill that her brother has in a very short-sprint special election,” one Republican operative told NOTUS. Exactly why Graham is in a bad position in the race “isn’t rocket science,” according to the source.
A lack of reliable or neutral polling has left much of the country’s electoral odds in the dark, including in South Carolina.
“Tomorrow’s election is the biggest black box in recent memory here,” a South Carolina–based Republican operative told NOTUS.
Whoever pulls through the runoff Tuesday evening will eventually have to face off against Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election. (Though the last time South Carolina elected a Democrat to the Senate was in 1998.)
But unlike other midterm-bound candidates who have been advised by party leaders to separate themselves from the president’s negative polling, Graham still needs to ride Trump’s brand if she wants to win big.
“Her only good is hyper-engaged Trump voters. There is no Darline Graham voter,” the operative told NOTUS. “No one’s voting for Darline because of Darline.”

sources.news_title: South Carolina U.S. Senate runoff election will test Trump's endorsement
sources.text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. — South Carolina Republican voters are returning to the polls Tuesday to decide who will replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on the general election ballot in November.
After no candidate in a crowded field won outright in a Republican special primary earlier this month, the state is holding a runoff between Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham, and Congressman Ralph Norman.
The outcome of Tuesday’s race will test President Trump’s influence in the state.
The past month and a half has been a scramble to replace the state’s senior U.S. Senator who had just secured the nomination in the June primary for his fifth U.S. Senate term before dying from a heart condition on July 11.
South Carolina’s GOP Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term following his death. She came in first place following a special election on Aug. 11 to replace him on the November ballot to run for a full term.
But Graham failed to secure the amount of votes needed to avoid a runoff election.
Loading...
A competitive primary tests President Trump’s influence
The race is shaping up to be one of Trump’s biggest bets of the midterm primary cycle. Trump encouraged Graham to run, endorsed her, and held a rally for her in South Carolina ahead of the runoff election.
Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., has also spent more than $827,000 on behalf of Graham.
“I’m doing this to honor Lindsey. That’s why I’m here,” Trump said at the Myrtle Beach rally on Aug. 21. “So, Darline, we got to win that race.”
Trump’s significant personal and financial investment into the race is rare.
His PAC wallet has been mostly shut during several close Republican primaries this election cycle.
And in some tough primary races, the president’s support hasn’t been a silver bullet. Trump has seen primary defeats in Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Minnesota, Michigan, Wyoming and even in South Carolina during the gubernatorial primary in June.
60-year-old Ray Saldi voted for Graham, but he said the endorsements from officials in support of her were not what solidified the decision. The familiar last name and near-blank political slate pulled him in.
“I really liked her brother, Lindsey Graham. I just wanted to make sure that she’s truly genuine to the people of South Carolina,” he said.
To Saldi, it felt as though Graham would be more willing to put South Carolina above all else.
An abbreviated GOP primary campaign
In the Aug. 11 special election, Graham received around 33% of the vote, while Norman got about 25%. A third candidate, U.S. Rep. Russell Fry placed third. The lack of an outright win for Graham shows GOP voters aren’t fully sold on the Trump-back candidate.
Despite her lack of political experience, Graham inherited a seasoned campaign machine. Her brother had been in elected office since 1995, when Lindsey Graham initially served in the House. She is also leaning on the legacy of her brother during the campaign, who had a state and Washington team with a solid reputation for their constituent services.
She told supporters in Aiken, South Carolina on Monday that her brother’s legacy is one she wishes to continue in a full term.
“I want to continue to fight to finish what he was doing. He helped this state. He brought resources to this state. And you know what? If we don’t bring them here, they’re going to go somewhere else, right?”
But Graham isn’t as hawkish as her brother. During the only candidate debate leading up to the runoff election, hosted by NewsMax, Graham caught heat for her answer on a question about the significance of Taiwan and the South China Sea.
“I’m just going to be honest here,” she said. “I’m not that informed on national security.”
The response from Graham prompted ‘boos’ from the audience. It also presented a weak spot. Lindsey Graham was known for his aggressive defense on U.S. national security and dedicated his career to foreign policy issues.
Rep. Norman, on the other hand, does have political experience as a five-term Congressman. Earlier this year, Rep. Norman ran for South Carolina governor but came in third place. During his short campaign for Senate, Norman has leaned on his political experience as a reason why voters should send him to the chamber.
Voting earlier on Tuesday, Rep. Norman leaned into his underdog role in this race.
“I love being an underdog,” he said. “I think our people are going to get out and vote. I think they’re excited. The electricity that we’ve had has been great.”
He also appeals to some Trump skeptics. While Norman aligned with the president politically, he endorsed his longtime friend former South Carolina governor Nikki Haley in her 2024 presidential bid against Trump.
Haley has returned that support to the tune of more than $700,000 in outside money from PACs aligned with her. That makes Haley the biggest outside player supporting Norman, with whom she also served in the state House of Representatives several years before being elected governor in 2010.
However, voters across parties have been bucking the political class by voting for anti-establishment candidates this election cycle. Graham has definitely used the fact she isn’t a career politician to her advantage.
“The critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Sen. Graham said during the Myrtle Beach rally. “By the way, President Trump has never served in elected office before and I think he’s done a damn good job.”
Whoever wins the runoff election will face the Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in November. The seat is considered to be a safe Republican win.
South Carolina Public Radio’s Luis-Alfredo Garcia contributed to this report.

Trump Unloads Campaign War Chest For The First Time Of 2026 — In A GOP Primary
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has unleashed his massive $400 million war chest for the first time this year in a hotly contested GOP primary as party officials worry the president has yet to focus on key battleground races.
On Monday, Trump Super PAC MAGA, Inc. made its first significant spending since November 2025, pouring $827,711 into GOTV calls and text messages for Darline Graham in Tuesday’s South Carolina Senate GOP runoff. The group last reported more than $403 million cash on hand.
The South Carolina race appears personal to the president, who hand-picked Darline Graham to fill the shoes of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, telling a tele-rally audience that he “got her into this whole thing” and “has to make sure she gets in.”
The last-minute push for Graham marks the first time Trump has tapped into his hundreds of millions since coming to the rescue of Rep. Matt Van Epps in Tennessee’s closer-than-expected 7th Congressional District special election.
The money dump in South Carolina highlights Trump’s increasing involvement in divisive and hotly contested GOP primaries as he continues to withhold money from key battleground states and races with just 70 days to go until Election Day.
“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump said, teasing his financial involvement in the midterms. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money, and my own money, for candidates that I think are good — Republican candidates that I think are good.”
MAGA, Inc. may be calculating that voter engagement will intensify closer to Election Day, making a larger spending push in late September and October more effective.
“When you add the $850 million to all of the other money that we’ve raised, we’re in very good shape,” Trump added in an August 21 gaggle with reporters.
Perhaps no candidate is more eager for Trump’s financial firepower than Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is locked in a tight Senate race with Democrat James Talarico.
Over the weekend, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott downplayed fears that Democrats could flip the Lone Star State blue this year and seize control of the U.S. Senate. “Well, let’s put it in context where Ken Paxton is in his campaign, and that is he was in a three-month-long runoff that demanded capital, it demanded campaigning, demanded his attention, and so he’s just now catching up in the campaign process with Talarico,” Abbott told ABC News.
“Talarico got away with something, and that is with Ken Paxton campaigning against John Cornyn as opposed to Talarico,” he added.
The Senate GOP’s fundraising arms have continued to withhold money from Paxton’s campaign after Trump led the effort to oust incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn, The Daily Wire reported. Since then, Talarico has dominated the airwaves while Paxton has struggled to raise money in one of the nation’s largest and most expensive states for statewide campaigns. The RealClearPolitics polling average gives Talarico a nearly two-point advantage.
With control of both the House and Senate up for grabs, Republicans face significant headwinds heading into Election Day, including elevated gas prices, the lingering war with Iran, and President Trump’s low approval ratings. The latest RealClearPolitics polling average gives Democrats a roughly 6.4-percentage-point lead on the generic congressional ballot.

sources.news_title: Live Election Results: Norman faces Graham for GOP nomination in South Carolina U.S. Senate race
sources.text:
With Trump’s backing, Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP Senate nomination
Interim U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won South Carolina’s special Republican primary runoff Tuesday, defeating U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman after a bruising campaign to determine who will seek to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
Graham received 52.5% of the vote, compared with 47.6% for Norman. Norman carried only the Upstate, his political base.
“What a night,” Graham told supporters at her victory celebration in Columbia. “South Carolina Republicans, I humbly accept your nomination to serve as the Republican nominee for the United States Senate from the great state of South Carolina.”
Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a Charleston physician, in the November general election. Republicans will be favored in a state where Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate race in decades.
Below video: Darline Graham addresses supporters after runoff win
Trump’s support helps lift Graham
Graham’s victory demonstrated the continued influence of President Donald Trump in South Carolina Republican politics.
Trump endorsed Graham before she formally entered the race, campaigned with her in Myrtle Beach and held a tele-rally on the eve of the runoff. MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump and allied Republicans, also spent nearly $830,000 on calls and text messages to voters in the final stretch.
“Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful,” Graham said in thanking Trump. “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
Trump had been a close political ally of Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly July 11. He praised the decision to appoint Darline Graham as her brother’s interim replacement and encouraged her to run for the remainder of the term.
Throughout the brief campaign, Graham emphasized her support for Trump’s agenda, including legislation that has become a priority for the president.
Her famous last name and Trump’s endorsement helped her overcome questions about her lack of campaign experience and previously little-known political views.
A difficult campaign shaped by grief
Graham began her victory speech by reflecting on the loss of her brother.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” she said. “But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room.”
She said she felt a mix of “grief, heartache and immense gratitude” after a whirlwind campaign that began shortly after his death.
Graham also thanked Norman and the other Republicans who entered the special election, acknowledging that the party had endured an intense and sometimes personal contest.
“As South Carolina Republicans, we are part of a large and sometimes disagreeable family of conservative voices,” she said. “If you supported another candidate in this primary, please know that I will work hard to earn your trust and your support.”
Below video: Darline Graham: 'I've worked hard for the people of South Carolina'
Norman’s experience falls short
Norman entered the Senate race after finishing third in the Republican primary for governor earlier this year. A wealthy developer and one of the most conservative members of the U.S. House, he made his experience a central argument against Graham.
Norman had served for much of the past two decades in state and federal office. He received endorsements from Republican Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action.
He also invested more than $1 million of his own money during the campaign’s final week.
Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley and groups aligned with her helped Norman, contributing or directing more than $700,000 toward efforts supporting his campaign. Norman backed Haley over Trump during the early stages of the 2024 Republican presidential primary, though he has generally supported Trump’s policies in Congress.
Norman portrayed Graham as an inexperienced and heavily managed candidate backed by Washington interests. His campaign highlighted her performance during the runoff’s only debate, when she struggled to answer a question about U.S. security interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea.
“National security is not my thing,” Graham said during the debate, adding that she was not well informed on the subject. Norman cited the response as evidence that she was not prepared for the office.
The criticism was not enough to carry Norman beyond the Upstate or overcome Graham’s support in the rest of South Carolina.
Graham quickly turns to November
Graham used much of her victory speech to pivot toward Andrews and the general election.
She portrayed Andrews as far outside South Carolina’s political mainstream, criticizing her positions on guns, health care, abortion and transgender issues. Andrews and her campaign did not immediately respond to Graham’s remarks.
“Tonight is a great victory, but it’s not the finish line,” Graham said. “In fact, it is the starting line for an even bigger fight which lies ahead.”
Andrews won the Democratic nomination outright in June. Her campaign had initially been organized around a challenge to Lindsey Graham but shifted its focus after his death.
South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in decades. Lindsey Graham won his most recent race in 2020 by 10 percentage points, despite a record-breaking flood of campaign spending.
Darline Graham told supporters she would campaign on growing the economy and helping South Carolina families, drawing on her years working for the state and leading a state agency.
“I understand the struggles faced by South Carolina families because I’ve faced them too,” she said. “As your senator, I will continue to work to grow our economy and put South Carolina families first.”

sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — Sen. Darline Graham — a political newcomer appointed to the seat held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — will win a special GOP primary runoff to replace her brother on the South Carolina ballot, The Associated Press projected Tuesday.
Graham, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman, a staunch conservative and member of the hard line Freedom Caucus, who had also advanced to the runoff following South Carolina’s special Senate primary earlier this month.

Speaking to a crowd of triumphant supporters Tuesday night in Columbia, South Carolina, Graham struck a reflective tone at times.
“The past few weeks have been an unbelievably challenging time for our family, but you know what? We did it,” she said, while adding that she was feeling “mixed emotions” given her grief over her brother.
As she thanked God, her key supporters and her family, Graham also effusively thanked Trump for his support and endorsement, describing the “bond” between her brother and the president and telling the crowd, to raucous cheers, “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
Graham framed her outsider status as an asset, while pointing to Trump’s support as one of the key reasons conservatives should support her bid for a full term. Trump threw more than just a social media endorsement behind her: he flew to Myrtle Beach for a rally on Friday, in one of his first major campaign stops during the 2026 midterms.
“Now, the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said during the rally to cheers. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”
Trump, later on, effusively praised Graham, saying “she only knows how to put America first.”
Norman, meanwhile, said that his experience is his “resume” and that conservatives in the Palmetto State could trust him more than a relative unknown like Graham.
“The establishment has already picked their candidate. Same old playbook, same old insiders. I’m not their choice. And this election is not for sale,” he said in a campaign ad.
He also questioned why Trump has gotten involved in the race in GOP-favoring South Carolina instead of focusing on ones where the GOP faces an uphill battle against Democrats. The White House, asked about some of Norman’s comments about Trump, pointed to Trump’s previous social media posts where he endorsed Graham.
Graham, on her end, faced scrutiny from many fellow Republicans over her lack of political experience and occasional missteps on the trail.
During a one-on-one debate she had with Norman last Tuesday, she was asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the United States. She answered, “I’m not that informed on national security. But I do support the military … I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
The comment, which contrasted with her brother’s major focus on national security, sparked criticism from Norman’s allies, including former Gov. Nikki Haley.
“Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate,” Haley wrote on X last week.
Norman, in an interview with local outlet WHNS posted on Thursday, called Graham’s answer “surprising” and hammered her for her lack of experience. “There’s no more important issue than national security … there’s no time for training on the job,” he said.
But Graham, while admitting she feels she got the answer wrong — telling Fox News she “tripped up on one question” — told voters at an event last week, “To me, as I’ve walked around this room and I’ve asked people, ‘Are y’all concerned about Taiwan?’ You know what they said? No, they’re concerned about the price of groceries, the price of gas, rising healthcare costs.”
She also said she believes national security is important and she will become more informed about it. “Everybody has a first day on the job. President Trump — was he a politician [when he was first elected]? Has he done a good job? Yes, he has,” she told attendees.
Heading into the runoff, David Woodard, a political scientist who also managed some of Lindsey Graham’s early congressional campaigns, but did not work on this Senate race, told ABC News that he expected relatively low turnout and that those showing up to vote in such an off-cycle election are likely among the most opinionated, plugged-in Republicans.
“I think on the first round, people I was talking to had sympathy for Darline, thought it was great she’d serve out Lindsey’s term,” he said, adding that some of them “think that Ralph Norman has credibility on issues that Darline lacks.”
But heading into Tuesday some voters said they find Trump’s endorsement of her, as well as her focus on the economy, a strong selling point.
Mike Funderburk, a contractor from Neeses, South Carolina, who voted early for Graham, said the economy is his top issue.
“I think she’s probably going to have a steep learning curve,” he said. “But I’m willing to give her the benefit of the doubt.”
ABC News’ Michelle Stoddart contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Famed strategist eyes South Carolina Senate race for potential upset
sources.text:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) won the runoff for the Republican Primary on Tuesday night, inching out a victory against Rep. Ralph Norman. One political strategist said that he doubts it would go to Democrats but urged folks to keep an eye on it.
“Normally, in South Carolina, we wouldn’t want to waste any dollars. But I want to build on something that Matt [Mowers] said that’s important,” said Rocha.
“Even the senator who was there, [Lindsey] Graham, the original Graham, got less than 50 percent in his own primary. An opposition got 40 percent,” said Rocha.
“And last night, even with the president’s endorsement, she only got 52 percent. That’s it. This is really important for everybody in a Republican primary, [but] not a general election. So that means there are people within the Republican Party who aren’t happy with their own Republican Party,” said Rocha.
When asked if a race like that could be competitive, he said that he thinks “it’s on the table. Just because we’re in an atmosphere where there’s been 25 special elections for state house in America, where Democrats have flipped Republican seats and no Republicans have flipped Democratic seats. Just because of history and the party in power. So, I think just watch it. I would just keep it on your watch list.”
Mowers got a big grin on his face, saying he would love to see Democrats dump millions and millions of dollars into deep red South Carolina. He said that six years ago, Democrats tried the same thing and it didn’t happen.
“I don’t see a single Ralph Norman voter voting for Annie Andrews,” Mowers said.
During his rally on Tuesday night, Norman mentioned Trump’s name and his rally burst into loud boos.
But Rocha explained they don’t have to.
“That’s important. A lot of them won’t. The majority of them won’t. But if 10 percent of them do this, place sits in play,” Rocha said.
His example was what’s unfolding in Texas, where a very unpopular Republican is running neck-and-neck with a Democrat in the polls.
“All I’m saying is if you look at Texas — and stay with me here in Texas — where you had this John Cornyn fight with [Ken] Paxton. Like, I don’t think all the John Cornyn people are running to [James] Talarico. But if 10 percent do just like in this race, at this moment in time. Six years ago, you’re exactly right, Matt. We got our clock cleaned when we spent a bunch of money against Graham. It’s just a different time now in America, where Republicans have been in charge of everything.”
