sources.news_title: Darline Graham wins primary to contest late brother's US Senate seat
sources.text:
Voters in South Carolina have chosen Darline Graham, the sister of late Senator Lindsey Graham, as the Republican candidate to contest his US Senate seat in November.
Graham’s bid received strong backing from President Donald Trump, who travelled to the state to campaign for her. Graham’s victory is being seen as evidence of Trump’s continuing influence over the Republican Party.
Graham is currently serving in the Senate as a temporary replacement for her brother, who died suddenly in July. She had never previously run for elected office.
Republicans and Democrats also held primaries in several other states on Tuesday, as they narrowed down their field of candidates for the midterm elections.
Political experts expect that Graham will now go on to succeed in the November election. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate for decades.
The midterms more generally will decide which party controls the US Congress – which in turn will have a bearing on the second half of Trump’s presidency.
Graham was running against right-wing Republican Congressman Ralph Norman, who sought to portray his opponent as a puppet of Washington politicians. The head-to-head was set up after the pair emerged as the top two from a wider field of candidates during an initial contest earlier this month.
Norman is a supporter of Trump and has voted in favour of many of his policies. But in 2024, he initially backed Trump’s primary opponent Nikki Haley as his pick for Republican presidential candidate.
With counting almost complete, Graham had received 52.5% of the vote, according to the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
In a post on X, she thanked her supporters and the president, and said she was “deeply honoured and humbled” by the result.
During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling during a foreign-policy question during a recent debate.
Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: “I’m not that informed on national security.” She added: “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”
Trump’s influence over the party was also tested in Oklahoma, where Mike Mazzei, a former state lawmaker endorsed by the president, took on Gentner Drummond, the state’s attorney general.
The winner is widely expected to become the next governor in the heavily Republican state.
South Carolina was not the only state that held an election on Tuesday to replace a deceased lawmaker.
In Georgia, voters in the Atlanta area were tasked with choosing a replacement for Democratic Congressman David Scott, who died in April.
Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late congressman, was among those seeking office. But projections in US media show she was beaten by opponent Everton Blair.
Blair will therefore serve out the remainder of the term, which ends in January. In November, two other candidates will run to take over his seat in the new year.

sources.text:
Darline Graham secured the South Carolina Republican primary runoff victory for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, defeating Representative Ralph Norman. Appointed after her brother Lindsey Graham’s death in July, she now advances to face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November for a full six-year term, backed by President Donald Trump.
Darline Graham narrowly won South Carolina’s Republican Senate primary runoff on Tuesday, edging out her opponent after a high-stakes sprint that drew heavy involvement from the White House. With 99% of the vote counted, Graham captured 52% of the ballots compared to 48% for Representative Ralph Norman, who represents a district in the northern part of the state.
The victory marks a milestone in a whirlwind political season. Graham was initially appointed by South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s term following his sudden death at age 71 in July. Despite having no prior public office experience before stepping into her brother’s Senate seat—having previously worked advocating for persons with physical disabilities—she quickly transitioned from a temporary placeholder to a formidable candidate for a full six-year term.
Trump Endorsement, Super PAC Funding, and the Campaign Trail
President Donald Trump played a decisive role in pushing Graham over the finish line. Beyond his vocal endorsement, Trump backed that support with large campaign contributions from his MAGA Inc. super PAC. According to Federal Election Commission filings, MAGA Inc. spent $827,711 to bolster Graham’s campaign through a phone bank operation over the final weekend. This financial deployment marked a rare instance of the president actively injecting substantial PAC funds into a midterm primary.
The alliance was on full display days before the runoff during a campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, where Trump and her vote to confirm Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Simply put, I’ve done more in 20 days than Ralph Norman has done in 20 years.”
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., via Fox News
Norman, a longtime real estate developer and member of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus who previously mounted an unsuccessful gubernatorial bid, carried his home base of Greenville but lagged behind Graham across the rest of the state. Despite a bruising primary battle where Graham accused him of bucking party leadership, Norman conceded defeat on Tuesday evening and pledged to back the nominee.
“As I said earlier, I’m going to support the Republican. I’m not supporting a Democrat. So, I will support her – Darline – as best I can.”
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., via Fox News
General Election Outlook and the National Midterm Landscape
With the primary runoff concluded, Graham advances to the general election in November. She will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Given South Carolina’s deep conservative leanings and history of overwhelming support for Republican candidates, Graham is widely expected to win the seat outright.
For the national Republican party, the primary served as another testing ground for presidential influence during a cycle complicated by voter concerns over inflation, trade disputes with Canada, and an unpopular conflict with Iran. While Nordone, who was appointed by South Carolina’s Governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term, earned the highest share of the vote on Aug. 11, she fell short of the majority she needed to win the race, triggering the runoff. Nordone earned nearly 33% of the vote on Aug. 11, while her opponent, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, came in second, with nearly 25%, sending both candidates to the runoff race.
President Donald Trump had championed Nordone in the race, publicly encouraging her to run for a full term before she had even announced her plans to do so. In a Truth Social post in July, Trump called Nordone “a spectacular person, and a true American Patriot.”

Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.”
Although Nordone was a strong supporter of her brother’s political career over the years, she had never before held elected office. sources.news_title: Graham Wins GOP Senate Runoff, But Anderson County Supported Norman — The Anderson Observer
sources.text:
Graham Wins GOP Senate Runoff, But Anderson County Supported Norman
Seanna Adcox/S.C. Daily Gazette with local results from The Anderson Observer
COLUMBIA — Voters elected Darline Graham to take her late brother’s place on November ballots, as the full backing of President Donald Trump helped overcome criticism of her political inexperience.
When The Associated Press called the GOP runoff election at 9:01 p.m., Graham had 52% of the vote over U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, with 89% of votes counted.
In Anderson County, Norman received 11,362 votes, or 57.27 percent of the vote to Graham’s 8,479 42.73 percent. Turnout in the county was just over 16 percent.
Graham’s win ensures the first elected female U.S. senator from South Carolina will be sworn into office in January. Sworn in exactly six weeks ago as the appointed senator, Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election.
The 62-year-old younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham led the 10-candidate primary two weeks ago with 33% to Norman’s 25%. But a runoff win was far from guaranteed. Some polling showed Norman ahead hours before precincts opened.
“We did everything we could do,” Norman, 73, said to a round of applause from supporters at his election watch party in Rock Hill.
He didn’t have a concession speech, since he didn’t expect to lose, he told the crowd. “But I accept it and I will forever be grateful for each one of y’all who supported us.”
Graham, who took the stage later in Columbia, said she had mixed emotions, including grief and “immense gratitude.”
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart,” she said. “But I know he’s looking down right now and he’s proud.”
Losing her brother was a tragedy for the entire state, Graham said.
“But tonight, you know what? We stand back up, the way South Carolinians have done and look forward to the future,” she said. “South Carolina was founded by fighters, and we are fighters.”
Trump, who urged Darline Graham to seek the next six-year term, pitched her candidacy as a tribute to her brother, his best friend: Lindsey Graham died suddenly July 11 in Washington, D.C., of a ruptured aorta, one month after trouncing five GOP opponents on his way to a fifth term.
“She’s the perfect person to carry on the legacy of her brother,” Trump told people who called in to a tele-rally Monday night. He congratulated her by phone Tuesday night before she walked on stage.
His all-in endorsement included traveling to ruby red Myrtle Beach, where he told thousands of supporters Friday to pretend his name is on the ballot. Voting for Graham, he said, is voting for someone who “fully supports the Trump agenda.”
He recognized he would take the credit or blame.
“I asked her to do it. I got her into this whole thing,” he said Monday night. “I have to make sure she gets in because there will be nobody better.”
In a state where Trump won every time he was actually on the ballot, the runoff results were expected to reflect his strength or waning influence. In November 2024, Trump won South Carolina by 18 percentage points. When Trump got behind Graham’s candidacy pre-filing, political commentators outside South Carolina assumed that made her a shoo-in.
But Trump’s surprise pick of a political novice caused many South Carolina voters to rebel. Graham was expected to be the honorary placeholder — an appointment that gave no one the benefit of incumbency in South Carolina’s first open Senate race in 22 years — not the handpicked successor.
Norman attempted to turn that into an advantage. The support and money lining up behind Graham “shows the elite establishment has already picked their candidate. Same ol’ playbook. Same ol’ insiders. I’m not their choice,” he said in an ad.
Following an unsuccessful campaign for governor when he sought the outsider label — repeatedly saying he’s not a career politician — Norman juxtaposed his record over more than two decades in elected office against Graham’s first-time candidacy. He’s the proven conservative, he argued: “You know how I’m going to vote.”
Graham embraced her status as unskilled at being a politician.
“They say I’m not a politician. I say guilty as charged,” she repeated Monday night.
Norman, first elected to the state House in 2004, has won two previous special elections, including the 2017 race that sent him to Congress. He opted to seek the governor’s office this year instead of re-election to the U.S. House but placed third in the June GOP primary.
She used that against him.
“He’s run for office 14 times, always chasing the next office. To me, this is just desperation,” Graham told callers Monday. “I am not a career politician.”
She pointed to 30 years of experience in state government, to include the last seven leading the state Commission for the Blind. And she emphasized her humble roots in relating to Americans’ economic struggles, saying that, like her brother, a childhood growing up in the back of their parents’ restaurant and pool hall also instilled a hard work ethic.
“Whatever it was that made Lindsey strong has made her strong,” Gov. Henry McMaster said during a campaign event with her Monday. The perspective she gained in her roles helping people with disabilities is also a strength, he added.
McMaster, who appointed her last month for the term ending in January, endorsed her for the full term on Friday, just before the Trump rally.
He called Graham the better candidate for keeping the Senate seat red.
Norman was the more polarizing candidate. A member of the hardline Freedom Caucus in the U.S. House, he ran for governor as the ticket furthest to the right on the political spectrum. His pick as a running mate was former Rep. Adam Morgan, founding chair of the affiliate caucus Norman helped launch in the state House in 2022, which has feuded with the majority GOP caucus ever since.
“Keep this in mind: There is another election after this one,” McMaster said. “We’ve got to win this election in order to win that election in November.”
For David and Ann Casey of Rock Hill, their votes for Norman came down to time spent in office. They also wanted someone who could push back against Trump.
“Darline’s a great person, but my vote was more for experience,” said Ann Casey, a 63-year-old dental hygienist, after voting at a church off Interstate 77 in Rock Hill.
“I had concern about Darline being a ‘yes’ person to the Trump administration,” added David Casey, a 64-year-old financial advisor. “(Norman’s) capable of hitting the ground running, and he’s not going to be told what to do.”
Graham’s non-response to a question about Taiwan during the only runoff debate sunk her for some voters.
Matthew Gusmer, a farmer in western York County, supported Norman in the governor’s race and in Senate GOP primary two weeks ago but was on the fence about whether to continue supporting him in the runoff — that is, until Graham’s performance in the Aug. 18 debate in Newberry.
“Probably the number one thing that swayed me was in the debate the other night with her comment about foreign policy,” he said.
Asked whether Taiwan is a national security issue for the United States, Graham blanked, eventually acknowledging she’s not informed on the issue.
“I’m just going to be honest up here,” she said. “I’m not a polished politician. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
“That really just kind of floored me,” Gusmer said. “With everything going on between Russia, Iran, every front, it just really turned me off.”
As a farmer, Gusmer said foreign policy and the impact it can have on things such as prices at the pump, fertilizer, and seed, as well as the cost of land in fast-growing South Carolina, are major issues and he wants a candidate who is well-informed.
But for Graham’s supporters, her lack of political experience was a plus.
“I like the fact that she’s not a politician,” said Tommy Wood, a 66-year-old engineer from Irmo. “She’s not seeking the job, so she’s willing to serve, where all the opponents are wanting the job.”
Graham kept the same staff as her brother, which brings their institutional knowledge, Wood said. He and his wife, Phyllis Wood, were longtime supporters of Lindsey Graham.
“That’s invaluable,” Tommy Wood said of his staffers committing to her.
When the Woods watched Graham flub the answer on Taiwan during the GOP debate, they felt bad for her, but their opinions never swayed, they said.
“She was nervous and blindsided, and it didn’t look good,” said Tommy Wood. But, as he heard someone else say, “I don’t care if she knows the difference between Taiwan and Timmonsville,” a tiny town in Florence County.
The couple noted that Norman ran for Senate only after losing the nomination for governor. If he wanted to be a senator, he should have made that his primary goal, they said.
“I didn’t like that,” said Phyllis Wood. “Not cool,” Tommy Wood added.
Sandra and John Jackson, of West Columbia, felt her support for South Carolina is more important than her opinions on foreign policy.
“She’s going to keep South Carolina at the forefront of her mission in Washington, D.C.,” said Sandra Jackson, a 69-year-old retired flight attendant.
What Graham lacks in political experience, she makes up for in life experience, the Jacksons said.
“She’s a mother, and she’s run the Commission for the Blind,” Sandra Jackson said. “She has experience.”
“Anybody who runs for office for the first time doesn’t have any experience,” added 78-year-old John Jackson.

sources.news_title: Dr. Annie Andrews Wants to Flip South Carolina
sources.text:
After Senator Lindsey Graham’s death in July, his sister Darline Graham was appointed to fill the seat and is now campaigning for a full term.
But, after her poor performance during a debate against Republican runoff challenger Rep. Ralph Norman, this Republican stronghold now sits on shaky ground, leaving an opening for Democrats.
Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democrat in the race, believes that South Carolinians deserve better than MAGA know-nothings and Republican extremists. Andrews’ background in pediatric medicine guides her views on freedom, gun violence, and healthcare affordability.

sources.news_title: Annie Andrews Statement on GOP Runoff Election Results
sources.text:
With the Republican runoff decided, South Carolina’s general election for U.S. Senate is officially underway. Democratic nominee Dr. Annie Andrews released the following statement, challenging her Republican opponent to meet her on the debate stage and make the case directly to voters:
“Tonight, Republicans nominated a candidate who was appointed to this seat because of her last name and elevated by Donald Trump’s endorsement and political machine. But no appointment, endorsement, or family connection entitles anyone to six years in the United States Senate. This seat belongs to the people of South Carolina.
“Now Senator Graham must answer to them. I am renewing my challenge tonight: Join me for at least three televised debates across South Carolina and explain how you will lower costs, protect health care, and keep our rural hospitals open. I’ll be there. Will she?”

sources.news_title: Graham vs. Norman: Voters Head to Polls in Critical Senate Runoff Today
sources.text:
Today South Carolina voters will decide the Republican nominee after longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham died July 11 from an aortic tear, forcing a new special primary in the state.
Sen. Darline Graham, his sister, then took the lead with about 33 percent of the vote. Rep. Ralph Norman finished second with about 25 percent. Meanwhile, Rep. Russell Fry received about 20 percent and later endorsed Graham.
Since no candidate made it to 50% of the vote, the 2 top candidates are facing off in today’s runoff election. The winner advances to the Nov. 3 general election against Democrat Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews.
Darline Graham is currently serving the remainder of her brother’s term as Senator. Before being appointed to the Senate by Governor McMaster, Graham built a public-service career managing teams. She directed communications for the South Carolina Vocational Rehabilitation Department, and in 2019, she became commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind. There she led roughly 100 to 150 employees. In 2026 she also won election as president of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind.
Graham holds major endorsements, both statewide and nationally, including Russell Fry and Governor McMaster. President Donald Trump and Sen. Tim Scott both backed her, and Trump even appeared with her at a Myrtle Beach campaign rally this past Friday.
In contrast, Norman represents South Carolina’s 5th District as a 5-term congressman. He draws strongest support from the Upstate and Piedmont, including populous Greenville County. Graham, however, performed especially well in central South Carolina and the Lowcountry.
Norman has faced growing criticism over the Silfab Solar factory in Fort Mill. He co-founded the Congressional Solar Caucus. Records show he took campaign contributions from Silfab’s lobbying firm, the Solar Energy Industries Association. He also personally called York County Council members and pressed them to approve the project’s fee-in-lieu deal.
At a 2024 public forum, Norman lied about the plant’s chemicals. He compared their operations to everyday products at Home Depot. Yet company documents identify over 2 dozen of the most toxic and explosive chemicals used in industry, including SiH4 gas and TMA, both which ignite on contact with air, as well as large amounts of hydrofluoric acid, boron trichloride, Pyrophorus oxychloride, anhydrous ammonia, sulfuric acid, and numerous other high-hazard substances in a building next door to 2 new Fort Mill schools, hundreds of homes, and a retirement community.
In addition, Norman’s district secured a $5 million federal Solar Energy Technologies Office grant for Silfab in 2024. Later, during debate on President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill, Norman initially voted against President Trump’s bill, then negotiated changes to protect Silfab and afterwards cast the deciding vote to approve the bill.
How to vote today in South Carolina
Voters can cast ballots today throughout South Carolina from 7am to 7pm. Anyone in line by closing time may vote.
Eligible voters include those who cast Republican primary ballots in June or on Aug. 11. Voters who skipped both June primaries may also participate. However, anyone who voted in the June Democratic primary cannot take part.
Voters should bring a valid photo ID. Acceptable forms include a South Carolina driver’s license, DMV ID card, photo voter registration card, federal military ID, or U.S. passport.
They can check their polling place and sample ballot at scVOTES.gov.
